Gets Greater “Ma! Ma!” I excitedly ran into the kitchen, out of breath. “I

when Mr. Mikhailov came to discuss The Great Parade? And that he wants to sponsor it this year, but only if 100,000 kids attend?” “Yes, I remember that.” “So Rabbi Benjaminson clarified that he doesn’t mean getting 100,000 kids to the parade here in New York, but 100,000 kids in parades all over the world! Everyone has to get someone to come! It’s—” my words were tumbling out fast. My mother smiled. She knew me well. “So how’s it going?” “Baruch Hashem! The plan is that each kid in Chayolei Tzivos Hashem gets a TGP (The Great Parade) T-shirt for himself, plus 20 more to give to kids who don’t yet know about the parade. Kinda like an invitation to come, and to spread the word to their own friends. And that’s what I was saying—I finally gave out all 20 T-shirts!” Whew, I was still speaking a million words a minute. Sloooow down! I took a deep breath. “So Ma, now I’m asking for your help. We need to reach parents to make sure that they bring their kids. Any ideas?” “Hmmm…” my mother thought for a moment. Then, her eyes sparkled as she reached for her keys. “If you want to reach mothers, Sruli, I know just the place!” A few minutes later, we pulled up to the largest supermarket in Brooklyn. Wow, I thought to myself, This place is huge! How can we get all of these shoppers’ and their kids to the parade?

I needed to find one commonality here…what could be used to reach everyonel? “Ma, can we walk quickly through the store? I want to look around for ideas.” “Of course, Sruli. I’m right here with you.” My mother is amazing—totally supportive of me and my creativity! We hurried up and down the aisles, but I didn’t notice anything in particular. When we neared the exit, I slowed my pace, my eyes lighting up. Shopping bags! Things moved quickly from there. With a wink to my mother, the two of us rushed to the door labeled “Staff Only”, and found the manager. I explained the parade to him, and asked if TGP logos could be printed on his store’s bags. Not only was he amazed, but he loved the idea. He even offered to speak to managers of other stores in the national chain! Numbers and equations started spinning in my head…10…20…30 million bags! Within a few days, every person coming out of that supermarket was transformed into a walking advertisement for The Great Parade. Well, bags are nice, but we needed something more. And I wanted every chayol and their family to feel responsible for the parade’s success. As I had learned many times, the Rebbe wants everyone to be a recruiter. That evening, I organized an emergency conference call with Tzivos Hashem bases across the world. Australia, England, Chicago, LA—even South Africa and Brazil. The world needs to know about the parade! Together, we brainstormed

ideas. Mr. Mikhailov's money was backing us, but what can guarantee people? After some discussion, a plan was born: plaster the world! Days later, trucks filled with all sorts of advertising material pulled up in front of every TH base. We’re talking flyers, bumper stickers, bags, T-shirts, and more, all sporting the TGP logo. Before they realized what was happening, the world media was bustling with excitement! Reporters all over couldn’t keep track of the largest advertising campaign ever seen. Pictures of malls, highways, parks, and even gas stations appeared in every form of newscasting. The plan was working! Chayolim across the globe were given a mission: pick an area, and cover it with TGP advertisements. Order whatever you need through your school rep, and you will receive it within four days. Chayolim picked highways, shopping malls, public parks, and every area in between. Those who chose highways contacted the billboard companies. Those who picked malls focused on bags; plastic, paper, canvas—you name it. (Can you imagine every person in the mall walking around with TGP bags?) Together with their parents or base commander, many chayolim drove up and down the streets, stopping at busy locations and handing out flyers and T-shirts to every Jewish kid in the area. A reporter standing outside the largest mall in America made headlines in major newspapers:

Behind him stood a giant 50-foot TGP banner, and each of the 50,000 cars parked in the lot had a TGP bumper magnet placed on their windshield. Similar news items went viral from Israel, Russia, and France. The world was vibrating with TGP excitement! As manager of the advertising campaign, the work was non- stop. Each day after school was spent ordering, coordinating, and making sure that things were under control. Three days before the parade, I collapsed into bed for some much-needed sleep. When I awoke, all I could see was a huge TGP logo. I thought I was still dreaming…until I heard my giggling brothers. While I was asleep, they had hung a huge TGP poster right on top of my head. Okay, I’ll give them credit— that was a pretty good prank. Sit back up, negel vasser, jump out of bed. Suddenly, I realized that I had forgotten one very important detail: the hookup! Our goal to reach 100,000 people was great, but we’ll need to connect all these people at the event! I frantically called Rabbi Benjaminson. He calmed me down and told me not to worry: with the

advertising taken care of, organizers of the actual parade focused on the rest— including the live hookup. Phhhhhyew! Baruch Hashem! The day of the parade finally arrived. No words can describe the surge of excitement. What a magnificent celebration of the Rashbi: True achdus, and abundantly powerful Jewish pride! As you probably guessed, the numbers soared far beyond 100,000. When the parade in Moscow was featured on the screen, I noticed Mr. Mikhailov smiling broadly, pointing to his TGP T-shirt. What a special z’chus he has in all of this! I marched alongside chayolim of my school, and saluted as I passed by the Rebbe’s place. I knew that the Rebbe was smiling with us, too. To be continued…

check out all of the other exciting things happening for Lag Ba’Omer. I heard that this year’s rides would be better than the ones they had last year! I started walking down Kingston, when I heard something ringing. At first, I thought it was just an after-effect of all the blaring music of the parade. But after I wiggled my finger in my ear once, twice, three times—but the ringing continued, I was quite confused. The friend I was walking with turned to me, “Sruli, your pocket’s ringing.” “Hu? What could be ringing in my pocket?” I wondered aloud. But when I slid my hand into my right jacket pocket, I realized that he was right; the ringing noise was coming from a phone after all! There’s just one problem with that: I don’t own a cell phone! Nor did I have any idea how this one ended up in my jacket pocket! “Hello?” I asked quizzically. “Sruli, hi. It’s me, Noam.” “Mr. Mikhailov? But how did you—I mean how did I get this—” “Sruli, I’ve been trying to get in touch with you all day. Realizing that it would be exceedingly difficult for Rabbi Benjaminson to get you into his office today,

home after all the festivities, I just asked an employee of mine to drop a cell

you a buzz when the parade ended.” My head was spinning. Mr. Mikhailov continued, “Sruli, I wanted to ask you something.” Pretending that I wasn’t totally baffled that such a thing was normal for him— besides for being in complete bewilderment as to how a cell phone had slipped into my pocket unnoticed—I responded, “Absolutely, Mr. Mikhailov. How can I help you?” “Shavuos is coming up very soon. You know what I’m thinking?” “Ten Commandments?” I asked. “Yes. And ice cream.The biggest ice cream party the world has ever seen. And as for the party guests, I will leave that up to you.” “It’s so cool that you said that, Mr. Mikhailov.” “Go on,” he requested. “You see,” I explained, “The Rebbe said that Shavuos is a holiday especially for us kids. When Hashem was ready to give the Torah to the Jewish people, He asked for a guarantor—someone who will make sure that we will never stop learning the Torah and keeping its mitzvos. After a few suggestions which Hashem turned down, we children were nominated as guarantors—and Hashem gladly accepted.” “What are you saying, Sruli?” He asked. “Since the Jewish people only got the Torah because of us children in the first place, this Yom Tov is kind of like our special party! And this being the case, I think it’s perfectly appropriate that we should work on inviting the guests ourselves.” “Bravo, Sruli! The more I get to know you chayolim, the more I’m impressed by your energy and devotion.” As our conversation continued, Mr. Mikhailov and I sorted out some more details. Turns out

he didn’t mean the biggest ice cream party in just one location, rather, a world-wide party wherever Jewish people live, work, and play. (Naturally…I should’ve known as much!) And here’s the coolest part—how we actually invited everyone: First, we compiled a guest list of every single Yid we could possibly involve on this special day. This was done quite simply—a call- text-email center was quickly put together, and we reached out to every shul and Jewish club we could find, asking them to please share the Aseres Hadibros kriah times and locations with their entire mailing lists, along with ice cream orders to be delivered to their groups. However, since there are sadly many Yidden who aren’t involved with a shul or club, and couldn’t be reached to come hear the Aseres Hadibros through these mailing lists, Mr. Mikhailov and I came up with a unique idea. We arranged for every Tzivos Hashem base to receive a giant shipment of boxes: Several refrigerated boxes (i.e. special containers designed to keep things frozen for a long time) containing the most amazing Cholov Yisroel ice-cream-on-a- cone imported from Eretz Yisroel; another box was stuffed with a huge assortment of awesome- flavored toppings, serving utensils and napkins; and in the final box was a portable cooler and a few lightweight folding chairs. We were determined to whip up the most incredible lead-up to Aseres Hadibros ever experienced. Bases worked hard organizing roles and coordinating routes for what would be the first-of-its-kind method of Shavuos mivtzoyim. Finally, Shavuos arrived! After an invigorating night of saying Tikkun Leil Shavuos, Chayolim across the world met up with their local teams at 8:00 am (after a brief sleep), and then

excitedly hit the streets with the clearly branded ice cream coolers, all necessary ingredients, and of course, stacks of maps highlighting every shul in the area and their Aseres Hadibros times. (Many bases even arranged with shuls to provide extra-early and extra-late Torah readings, to accommodate the not-yet- frum families still planning to attend school or work that day.) Chayolim positioned themselves on sidewalk benches, while others brought folding chairs to busy street corners, where they set up their cooler station. “FIND OUT WHERE TO HEAR THE TEN COMMANDMENTS!'' yelled out a few chayolim of the group. Others shouted, “GET YOUR SHAVUOS ICE CREAM HERE! TEN DIFFERENT TOPPINGS TO CHOOSE FROM!” Tens of Jewish mothers, fathers, and their children crowded around the coolers. And that’s when the fun really started! Chayolim instantly got into position, some handing out the ice cream—after carefully opening the wrappers to help recipients avoid ripping letters on Yom Tov—while others sprinkled on the toppings, and the rest of the team explained to families about the importance for every Jewish man, woman, and child to hear the Aseres Hadibros on Shavuos Day (while handing them the mapped-out shul directions, of course). After 2 hours of this electrifying mivtzoyim, chayolim rushed to shul for the main minyan at 10:00 am and to hear the Aseres Hadibros read properly, followed by a yummy milchig kiddush. We eagerly returned to our mivtzoyim posts during the afternoon hours as well, encouraging any Yidden who didn’t yet hear the Aseres Hadibros to attend the specially- arranged afternoon leinings. What can I say, we simply had

the time of our lives on that Yom Tov day as we proudly carried out the Rebbe’s work! Every so often, whenever I had a moment to pause, I’d look up at the Jewish parents and children walking off. I could feel my whole being fill with joy at their eager faces, each proceeding to fulfill today’s special mitzvah in a most glowing and delightful way. And during the hours spent tending to those ice cream coolers, my fellow chayolim and I exchanged many happy glances, feeling so grateful for the zechus to fulfill the Rebbe’s order-of-the-day so thoroughly. I can only imagine how lucky Mr. Mikhailov must have felt at his great privilege of funding this mivtzah! It truly was the best Shavuos of my life. I mean, where else could a boy like me get to use my creativity, energy, and excitement to the fullest, all while doing what Hashem wants, if not for mivtzoyim?! As I lay in bed on Motzei Yom Tov, I wondered how many other children like me have awesome mivtzoyim adventures to share. Chayolim who come up with out-of-this-world ideas and ways to inspire others, doing what it takes to bring Moshiach. The more I thought about it, the more I was convinced that they’re out there, way more than the world knows. And next year, I’m gonna find them!

we followed a boy named Sruli as he filled his year with extravagant escapades and unthinkable pursuits.

This year, Mivtzoyim Mania is back - but the shtus d'kedusha that's described actually happened! We will be featuring stories of real chayolim and their families who bring the

Two years ago was no different. After davening and the Yom Tov meal, my father and I set out for Dave’s house with our shofar in hand.

He lives two long miles from our Chabad House. It was a scorching hot day, and we arrived tired, sweaty, and eager to help a fellow Yid. We knocked on the door, but nobody answered, so we walked around to the back of the house. There we saw Dave’s wife and daughter relaxing.

“We’re so sorry that you can’t blow the shofar for Dave this year,” they said. “He’s out surfing.”

“No problem,” Tatty said. “I’ll blow it for just the two of you. But if you don’t mind, let’s walk towards the beach so we can get as close to Dave as possible.”

When we got near the water, we could see Dave out in the distance, riding the waves with some friends. Tatty turned to Dave’s wife and said, “I’m going to try blowing the shofar so loud that Dave can hear it all the way out in the ocean!”

Tatty took a deep breath, and blew the shofar with all of his might. Again and again he blew, until all of the tekios were finished.

He turned to Dave’s wife and cheerfully concluded, “I hope that when Dave comes home later, he’ll say, ‘Y’know, I think I heard the shofar while I was surfing!’ And you can say, ‘You sure did!’”

We all laughed, and then wished Dave’s wife and daughter a “Shana Tova!” as we headed back to the Chabad House for Tashlich.

Months passed, and we forgot all about the shofar blowing on the beach. Summer time came, and soon it was Tisha B’Av.

Like I said before, Dave always comes to shul on Tisha B’Av. Why then? Well, there are many Yidden who go to shul only once each year—on Yom Kippur. Dave promised his mother that he wouldn’t be a “once-a-year Jew” like all the rest; he would at least be a “twice-a-year Jew”. So he searched the calendar for a second time to show up to shul, and decided that Tisha B’Av was the day. (Why he didn’t choose a happier time like Simchas Torah, Purim, or Shavuos, I have no idea, but he didn’t ask me…)

That Tisha B’Av afternoon, however, Dave had brought someone else along with him—a teenage boy with a tefillin bag in hand. The boy put down the bag, reached for a Siddur, and started putting on his tefillin.

A local Yid who owns tefillin? Tatty curiously walked over to their table. “Dave! I’m happy you’re here! And who is this young man?”

The boy told Tatty his name, and then added proudly, “I put tefillin on every day, and it’s all because of you, rabbi!”

Quite surprised, Tatty asked him to explain. This is what the teenager said:

“Ten months ago, my father, twin brother, and I went out

surfing with Dave. We were having a great time on the waves, when I suddenly heard a noise that sounded like a shofar’s blast. ‘Impossible!’ I thought to myself, ‘There’s no way I’m hearing a shofar out here in the ocean!’ But then I heard it again, and again. By now, there was no mistaking the noise—it was definitely a shofar. And as I learned later that day, it was your shofar; the one you blew for us as we surfed those ocean waves.

“Hearing that heavenly sound shook me to my core. Right then and there, I decided that I want to go to Israel to study Judaism. As soon as we returned to shore, I told my father how I felt, and we began looking into options. Before I knew it, I was on my way to the Holy Land!

I enrolled in a beginners' yeshiva, and spent the next few months soaking in everything I could about my new heritage. Hands down, those were the best months of my life. Back at home, I now put on tefillin every day!”

Tatty was amazed that someone who was completely not observant just a few short months ago, would begin to wear tefillin on his own. He invited the boy to spend a Shabbos in our home. One Shabbos led to another, and he became fully shomer Shabbos.

Today, that boy’s twin brother and father are steady visitors at Chabad, and each have their own pair of tefillin. The teenager himself lives in Eretz Yisroel, and is completely frum —all because of the power of shofar.

We are inspired by their newfound commitment to Yiddishkeit, and even more inspired to strengthen our commitment to mivtzoyim. We can’t wait to get back out there, and blow shofar for every Yid!

Over the years, he’s had many special experiences with the Rebbe, but this story is a favorite. (Rabbi Groner, the Rebbe’s secretary, who also appears in this story, is our zeidy, too!)

It was the middle of the night in the early 5740’s (1980’s),

and Zeidy Benjaminson was fast asleep. Suddenly, his phone began to ring. It rang and rang until it woke him up.

Looking at the clock next to his bed, he saw that it was two o’clock in the morning! Zeidy thought to himself, “Who could be calling at this hour? It must be important!”

Curious and a little concerned, Zeidy answered the phone.

“It’s me, Leibel Groner,” said the voice on the other end of line. Rabbi Groner? Wow! Zeidy knew it must be urgent.

“Rabbi Groner,” he quickly responded, “What can I do for you?”

Zeidy Groner replied, “Rabbi Benjaminson, are you in your office by any chance?”

“Rabbi Groner, I’m not at my office. I’m at home—it’s two o’clock in the morning!”

“Well then, I need you to go there immediately. The Rebbe has an urgent mission for you to complete at your office.”

Of course, as soon as Zeidy Benjaminson heard that, he immediately reached for his clothes and prepared to leave. “What does the Rebbe need me to do?” he asked.

“A young girl was in a terrible car accident tonight,” Zeidy Groner explained. “She’s now at the hospital, and in critical condition. The Rebbe says that in order for her to recover, she must be promoted

immediately to a higher rank in Tzivos Hashem. This will lift her up b’ruchniyus, and it will help her get better b’gashmiyus.”

“I’m on my way!” Zeidy Benjaminson assured him, and ran out the door.

In those days, there were no computer systems to record everyone's rank on the internet. Instead, Tzivos Hashem used index cards to store each chayol’s information, including their name, address, and rank. Zeidy’s office had over 60,000 index cards stored in filing cabinets. When Zeidy got to the office, he searched and searched until he finally found the sick girl’s card. He took a pen, crossed out the old rank, and wrote in her new, higher rank. He then went home and got back

A few days later, Zeidy Groner called Zeidy Benjaminson again. “Baruch Hashem, a miracle has happened for the little girl! She has fully recovered from her injuries! I just got off the phone with her mother; they’re on the way home from the hospital now.”

“Baruch Hashem!” Zeidy Benjaminson exclaimed. How grateful he was to have played a part in her refuah shleima, and how lucky he felt to be directing Tzivos Hashem, the most powerful army in the world!

Indeed, the Rebbe spoke about the power of Tzivos Hashem many times, telling us that it is not just a game or a fun idea. Tzivos Hashem is a serious matter. We are real soldiers in a real army.

In this story, we see clearly how important it is to be part of Tzivos Hashem, and how much it can truly affect the life of every chayol. Every time we hear this story, we feel re-inspired to strengthen our commitment to Tzivos Hashem. How important it is to succeed in our missions, move up in rank, and help others join this powerful army too—so that together, we can bring Moshiach NOW!

Our bubby and zeidy, Rabbi and Mrs. Yerachmiel Benjaminson, got married in the early 5740’s (1980’s). As dedicated chassidim, they wanted to go out on shlichus. While they were looking into various ideas, Zeidy was approached and asked if he would instead stay in Crown Heights and take charge of the Rebbe’s army, Tzivos Hashem. Zeidy didn’t know what to do, and turned to the Rebbe for advice. The Rebbe’s answer was clear: He should accept the position.

And so, Zeidy was hired to be the Executive Director of Tzivos Hashem.

Levi Yitzchak ,10 Shaina, 8 Tzemach Groner, 7 MyShliach, Calgary, Alberta, Canada

Rabbi Hershberg consulted with the Frierdiker Rebbe about becoming the rav for a Lubavitcher shul in Chicago. At that time, the Frierdiker Rebbe sent him to speak with our Rebbe as well.

"I spent almost the entire night with the Rebbe,” he later recalled. “The Rebbe's knowledge and brilliance was astonishing. From that night onward, we maintained a close relationship, and I consulted with the Rebbe about many personal and public matters."

Eventually, Rabbi Hershberg moved to Mexico and became the Chief Rabbi. He established the Beis Din of Latin America, and worked hard to build up Latin Jewry. Because of this, he had many unique opportunities to help Yidden around the world.

In תשל”ט(1979), the American embassy in Iran was seized by a group of Iranian students. 52 people were taken hostage, including six Yidden. In תש”מ (1980), the UN arranged a religious visit for the hostages. Leaders of all religions were allowed to come, including rabbis—but not Americans or Israelis. And so, as the Chief Rabbi of Mexico, Rabbi Hershberg was asked to make the courageous trip.

Of course, it was dangerous for a rabbi to travel to Iran, and Rabbi Hershberg wanted the Rebbe’s bracha.

“Go with Jewish pride,” the Rebbe encouraged Rabbi Hershberg, “You mention that you’ll be there on Chanukah, when the menorah is lit towards the outside. It should be with the strength of “אַל יֵבֹוׁש מִּפְנֵי הַּמַלְעִיגִים”—no shame to be a Yid in front of anyone. Hatzlacha Rabba, and may you bring besuros tovos!”

Deeply uplifted by the Rebbe’s words, Rabbi Hershberg made his way to Iran, proudly armed with his menorah and holy mission.

He developed a relationship with some Iranian officials, and asked if he could light the menorah with the Jewish hostages.

"Just as we have granted permission for a priest to meet with the Christian hostages on their holiday," the Iranians replied, "we will allow you entry as well."

Rabbi Hershberg eagerly brought his menorah to the Yidden in captivity. “It was a very uncommon scene,” he related. “It’s hard to describe their excitement when they saw me and the menorah. After lighting the candles, we sang and danced together—in the middle of Iran! They were full of joy.”

The next day, Rabbi Hershberg and the other religious leaders were invited to join a massive prayer service attended by Khomeini, the ruler of Iran,

and thousands of his people. Rabbi Hershberg and his colleagues were prominently seated in the front row.

At a certain point in the prayers, everyone in the audience bowed to the ground. All of the visiting religious leaders did the same. All, except for Rabbi Hershberg.

Khomeini sent a messenger to Rabbi Hershberg demanding an explanation. “How dare you not bow during the public service?” he was asked.

With the help of a translator, Rabbi Hershberg calmly responded, “I am a Jew, and I don’t speak your language. How could I bow, without knowing who you are bowing to?”

reply. A few minutes later the messenger told rabbi hershberg that khomani has called him over Everyone held their breath, certain that Rabbi Hershberg’s life was in danger.

But then, Khomeini’s expression relaxed., “This is a true commitment to his beliefs. This I can respect.” here i guess he is speaking to him in person

Of course, the incident created an enormous Kiddush Hashem. Rabbi Hershberg used the incredible opportunity to arrange an official meeting with the ruler himself, and was able to help the Iranian Yidden in many ways.

Even in the darkest of places, our Yiddishe pride can shine bright. With the Rebbe’s brachos, Rabbi Hershberg openly lit the menorah for Yidden in captivity, and stood without fear before the highest Iranian officials.

We, too, must fulfill our mission loud and proud. We light public menorahs for all to see, and won’t stop until every last Yid is reached.

So grab your menorahs, light up that Yiddishe pride, and hit the streets.

The story that I will tell you happened to my great- great-grandfather, Rabbi Avraham Mordechai Hershberg, former Chief Rabbi of Mexico, where my family is zoche to be on shlichus.

The clock had already struck midnight, but the girls decided to do a final status report and make sure that everything was in place for the next day's operation. Mivtzoyim supplies? Check. Metro cards? Check. Routes for each group? Check. Letter written to the Rebbe? Silence…

In all of the hustle and bustle, no one had taken the time to write about the campaign to the Rebbe, our general, and to ask for his bracha. “We can’t move forward without informing the Rebbe!” they all agreed.

“Look,” said one girl, “We all need to get some rest. Why don’t you two head to bed, and I’ll write to the Rebbe on our behalf?”

“It’s a deal,” replied the other two, and off they went, confident that with the Rebbe’s bracha,

their mission would be a success. And even though it was late, their friend made sure not to go to bed until the letter was written.

“Rebbe,” she wrote, “Please give us a bracha that everything will go smoothly, and it should be with hatzlacha.”

Girls were giving each other worried looks, and umbrellas could be seen everywhere. “Are we still going in the rain?”

But the organizers were adamant that nothing will get in the way of soldiers fulfilling their mission. “We have the Rebbe’s bracha,” they told everyone, “and we know that no rain can stop us.”

Outside, dark clouds were gathering, and a light drizzle was beginning to fall. Inside, however, preparations for the operation were in full swing. Girls were gathering from schools all over Crown Heights, picking up their gear, and joining up with their units. By the time the first team headed out at 12:30, the rain was gone.

The Mivtzoyim groups headed all over Brooklyn, spreading light in their specific target area. Group #7 was in Park

Slope, operating at full power. They even carried a secret weapon: in addition to their regular mivtzoyim supplies, they had brought along homemade challah to give every Yid a taste of Shabbos.

Soon, they spotted an old lady walking down the street. “Excuse me, are you Jewish?” they asked.

The girls were not deterred. “Would you like some challah?” they persisted.

The woman’s face lit up. “I love challah!” she exclaimed.

The girls continued walking down the street, happy to have found another Yid. They got to the end of the block when they heard someone calling behind them.

They turned around to see the old lady they had just met. “Girls, actually, I do want candles to light this week—in honor of Israel.”

The girls were amazed at how this woman’s neshama had been lit up from their small act of Ahavas Yisroel. Indeed, all over the city, Tzivos Hashem soldiers were illuminating the dark.

The battle plan called for the girls to head back to base at 2 pm. At 1:57, a light rain began to fall. By 2:30, all units were on their way back to headquarters. At 2:35, it started pouring.

The girls laughed together, sharing stories of the people that they met and the lives that they touched. Each chayol knew without a doubt that she had helped inspire another Yid that day—with the Rebbe’s bracha. Mission accomplished. Now it’s your turn, soldier. Get out there and spread the light!

The night was cold and the hour late. In a doorway on Kingston Avenue, three girls huddled together. Their attention was focused on a pile of boxes loaded with weapons. These weapons were not guns or bombs; the boxes were filled with Neshek—the Yiddishe weapon.

It was a Thursday night, and the girls were preparing for a large-scale offensive. The next day, 50 elementary- aged girls would be hitting the streets for a massive mivtzoyim campaign, to strike a blow against the Golus with weapons of light. They would be fully equipped with Ois B’Sefer Torah brochures, Sheva Mitzvos cards, pushkas, and of course, Shabbos candles.

Chayale Minsky, Mussie Simon, Riva Sandhouse, DL Lagziel, Goldie Wilschanski, Aidel Perlstein, Shaina Morosow 5th Grade, Bnos Menachem CH

Suddenly, the jeep screeched to a halt. Zeidy looked outside, where an intimidating scene met his eyes. Arabs had blocked the road with large stones. Burning tires nearby filled the air with thick black smoke.

“We must turn around and go home,” said the driver. “It is too dangerous for us to continue.”

“No!” Zeidy firmly replied. The Rebbe had assured Zeidy’s group of shluchim that he was taking full responsibility for their safety. Confident in the Rebbe’s protection, Zeidy told the driver, “I’m not afraid. We won’t abandon our mission!”

The driver looked at him as if he was crazy. “You’re welcome to fulfill your mission another time, but I cannot take responsibility for your safety.”

Zeidy smiled. “Don’t worry,” he said. “The Rebbe is taking responsibility for us.”

“We are,” Zeidy and his friends emphatically replied.

The jeep rocked dangerously from side to side as it made its way over the boulders. As they continued driving, a group of Arabs began throwing rocks at the jeep. The vehicle shook violently as if it was caught in a hailstorm.

“We must turn back!” yelled the driver. “This situation is completely out of control!”

Zeidy didn’t back down. He had a shlichus to do. “If you turn back, I will get out and continue on my own.”

The Rebbe often said that Yidden need to stand strong and not give in to Goyim. Zeidy knew that he had an opportunity to show just that: Yidden were on their way to Shechem for a mitzvah, and nobody else would decide otherwise.

By now, the Arabs had surrounded the jeep. Left with no choice, the soldier on board opened his window and fired his weapon into the air. Poof! The crowd scattered instantly. The driver inched forward until they were clear of the rubble, and then sped up the highway with a deep sigh of relief.

Baruch Hashem, they arrived safely at the army base. With

shining faces, the devoted chassidim gave those soldiers a Purim to remember. The megillah was proudly read, graggers loudly whirled, and mishloach manos gratefully enjoyed. The army base in Shechem was permeated with the festive Purim spirit.

When the crew finally returned home, they called the Rebbe’s office to inform him of the day’s events.

After such an experience, they thought that the excitement was over. Boy, were they in for a surprise!

Hours later, at around 4:30 am, Zeidy was still awake— tuning in to the Rebbe’s Purim farbrengen. Eretz Yisroel time is seven hours ahead of New York, so Zeidy, together with many other bochurim, stayed

Suddenly, his eyes opened wide in disbelief. The Rebbe was telling his story!

“We just heard a story which happened today in Eretz Yisroel,” announced the Rebbe. The Rebbe proceeded to tell all the details, proudly comparing the chassidim to Mordechai HaYehudi. The megillah tells us, “ֹלא יִכְרַע וְֹלא יִׁשְּתַחֲוֶה—Mordechai didn’t bend or bow before Haman”. This group of shluchim, too, didn’t bow or give in to anything that tried disturbing their shlichus.

“In the end,” concluded the Rebbe, “neither the Yidden nor, lehavdil, the Arabs were harmed in any way. When a Yid remains firm and proud, we see clearly that no one gets hurt.”

Can you imagine the feeling of pride and joy that filled Zeidy’s yeshivah? Their very own shliach had given the Rebbe tremendous nachas! You can be sure that they did mivtzoyim with even more chayus, long after Purim was over.

Chayolim, we all have challenges. Going out on mivtzoyim can be hard. Remember this: You’re on a mission from the Rebbe, and he is right there with you. Be proud, and don’t let anything stand in your way! You’ll be amazed at how the difficulties can disappear.

“Purim Same’ach!” smiled the driver as he welcomed the unusual crew aboard his army jeep. Up climbed a group of passionate chassidim: two Bar Mitzvah boys, the gabbai of their shul, and our zeidy, R’ Yosef Yitzchok Gurevitch, who was then a bochur on shlichus in Eretz Yisroel. An Israeli soldier joined as well for added safety.

“To that end,” Rabbi Wolf said, “We are giving each one of you a pushka. Right now, it’s empty. Your job is to fill it! Well, she called him, and Baruch Hashem, she received a check from the Ma’os Chitim fund. It’s really thanks to the incredible work of your students,” she said with tears in her eyes.

I am so proud of my school for having this wonderful project which helps so many Yidden. Last year, we raised ten thousand dollars! And as for me, I got the biggest gift in the world: the incredible feeling that I helped another Yid.

The Rebbe then asked him, “You live in the Bronx. I’d like to send matzah to people in the Bronx. Is it too far for you?”

When Zeidy got the address from Rabbi Hodakov a couple of minutes later, he was quite surprised. It was actually on the other side of the Bronx, quite far from his house. He called his mother and told her, “Ma, I’m going to be late for the Seder. Don’t wait for me.” With that, he was off to the train station.

After a long and complicated journey, he finally made it to the address. Zeidy noticed that this particular building was set aside for families with blind children. He looked again at the paper in his hand. It read, “Apartment 3D.” He climbed the stairs, found the right door, and knocked.

‘Hi, are you Mr. So-and-So?” Zeidy pleasantly asked.

“The Rebbe sent something very special for you and your family.” Zeidy told him.

The man’s face instantly lit up with excitement. ‘‘The Rebbe? Oh, please come in!’’

Zeidy walked in. As they were about to sit down, the man’s family came in. His wife was visibly pregnant, and his two daughters were both blind.

“Ok,” Zeidy announced, “We’re going to make a Pesach Seder together right now.”

They each took a piece of the matzah that the Rebbe had sent, and, instead of four cups of wine, they had paper cups of water. Zeidy took the yarmulka from under his hat, and placed it on the father’s head. He looked around the table, wondering what to say. He asked himself, “What would the Rebbe say?”

Zeidy took a moment to gather his thoughts, and then began. He spoke about emunah, about how Hashem freed our ancestors from slavery, and that He gives us freedom, too. We each have our own personal Mitzrayims to get through. Yet, even when it feels extremely hard, Hashem never gives us more than we can handle. And He is right there, lovingly holding us throughout the challenge. Once you know that—and when you really believe it— you’re already free.

They spoke, sang, and cried together until late at night. Finally the girls went off to bed, and Zeidy got ready to leave. Before he could go, however, he needed the answer to one question that was glaring in his mind. He turned to the

man and asked, “What is your connection with the Rebbe?”

“I work in a slaughterhouse,” the man replied, “and one of my co-workers is a rabbi. One day, I came into work feeling completely lost. I was very worried and confused. I guess it showed on my face, because my rabbi friend immediately asked what was wrong. I explained to him that my two children are blind, and my wife is now pregnant again. The doctors are pressuring us to terminate the pregnancy, chas v’shalom, because otherwise the new child may be born blind, as well.

“After hearing my story, my rabbi friend lovingly urged me to write to the Lubavitcher Rebbe and ask for blessings and guidance. I had nothing to

lose, and I did as he suggested. After a short while, I received a response. The Rebbe said that the baby will be fine, and what’s more, it will be able to see.

“But until you came tonight,” continued the man, “I didn’t know how to have faith in the Rebbe’s blessing. But now, after hearing everything you shared, we understand.”

Zeidy was extremely touched by the story. He wished them a warm “Gut Yom Tov!”, and finally headed home for his own seder.

Over the years, they stayed in touch. Baruch Hashem, the baby was born healthy and able to see, just as the Rebbe promised. The family grew more in their Yiddishkeit, and have become frum Yidden. Both the daughters and the son have created Jewish families of their own, full of beautiful children who can all see.

Chayolim, the lesson for us is clear. Matzah is the food of emunah and refuah. When you reach out and give Shmurah Matzah to your fellow Yid, you are deeply touching his/her neshama. You are giving them power to have trust in Hashem!

They sat at the edge of their seats, full of stress and confused by the unknown. Their eyes constantly moved between checking the clocks and watches, and looked towards the door. Their young son was having heart surgery in the next room over.

And, as their own hearts pounded with fear, the worried parents hoped desperately for good news.

After what seemed like forever, the door to the operating room opened. Both parents jolted up out of their seats as the surgeon walked towards them. Sadly, he did not look like he was bringing good news.

“As far as your son’s heart is concerned, the operation was successful,” the surgeon slowly began.

“But during the operation, an important nerve that helps the body breathe was damaged.

“This means that in the worst case, your son will be paralyzed for life and will need a special machine in order to breathe.

“In the best case, he may recover in a few years and start to breathe on his own without the machine, but he will not be able to speak. And even if he does speak, he will remain disabled forever and will need constant medical care.”

The surgeon paused, and then added, “I know that this is not easy for you to hear. We did the best that we could. Your son will be brought to the recovery room shortly. You can see him then.” With that, he turned and walked back into the operating room.

As soon as the surgeon left, the parents collapsed into their seats and burst into tears. It felt as if their whole world had come crashing down on top of them.

By Hashgacha Pratis, the chossid Reb Moshe Rabinovitz was also in the waiting room at the time. When he heard the parents’ heart-breaking sobs, he himself was filled with pain.

There must be something I can do to help them! Rabbi Rabinovitz thought to himself.

Just then, he remembered about Mivtza Ois B’Sefer Torah. The Rebbe said many times that children having their own letter in the special Sefer Torah brings brachos to them and to the whole world.

This is a way I can help! The chossid thought to himself. Armed with the Rebbe’s mivtza and kind words of support, Rabbi Rabinovitz approached the parents.

He gently told them about the Children’s Sefer Torah, and suggested that they should buy their son a letter for protection and brachos. The heartbroken parents were grateful for the idea. They immediately bought a letter for their little boy, hoping that it would bring the brachos he so desperately needed.

A few hours went by. Finally, the boy woke up from the operation. To his parents’ surprise and delight, there were no signs that he had trouble breathing. It seemed that there were no problems at all! The boy’s body had responded well to the surgery, and was working just as a healthy body should. He was a bit weak during his recovery time, causing him to speak in

a quiet voice, but the surgeon’s words did not come true at all. Nothing short of a miracle!

As the boy got back into regular life, his parents told him how Rabbi Rabinovitz’s suggestion had brought such an incredible turn-around. The family remained forever grateful to the Rebbe and his devoted chossid.

Chayolim, do you have an ois in the Children’s Torah? Have you or your parents received the certificate in the mail listing your special name and the parsha containing your letter?

Think of a relative, friend, or neighbor who might not yet have a letter of their own. Reach out and tell them about this special mivtza. As the Rebbe says, and as Rabbi Rabinovitz told the parents in the story, these letters are extremely powerful and important for the child who buys it and for the safety of the whole world!

Whenever we look at our Ois B’Sefer Torah certificates, we remember that the Rebbe looks after his beloved Yidden and knows exactly what we need for a healthy and happy life. We hope that you’ll spread the word, too!

For more information and to sign up, visit www.kidstorah.org.

We’re very lucky that our zeidy, Reb Shmuel Greisman, is the director of Mivtza Ois B’Sefer Torah. His shlichus is a special one, and there have been many stories of how buying letters for children brings brachos and protection.

Personally, though, our family signed up on our own. We did our missions online, but that was it. No rallies, no excitement in school, and no sense of doing it together. It’s a big job that comes with many different responsibilities: leading rallies; helping with missions, promotions, and programs; and communicating with teachers, students, parents, and Tzivos Hashem HQ to make sure everything runs smoothly. But here’s the challenge: Most people in Brazil speak only Portuguese, but a base commander must also speak English. Mrs. Sigal knew that most of the English speakers in our school were busy shluchos, so finding the right person wouldn’t be easy. What would we do? Without a base commander, we couldn’t have Tzivos Hashem! One day, our amazing mother (who is a native English- speaker from Australia) made a bold decision. “I’ll be the base commander,” she told Mrs. Sigal. Even though Mommy was quite busy herself, she decided to do it as a z’chus for our bubby, who wasn’t well, and later, she continued in Bubby’s honor.

Was there ever something that you really wanted to do, but it felt impossible? Something that seemed so easy for other people but so hard for you? That’s how our school felt about joining Tzivos Hashem. We knew that other schools had exciting rallies and great base commanders. Their students could complete their missions and go up in rank, earn cool prizes and medals, and join Chidon. But our school wasn’t part of any of that. We’re far away in Brazil, and joining Tzivos Hashem seemed way too complicated.

Now we could finally begin! Mrs. Sigal, our mother, and other staff members got to work putting everything into place. They showed everyone how to fill out their missions, made it super exciting to join the rallies, and arranged for the prizes and medals to reach us all the way in Brazil. But it wasn’t simple. There were still many differences between our school and other Tzivos Hashem bases. We didn’t let that stop us, and instead, found creative ways to make it all work. One challenge was the language. Our mother tried translating the rallies into Portuguese, but it was hard because she isn’t totally fluent yet. Instead, she asked students who know English to help translate. (In fact, one time, on our mother’s birthday, our six- year-old sister announced, “Mommy, I give you a bracha to speak perfect Portuguese, so that you can translate the rallies all by yourself!” We all laughed. That was what she wanted most!) Another challenge was the calendar. The seasons in Brazil are opposite the ones in half of the world. For some parts of the year, schools in America are open and Tzivos Hashem campaigns are running at full force. So while they’re all busy memorizing Tanya, learning niggunim, and fighting V’halachta Bidrachav battles,

we aren’t even in school; it’s our summer break! But of course, we don’t want to miss out, so we instead learn everything during our winter months (when American kids are on their summer break). Baruch Hashem, our entire school is proud to be part of Tzivos Hashem. When Chidon started this past year, every single student who was able to participate, did! Kids from our school made it to the game show finale in New York—and some of us even won trophies!

It wasn’t easy, because all the Chidon books and tests are in English. But that didn’t stop us! One girl signed up for English classes, some families hired tutors, and some of our friends used AI translations to help them study. Everyone was excited to be involved. One day last year, something unbelievable happened. General Shimmy Weinbaum came to our school for a visit—in person!

Music blasted, Tzivos Hashem flags waved, and the boys even performed with a marching band! General Shimmy first led a special rally just for us, and then, at a Tzivos Hashem-themed lunch, he farbrenged with us, sharing uplifting stories and powerful messages. We even got to play soccer together! (And boy, is General Shimmy an excellent goalie!) After he left, each of us got a special gift: a picture magnet showing each chayol receiving rank medals from him. We still have them hanging on our fridge at home, and so do all our friends! The magnets remind us of those two special days spent with General Shimmy and the excitement he gave us to keep fighting our Yetzer Hara and continue on as a proud Tzivos Hashem base. Today, every one of the 70 children in our school who are eligible to join participates in Tzivos Hashem! We cheer each other on, work hard on completing our missions, and feel so proud to be part of Hashem’s Army. It’s hard to believe that not so long ago, it had all seemed truly impossible. Butas we say in the pesukim ""יגעתי ומצאתי תאמין

Local Yidden and tourists passed through it every day, and the ghetto was alive once more.

Then Chanukah came, and an elderly man walked in. He was about ninety years old. Tatty greeted him warmly and asked, “Did you ever have a bar mitzvah?”

A short while later, another elderly man came in. His name was Gabriel, and he was eighty- six. When Tatty asked him the same question, Gabriel gave the same answer: “No.”

Tatty didn’t wait. Together with the bochurim who had come to help for Chanukah, he quickly made a minyan and took out a Sefer Torah.

The narrow building stood quietly in the Roman ghetto. Its walls were hundreds of years old, filled with a long and painful history.

But now, something new was happening inside. It was our family’s Chabad House!

Slowly, the building began to fill with life, as people came to daven, learn, and take part in programs.

For the first time in their lives, the two elderly men put on tefillin. Then, they got aliyos to the Torah and celebrated their bar mitzvahs right there in the Chabad House. Everyone sang and danced with excitement and joy.

A few days later, on the last night of Chanukah, Tatty organized a small menorah lighting outside the Chabad House. He thought that only a few people would come, but when he stepped outside, he saw that an entire crowd had gathered!

Seeing that Gabriel was there, too, Tatty announced,

survivor, no less. We want to give him the honor of lighting the menorah.”

Gabriel stepped forward, and the crowd grew quiet as they looked. He lit one candle, then another, and another, continuing until all eight flames were burning brightly. The menorah stood tall and proud, in a place where, not so long ago, it wasn’t even safe to be a Yid.

After the lighting, Gabriel turned to Tatty and said quietly, “I need to tell you something.” He took a deep breath and began.

“When I was four years old, I lived right here in the ghetto. War raged on all around us, until the Nazis had taken over our city. But I continued to play outside with my sister, too young to understand the

was happening. He ran outside and began shouting loudly at us, ‘'I’ve been looking for you everywhere! Your mother is so worried!’

“He acted like an angry father and even slapped my sister to make it

look real. The Nazi stopped and asked, ‘'These are your children?’ The man answered, 'Yes.’ The Nazi nodded and let us go.”

Gabriel looked up at the building as he finished his story, his voice full of emotion. “That dairy shop was right here,” he said, pointing to our Chabad House. “Eighty-two years ago, this is the exact spot where my sister and I were saved.

“And tonight”, he continued, wiping away a tear, “I stood here as a proud Jew and lit the Chanukah menorah for all to see.”

The flames of the menorah flickered quietly against the moonlit sky. So many years had passed with so much darkness, but now, there was light again.

From then on, Gabriel kept coming back to the Chabad House. He returned every day to put on tefillin. In the place where his life had once been saved, his neshama began to shine once more.

Fellow Chayolim, this Chanukah, let’s all go out and help one more Yid light the menorah. A small flame can reach further than you imagine, and who knows what story it might complete. It’s up to us to spread the light!

own Shabbos candles! And they were princess- themed; her favorite!

Bnos Menachem’s fourth graders headed to the subway station with a bounce in their steps. It was Friday, and that meant one thing: mivtzoim!

At the station, they made a rally and said pesukim. Soon, the familiar screech of the subway filled the air. Their train sped down the tracks, slowed to a stop, and opened its doors.

At the subway station, they gathered for their usual rally, with Group 8 joining them for pesukim. Soon they were on the train, listening to a story about chassidim who spent Shabbos in a gas station.

One of the first people they met was a jogger, hurrying down the path. She slowed down just long enough to take Shabbos candles and then hurried on.

The girls smiled at each other. “Joggers never stop for long,” one girl said. “They don’t want to slow down!”

Wow, we did it! The Rebbe made a grand siyum for the first cycle of learning!

Phew, am I glad about Track Three! After opening the Mishneh Torah, I wasn’t sure I was old enough yet to learn it by myself… Sefer Hamitzvos lists short summaries of every mitzvah—much better for a kid like me!

The Rebbe said that everyone learning and discussing the same part of Torah each day will unite all Yidden! The cycles start tomorrow.

While learning today’s three perakim of Rambam, my roommate, Menashe, asked me which perakim we’re up to.

“Guys!” Dovber called from the corner of the room, “Did you know today is exactly ten years since the Rebbe first spoke about learning Rambam?”

Mivtza Shofar

Shofar
Print PDF

My feet have never hurt this much! But boy, was it worth it.

After shacharis this morning, I joined my cousin and some other bochurim on a long trek to blow shofar in a hospital. He kept asking me if I was sure I could walk it since I’m only 11, but there

was no way I was gonna say no! And guess what? I was so excited to help people do this mitzvah that my feet didn’t even hurt one bit. (Well … maybe a bit. A-lot-a-bit, actually. But I didn’t tell Naftali that.)

Afterwards, we ran back to 770 to join the tashlich parade up Eastern Parkway. By then, my feet were so numb that I couldn’t feel them anymore.

Mivtzoim—they feel like they’ve been around forever! Can you even imagine life without them? Yet, unbelievably, before the Rebbe introduced each of the mitzvah campaigns that we know so well, they simply didn’t exist.

Join us as we explore imaginary old diaries that could have belonged to kids just like you— kids who might have lived during the time when the Rebbe first announced many of these mivtzoim.

Shofar was the first mivtza to be established! As you can imagine, the idea of blowing shofar in the streets just blew people’s minds away. Lucky Yitzi, because he lived when this mivtza first started—and lucky you, because you get to read about it!

I feel like my head is inside the biggest shofar in Crown Heights while it’s being blown, and it’s not because I’m fasting (because I’m just seven, you know). It’s because I think I just heard the shofar four bajillion gazillion times this Rosh Hashana!

I’ll start from the beginning. Tatty came home the other day with big news: The Rebbe wants us chassidim to go out to the streets and blow shofar for people. Imagine that! Shofar outside of shul! Who ever thought of such a thing?!

It made me wonder—what’s next? I mean, if you can blow shofar in the street … I just can’t wait to find out!

Eastern Parkway early Rosh Hashana morning, asking people if they were Jewish. But more than that, it was so special. Tatty asked an old man sitting on a bench, his hand on his cane, if he could blow shofar for him. “אִיְך האָב פאַרגעֶסן אִינְגאַנצֶן—I completely forgot about shofar! ” the old man exclaimed.

P.S. By the way, if you are wondering why I’m starting a diary, it’s because Tatty told me that amazing things are happening now, and I should write them down for my grandchildren to read. I asked Tatty if he also writes a diary, but he laughed and said, “Yitzi look at my gray hairs! You think I have time to write a diary?”

What do gray hairs have to do with writing a diary? I’m not sure, but I’d better get in as much as I can before I go gray!

Wow, you’re dusty. I’m seeing that my last entry was quite a few years back! I’m already thirty- four now … It’s been a while since I’ve picked you up, old pal. And for good reason! I'm a busy tatty, rebbi, and bus driver on the side.

Well, if you are wondering why I remembered you today, it’s because this morning, seven- year-old Chaim came up to me and asked, “Tatty, I also want to have mesiras nefesh to leave the Rebbe for Tishrei just like cousin Chanan, and travel to Paraguay to blow shofar for people!”

I think he was more excited about the plane ride, but, suddenly, I whooshed right back to when I was seven years old and mivtza shofar was first established. It made me realize that I haven’t written in a while, and I think it’s time to catch you up.

Since I last wrote, I have been zoche to hear the Rebbe speak publicly about mivtza shofar several times. Two years ago, the Rebbe spoke about how we should blow shofar in prisons (!) and anywhere Yidden can be found, so that they, too, can crown Hashem as King. Personally, I haven’t done that yet, but some of my nephews have!

The year before that, the Rebbe declared that blowing shofar for patients literally gives life to their neshamos. Indeed, that year, when I went on mivtzoim, I was so moved to hear a patient say, “I knew Lubavitch would not let us down.”

In a different farbrengen a few years back, the Rebbe also asked that chassidim in Eretz Yisroel blow shofar for the soldiers in the IDF. My Israeli cousin, Mendy, lives near an army base, and has walked there in the heat every year since.

To think that in just 27 years we’ve gone from blowing shofar on the parkway to—one sec, is that Dovber crying? I’d better run and give him his pacifier.

P.S. Hey, what’s Chaim writing over there? It doesn’t look like homework. Is that a diary?!

I’ve been so busy these days in yeshiva that I barely ever have time to write. Thing is, I just heard something really amazing, and if my grandchildren do discover my diary one day, I want them to know about this:

I heard that just about every Jewish patient in Brooklyn hospitals heard shofar this year! The Rebbe’s goal is being fulfilled! Even the hospital officials gave permission for chassidim to go to the rooms and blow shofar for people, because they realize that having a refuah shleima in ruchniyus helps the patients to have a refuah shleima in gashmiyus, too!

Do you understand?! Many patients who are stuck in bed had given up on hearing the shofar this year. And yet, the Rebbe’s chassidim were there for them.

The first thing they needed to do was buy menorahs to give out. They tried asking different stores and companies, but none of them had enough menorahs, and it would be impossible to make them in time. This mivtza was launched so soon before Chanukah! Not only that, but there is also a metal shortage. (“Shortage” is a new word I learned. It means there isn’t enough of something.) So factories could hardly make any menorahs, even if they wanted to! I didn’t know we’re having a metal shortage now. Did you? Anyways, a neis happened, and the chassidim found a Jewish man named Tibor Kupferstein who owns a factory. Mr. Kupferstein’s factory normally makes supplies for the American army, but he agreed to pause everything in order to make 10,000 lightweight menorahs! His factory has already begun making menorahs 24 hours a day! When Tzach reported this to the Rebbe, the Rebbe responded in pleasant surprise, “Ten thousand?!” I hope I get to give out some of these menorahs tonight! Love, Yehudis P.S. MOTZEI SHABBOS Dear Diary, What a rollercoaster of a year this has been, and it’s barely begun! First there was the war, which you know already … I wrote so much about the surprise attack on Eretz Yisroel that happened on Yom Kippur. At first, we were petrified, and then we saw incredible nissim. And now this! A new mivtza! Let me backtrack. Thursday night, Friday, and Shabbos have been packed with Yud-Tes and Chof Kislev celebrations. During the farbrengens, the Rebbe started talking about the next exciting Yom Tov—Chanukah! The Rebbe declared that we must help other Yidden celebrate, and that there should be at least one menorah per house. “If you meet anyone who doesn’t have a menorah, you should give one to them. And it would also be good that every child lights their own menorah,” the Rebbe said. Wow! To knock on people’s doors and bring Chanukah to them? I’ve never heard of such a thing! Mommy excitedly told us at our family’s Melave Malka that it shows how much the Rebbe cares for and remembers every single Yid. Which reminds me: The Rebbe also said that in Eretz Yisroel, there should be a menorah at every army base and watchtower, even if just one soldier is stationed there. Just one! Plus, chassidim are to visit the homes of widows, orphans, and wounded soldiers, so they, too, can feel the light of Chanukah. The Rebbe ended the Shabbos farbrengen by saying that a meeting should be held right after havdalah to start making plans. There’s no time to waste. Chanukah is just four nights away! Love, Yehudis

On Zos Chanukah, the Rebbe called for a special Chanukah rally for kids! My friends and I all went.

Plus, that night, there was a surprise farbrengen! The Rebbe said that the Chanukah pe’ulos were super successful, and everyone should say “l’chaim". The Rebbe even sent wine & mezonos to the ladies section because we were very involved, too!

On Shabbos afternoon, I visited my friend Fraida’s house, and her tatty told us that Tzach had to keep asking Mr. Kupferstein for more and more menorahs. By the end of Chanukah, 60,000 were given out! That’s enough menorahs for almost 1,300 school buses filled with kids!

After being busy with menorahs for days on end, I’ll bet Mr. Kupferstein also dreams about menorahs at night!

Anyone over bar and bas mitzvah who went on mivtzoim was allowed to get, and gelt was even sent to Eretz Yisroel!

Don’t forget, dear diary, that hardly anyone gets a dollar or coin from the Rebbe, so it was a very special thing!

My parents are going to frame their Chanukah gelt to remind the whole family how important Mivtza Chanukah is to the Rebbe.

You definitely need an update on how this new mivtza is going!

Since the minute Chanukah began, chassidim have been in high gear. Busloads of bochurim and tatties have been pouring out of 770 and driving all over to spread the light of Chanukah. They’ve been visiting people in their homes, going to businesses, and giving out menorahs in the streets.

I went with my mother and sisters to Manhattan, and gave out 14 menorahs that Mr. Kupferstein made! People just love Chanukah, and are so excited when we offer them these menorahs.

And get this: Someone had a wild idea to put a menorah on top of a car! So they built one and parked the car in front of 770. When the Rebbe saw it, he told them to light it! A car menorah- -imagine that! Later, bochurim drove it to Fifth Avenue in Manhattan for more mivtzoim. One night, the mayor of New York, Mr. John Lindsay, came to see it. As the newspaper cameras took pictures, he gave each bochur a handshake.

Can you imagine? It was in the newspapers! The whole city saw the light of Chanukah!

I gotta go, because we are heading to the bookstore now!

Dear Diary, The Rebbe held a surprise farbrengen yesterday! Tatty told me that 770 was packed. The Rebbe again announced the same message—this time, to the men, too: that the solution for ruchniyus darkness around us is the Shabbos candles of young girls. Hashem gave us the power to light up the world! Chassidim must reach out to women and girls around the globe, telling them to light Shabbos candles. The Rebbe ended with a bracha that all of the small flames should join together into a big torch that will burn down the rest of Golus. Amen! It’s only 2 o’clock in the afternoon, but my shiny candlestick is already set up and waiting to be lit tonight for the very first time. I am way too excited! Imagine … My flame can light away the terrible darkness in the world, and it will join the flames of so many other meidelach who will also be lighting for the first time ever! Love, Chaya P.S. Can you guess why the Rebbe said the surprise sicha about this new mivtza yesterday, instead of waiting to speak on Shabbos?

Mivtzoim—they feel like they’ve been around forever! Can you even imagine life without them? Yet, unbelievably, before the Rebbe introduced each of the mitzvah campaigns

could have belonged to kids just like you— kids who might have lived during the time when the Rebbe first announced many of these mivtzoim.

Chaya used to stand and watch as her mother lit candles every Erev Shabbos. Then, one day, the Rebbe said a sicha … and Chaya began to light her own flame, too! Today, her grandchildren can’t believe there was ever a time when

mothers were the only ones who lit candles. Let’s dive right in

and hear about this historic mivtza through Chaya’s eyes.

My 10-year-old sister, Sheina, and I just bought our own Shabbos candlesticks! Are you confused, Diary, because you thought that only mommies light Shabbos candles?

Well, yesterday the Rebbe spoke to N’shei U’bnos Chabad, like he does every year before Rosh Hashana. Sitting in the big shul downstairs with just women and girls already felt special, but I didn’t realize how special I would feel after hearing the Rebbe’s sicha!

The Rebbe spoke about how the world has become darker, and the solution is to create more light. How? With Shabbos licht!

And why do I feel special? Because the Rebbe said that even unmarried girls—even girls under bas mitzvah— should light candles!

So, even though Sheina and I are just 10 and 8, we’re both gonna light with Mommy this Friday!

Something has been making me feel a bit funny inside.

You know how Sheina and I have started lighting Shabbos and Yom Tov candles, even though only Mommy used to light?

Well, at the Yud-Tes Kislev farbrengen last night, the Rebbe said that some frum people are upset about this! They think that lighting is just for married women—not girls. They say that girls bentching licht is a “new thing”, not part of our Yiddishe mesora.

But the Rebbe said they don’t realize that this is actually a very “old thing”! Many years ago, girls also used to light, but this minhag was somehow forgotten. The Rebbe even described how a young girl lighting Shabbos candles has caused her entire family to become frum!

We’ve got to get the message to every Yiddishe meidel! But how?

Maybe I can think of a good idea to tell Mrs. Sternberg…

I forgot to tell you! Mrs. Sternberg and the other Mivtza Neshek organizers created a candlestick for mivtzoim!

Everyone’s excited— thousands have already been given out! I’m proud to say that I gave out twelve candlesticks on the street corner today.

A helicopter flew around the city pulling a banner with candle-lighting times, bochurim traveled with candlesticks to Pesach hotels, and there were announcements on the radio and television—every possible way to reach people!

Every Friday after day camp, my mother, Sheina, and I give out candlesticks and encourage people to light Shabbos candles.

We heard that Mrs. Sternberg would be making the Rebbe a gold-plated candlestick engraved with the total number of candlesticks given out so far, and we wanted that number to be as high as possible!

Just moments before the Yud-Gimmel Tammuz farbrengen yesterday, the number “245,001” was engraved on the candlestick. That last “1” is for a candlestick that I gave it out, I’m sure!

After the farbrengen, the Rebbe walked out with the candlestick. I bet it made the Rebbe proud.

Cheder Tzivos Hashem

Cheder Tzivos Hashem
Print PDF

What an amazing Chanukah rally! It’s already quite late, but I have to tell you about it!

The Rebbe said that we must make our home into a Beis Tefillah (a place where we ask Hashem for everything we need), a Beis Torah (a place where Torah is learned and reviewed), and a Beis Gemilus Chassadim (a place where tzedaka is given). This way, it’s a place where the Shechina can rest.

After the rally, Mommy picked me up from 770. As soon as I got in the car, I asked

her—respectfully, just as the Rebbe had taught us—if she could help me do this as extra “Chanukah gelt” (not real money, but the special “gift” of making our home full of holy light).

“I would love to help you!” Mommy gushed. (She was even more excited than if I had asked her to help me with homework!)

We started brainstorming on how to add in all of these three things to make our home the brightest on the block!

Mivtzoim—they feel like they’ve been around forever! Can you even imagine life without them? Yet, unbelievably, before the Rebbe introduced each of the mitzvah campaigns that we know so well, they simply didn’t exist.

Join us as we explore imaginary old diaries that could have belonged to kids just like you— kids who might have lived during the time when the Rebbe first announced many of these mivtzoim.

Join Sara as she transforms her bedroom from ordinary to extraordinary; from just a place to sleep and relax into a full-on Cheder Tzivos Hashem a mini Beis Hamikdash! כ"ו כסלו, תשמ"ז

I was sitting cross-legged on my bed this afternoon, spacing out (as usual), when I started looking around my room. The soft pink curtains, the decorations on the wall … that’s when I noticed the picture I had drawn of my friend Leiba and me in Tzivos Hashem uniform. I continued looking around—my mirror, headbands, and art set. Hmm… I thought to myself. I’m a soldier in Hashem’s Army. If that’s the case, then my room must be my army base!

Did you know that when a Jewish home is a Beis Torah, Tefillah, and Gemilus Chassadim, it actually becomes a mini Beis Hamikdash (a.k.a. a Mikdash me’at)? I just found that out from a letter the Rebbe wrote to all chassidim! In another letter just for the kids, the Rebbe said that our bedrooms should have these three things, as well! When we learn Torah, daven and give tzedaka in our bedroom, it also becomes a home for Hashem! So, every bedroom needs to have:

1. A Chumash 2. A siddur 3. A pushka In the sefarim and on the pushka, we should write “לה' הארץ ומלואה” (or, “לה"ו” for short) and our names underneath. I’m heading to Kingston Avenue to buy myself a new, pink pushka and a good marker to write with. Love, Lieutenant Sara

My class and I just went on the best trip to 770 ever! The Rebbe gave out nickels just to us children to put right into our new bedroom pushkas! We all came wearing Shabbos clothes and pushka-decorated crowns, and proudly held our new pushkas.

I felt like a million dollars when the Rebbe focused on me as I passed by his shtender. Of course, I put the nickel straight into my pushka so the Rebbe could watch me do the mitzvah.

Mommy even brought my baby brother, Tzemach, to get a nickel from the Rebbe. The Rebbe put the coin into his teeny tiny hand, and Mommy helped him place it into his new pushka! Precious!

I’m heading over to buy myself a new hagadah, because the Rebbe just said that our bedrooms need a hagadah, too. I’m actually going to get a couple more sefarim besides that, because I want my room to be my Bayis Malei Sefarim, and no way are three sefarim enough.

On Shabbos, the Rebbe gave us a powerful strategy for fighting the Yetzer Hara. I tried it out, and it worked! Here’s how it goes: On Sunday morning, I hung a brand new sign on my bedroom door that says "Cheder Tzivos Hashem". I taped it right at eye level so I can see it every time I walk into my room. After all, my room—and everything in it—is a place for the Shechina to rest! When I was walking into my room to pick up my Chumash and learn, the Yetzer Hara tried to stop me with his kvetchy voice, “Why are you working so hard to learn Torah? You don’t even understand everything yet like your parents and teachers! Go relax and play like a 9-year-old should!” But have no fear: I saw the sign on my door. I told him, “It doesn’t matter that I’m so young! I’m part of Tzivos Hashem! In an army, what matters is kabbalas ol and ma’aseh b’po’al—doing what Hashem wants. And in that, every soldier is equal!” Boom! Kvetchy voice stopped. It felt so good to win the battle.

It’s been quite the week! Last Tuesday, the judge ruled that the sefarim belong to the chassidim (Didan Notzach!) and we danced like it was Simchas Torah. Then, yesterday, at an extra- special Didan Notzach Shabbos farbrengen, the Rebbe said that everyone, big and small—actually, davka the littlest kids—should get involved in making their homes a Beis Chabad. How proud I feel, knowing that my little Beis Chabad is connected to the giant Beis Chabad of 770, and from there to all Chabad Houses around the world! I could never be lonely again! And here’s the best part: The Rebbe shared that one Mommy and Tatty wrote a nachas note to the Rebbe, describing how their son was so excited to turn his room into a Beis Chabad that he hung a sign on his bedroom door with the words “Beis Chabad”! I’m getting my markers out right now. Love, Lieutenant Sara

I continued thinking: What would a Tzivos Hashem army base look like? Full of heilige things, that’s for sure. Well, I already have a mezuza. I wash negel vasser by my bed. My closet is full of tzniusdik bas-melech dresses. What else should I add? Love, Lieutenant Sara

Hadassah was just five years old when Mivtza Purim began, and while

her handwriting became smaller and neater over the years, the mivtza grew

bigger and more dramatic. Just make sure not to read her diary upside down!

My siblings and I just spent the whole day pretending to be airplanes. We jumped off the couches—dropping papers on each other's heads—and then ran to catch as many as we could.

Don’t think we spend every Sunday doing this! After a Purim like this one, though, it’s all we can think about!

You must have heard about it, Diary! On Purim morning, Chassidim flew an airplane over a huge area in Eretz Yisroel, dropping flyers onto people’s heads! The flyers had a Purim sicha about being like Mordechai—not bending, not bowing, and doing mitzvos with Jewish pride—and people were running in all directions to catch them.

It’s been ten years since Mivtza Purim began, and it just grows every year. This Purim, Chassidim in Eretz Yisroel (some of them in their soldier uniforms!), flew in an army airplane to bring the mitzvos of Purim to faraway army bases.

They brought tens of thousands of Mishlo’ach Manos, and also Megillos to lein with. The soldiers were so moved! Each Mishlo’ach Manos had a picture of the Rebbe in it, and many soldiers stuck it next to their beds.

In fact, on Motzei Purim, the Rebbe came late to the farbrengen, and began by telling everyone in 770 that the Chassidim who had gone on this special mivtzoim in Eretz Yisroel had all

choked up with tears as he shared how the army officials made sure that the

This year, the Rebbe wanted the mivtzoim with soldiers to be even bigger and better. He explained that the Purim activities with bereaved families (families who are sad because someone passed away) should be done with a k’nak (extra excitement)!

I also heard that the Rebbe didn’t start the Purim farbrengen until he knew that the Chassidim who had flown to the Sinai desert for mivtzoim with soldiers— and got stuck there—were able to listen to the farbrengen through the live hookup.

Just when we thought Mivtza Purim couldn’t get any bigger, the Rebbe said we must include the prisons. Wow! That sounds complicated.

B’ezras Hashem, in the z’chus of all of these mitzvos, Klal Yisroel will be released from the prison of Golus, and Moshiach will come right now!

Rabbi Dovid Raskin just made an announcement after davening that everyone who goes on Purim mivtzoim this year will get a dollar from the Rebbe! That doesn’t happen often, and it shows how special Purim mivtzoim are to the Rebbe!

The Rebbe just held an unusual weekday farbrengen last night, encouraging us to go on Purim mivtzoim. Why on a weekday? So it can be broadcasted for everyone to hear the words straight from the Rebbe!

The Rebbe said that since Mishlo’ach Manos must be given from man to man and woman to woman, we women and girls are super important for this mitzvah.

The Rebbe also emphasized that Mivtza Purim isn’t just for Lubavitchers. It’s for all of Klal Yisroel!

Today, Tatty came into the kitchen as I was putting a wafer and a tangerine into my Mishlo’ach Manos bags. “Hadassah, I’m so glad that you are making your own Mishlo’ach Manos!” he said. “You’re so big now, already five years old!”

“Of course, Tatty. It’s my favorite mitzvah! And look,” I told him, pointing to four pennies on the counter. “I have Matanos L’evyonim ready, too!”

“It’s because of the letter from the Rebbe,” I explained.

“That’s right!” Mommy piped in. “As soon as I heard about the Rebbe’s letter that young children should do Mishlo’ach Manos and Matanos L’evyonim by themselves, we jumped into action and went straight to the grocery store!”
