Mivtza Yom Huledes

Yom Huledes
Print PDF

Mivtzoim—they feel like they’ve been around forever! Can you even imagine life without them? Yet, unbelievably, before the Rebbe introduced each of the mitzvah campaigns that we know so well, they simply didn’t exist.

Join us as we explore imaginary old diaries that could have belonged to kids just like you— kids who might have lived during the time when the Rebbe first announced many of these mivtzoim.

Most people didn’t pay attention to their birthdays, until the Rebbe changed all that. Join Simcha as he learns to celebrate his birthday … the Yiddishe way! )1988( כ"ה אדר, תשמ"ח

Tonight, over chicken and potatoes, Tatty said, “Kids, are you ready to hear something unbelievable that happened after shacharis today?”

Diary, I’m sure you know that since Rebbetzin Chaya Mushka was niftar, the Rebbe has been davening in his home with a smaller minyan. So anyways, Tatty goes to this minyan sometimes.

“It seemed like an ordinary morning,” began Tatty. “We finished shacharis, people were leaving for work, the Rebbe had already gone up to the second floor, I was folding up my tallis… Then, suddenly, everyone around me stopped what they were doing. I looked up, and I couldn’t believe my eyes.

At the Moshiach seuda on the last day of Pesach, the Rebbe spoke more about birthdays! The Rebbe showed us different places in the Torah that tell us about the importance of birthdays.

A couple of days ago, a proper organized list of all the birthday minhagim was given out, with ten different sections. The Rebbe himself edited it! I’m writing everything down with checkboxes so that when it’s my birthday, I won’t even miss one thing.

But Diary—don’t think Mivtza Yom Huledes is staying a secret! A full- page ad was published in the New York Times, which is a huge newspaper,

ALIYA Get an aliya on the Shabbos before your birthday. This one will have to wait. TZEDAKA Give extra tzedaka before shacharis and mincha. I put a whole load of coins into the pushka! TEFILLA Daven with extra kavana and say the whole Tehillim (or at least a sefer). I davened beautifully today! KAPITEL Learn and say your new kapitel. Yup!

saying “Birthdays Matter.” There was also a Yiddish ad in the Algemeiner Journal: “Do not miss out on observing the most important day of your life!” And more ads—too many to write down—were published all across the globe! I heard that in Eretz Yisroel there’s a full-blown campaign going on!

I heard that at dollars, the Rebbe sometimes even reminds children to have a party or a farbrengen in honor of their yom huledes! I can’t wait to go for dollars before my birthday!

It’s really special that keeping the minhagim of a Yom Huledes is a z’chus for the aliyas haneshema of Rebbetzin Chaya Mushka. It makes Mivtza Yom Huledes extra special for us chassidim.

TORAH Learn extra Torah—both Niglah and Chassidus. I learned a few extra lines of Tanya Baal Peh, and Sefer Hamitzvos, too. MAAMAR Chazer a maamar (or part of a maamar) baal peh. I think I’ll do this when I’m a bit older. HAFATZA Encourage other people to grow in their Yiddishkeit and Chassidishkeit, even more than we usually do! I was feeling a bit shy, but I invited a neighbor to my birthday farbrengen so he could hear some

Chassidus and learn about mivtza yom huledes! HISBODEDUS Spend some time all alone thinking about the past year: what I did well, and what I need to do better next year. I did a great job sharing my Shabbos treats with my younger siblings. And I definitely need to stop talking so much in class. HIDDUR MITZVAH Do something even better than before! I took on a hachlata to say Asher Yatzar with more kavana for a whole month. I’ll do this by standing in one place when I say it.

I announced that to everyone at my farbrengen, so they can all help me remember to keep my hachlata! FARBRENGEN (My favorite one!) Have a farbrengen with family and friends to thank Hashem for this special day, take on hachlatos, and make a bracha ׁשֶהֶחֱיָנּו on a new fruit. You should have seen the seven-layer cake Mommy baked me … with the special fruit right on top!

“The Rebbe walked over to the shtender, and started saying a sicha!”

“What did the Rebbe say?” asked my older sister Shaina.

“Today is actually Rebbetzin Chaya Mushka’s birthday, and the Rebbe spoke

“Yes.” Tatty answered. “Would you believe it? I don’t know if Zeidy even knows when his birthday is. Wait—when’s mine again? Sometime after Pesach, no? Chof-vov, chof-zayin…?”

“It does say in the Hayom Yom for Yud-Alef Nissan that your birthday is a day of cheshbon hanefesh and teshuva,” my older brother pointed out. He always knows everything.

“Right,” Mommy said. "And there was a point some years ago where bochurim would have a yechidus on their birthdays, but no one really pays much attention to birthdays b’chlal! It’s more of a private, quiet thing.”

“Yes, that’s all going to change now!” chimed in Dovi.

“That’s right!” responded Tatty. “The Rebbe said that we should be celebrating our birthdays! We should make joyful Chassidishe farbrengens with friends and family, taking on new hachlatos, and doing extra mitzvos. Kids, too!”

Mivtza Matza

Matzah
Print PDF

Mivtzoim—they feel like they’ve been around forever! Can you even imagine life without them? Yet, unbelievably, before the Rebbe introduced each of the mitzvah campaigns that we know so well, they simply didn’t exist.

Join us as we explore imaginary old diaries that could have belonged to kids just like you— kids who might have lived during the time when the Rebbe first announced many of these mivtzoim.

Starting from when he was just four years old, Ahrele_who would probably be an Elter Zeidy by now_wrote down these memories (with the help of his tatty), bringing us into the moments when Mivtza Matzah first began. ראש חודש ניסן, תשי"ד

“I’m so excited that it’s almost Pesach! ” I exclaimed to Tatty, who was helping me and Dovi wash the toys in the bathtub. “You know why Pesach is my favorite Yom Tov? It's because I love eating giant, crunchy, round matzah.”

“Every Yom Tov is your favorite!” insisted Dovi, who thinks that just because I’m four and he’s seven, he knows everything. “Purim was your favorite because you love eating little, tiny, triangle hamantashen, and Sukkos—”

“Oy, I didn’t even tell you what the Rebbe said in the sicha on Shabbos about matzah. Gevaldig!” interrupted Tatty just in time. “Listen up. In the olden days, the rav of every place would sell Shmura Matzah to the people in his shul, and that way everyone had proper, kosher, mehudar matzah for Pesach. Sadly, this minhag stopped. The Rebbe asked that it should start again—all rabbanim and leaders should send Shmura Matzah to their community members. If there is even one Yid who doesn’t have Shmura Matzah, we should send it to him!”

“Davka Shmura?” asked Mommy as she passed by, carrying a hamper full of stuffed animals to bring to the washing machine.

“Yes. This way, the Rebbe said, hundreds of thousands of Yidden will do the mitzvah properly! Matzah is called the “bread of emunah” and the “bread of healing.” Making sure all Yidden do this mitzvah b’hiddur will make it a healthy year in ruchniyus, which will make it a healthy year in gashmiyus!”

As any seven-year-old like me knows, there are four sons who come to the seder.

Well, anyways, that was until now. The Rebbe just told us that … wait for it … there is a fifth son! This son doesn’t even know it’s Pesach and doesn’t come to the seder at all!

Our task is to make sure to reach out to every Yid who doesn’t know about Pesach, and to make sure they celebrate the Yom Tov.

And that’s what giving out Shmura Matzah is all about! That’s why Yidden in Eretz Yisroel have been giving matzah to soldiers, government people, and not-yet-frum students.

And it’s not just happening in Eretz Yisroel. It’s all over the world!

P.S. I’m even big enough to write in my diary by myself now!

I want to fly to Eretz Yisroel to join in their new “Matzah For Every Student” campaign. Thousands of school kids went on trips to the matzah bakery in Kfar Chabad to experience making matzah, and even got to take a matzah home with them.

Man, that’s even better than a trip to the Yam Hamelach!

The way the Rebbe cares about every single Yid is unbelievable. The Rebbe said in a sicha yesterday that we can’t just be happy with giving out matzah to the people in our communities or to people that we know. The Rebbe said, “As long as there is one single Yid, man or woman, child or adult, in your surroundings— and the meaning of “your surroundings” is the entire world (!)— who does not have Shmura Matzah, or has Shmura Matzah but is unaware of its importance and message, there is no doubt that you must do something about it.” י"ב ניסן, תשל"ז

Remember when I traveled to Kentucky before Pesach when I was 24? My younger cousin Moish is doing something even

more extraordinary—he is going to help Yidden in prisons

The Rebbe said in a sicha yesterday that we can’t forget Yidden who are bedridden in hospitals and old age homes, and, of course, Yidden who are stuck in prisons. We have to help them celebrate Pesach, too. And that in this z’chus, the sick Yidden will get better faster, and the prisoners will get freed earlier! Amen!

Gotta run—I am heading to the mall near my house to give out Shmura Matzah, and then right back home to help my wife with Pesach prep!

My Yitzy is so excited! The Rebbe has launched a massive campaign to get the kids involved in Mivtza Pesach as well! This actually turned into a contest called “The Matzah Ball Contest.”

Involving the kids is so awesome! I wonder what “The Matzah Ball Contest” will lead to next!

(Oy, my toddler just woke up my baby in the middle of her nap! Gotta run!)

Mivtza Lulav

Lulav
Print PDF

It all started when my brother Sholom zoomed into the living room on his roller skates, waving a messy tree branch and a lemon from the fridge. He skidded to a stop right in front of my doll tea party.

“Rina!” he exclaimed, thrusting them toward me. “Here, shake them!”

I blinked at him, flicking a leaf off my toy teapot. “Sholom, it's not Sukkos yet!”

Sholom grinned. “Nope. But I’m just way too excited! The Rebbe has just introduced a completely new idea: to go out and help people bentch lulav and

esrog! All the bochurim in yeshiva are getting ready to go. And I need to practice!”

I tilted my head. “Wait, you’re going to take these to other people?”

“Yep!” he said proudly. “Well, not these,” he laughed, “A real set. We’re going to show Yidden how to make the bracha and shake the arba minim. Isn’t that amazing?”

I felt a little shiver of excitement. “Wow,” I whispered. “The Rebbe really cares about every single Yid.”

P.S. Today, a new girl joined my class. Her name is Ahuva, and she just moved here from somewhere called Vermont. She’s … different. Her uniform isn’t quite right, and during Chumash, she didn’t seem to know where we were up to.

(1953( י״ז תשרי, תשי׳׳ד MOTZEI SHABBOS - 2ND NIGHT OF CHOL HAMOED SUKKOS* Dear Diary,

It’s so late at night, but now that the first days of Sukkos are over, I must tell you about it!

On the first day, Tatty took me and Sholom to do what the Rebbe asked! We walked all over Crown Heights, stopping people on the streets to see if they wanted to bentch lulav. We saw tons of bochurim holding their lulavim too. Some of them were even walking all the way to Brownsville or the Bronx … anywhere a Yid could be found.

Sholom was so brave, running up to people and saying, “Excuse me, would you like to do the mitzvah of lulav and esrog?” At first, I was nervous, but after a while, I joined in. We even knocked on some doors!

Lots of people gave us strange looks. They couldn’t understand why we cared if they did the mitzvah or not.

But other people were very happy to see us. One man told us he hadn’t done the mitzvah since he was a little boy. He went back into his house to put on a yarmulka and wash negel vasser, and then bentched lulav with tears in his eyes.

A lady told me, “Thank you so much for doing this. Please come back every day of Yom Tov!”

After all the walking, asking, and bentching, I went to my class Sukkos party.

Morah taught us that even though the lulav, esrog, hadasim, and aravos are so different from each other, we hold them all together. That is just like the Yidden. We may look different from each other, but we are really all part of one people.

P.S. Ahuva came, which is nice, because she’s been too shy to come to class parties until now. I asked her if she wanted to sit with me. She smiled and said yes.

)1957( י״ז תשרי, תשי׳׳ח MOTZEI SHABBOS - 2ND NIGHT OF CHOL HAMOED SUKKOS* Dear Diary,

Wow, what a Yom Tov this was! It’s already 10:30 at night, but I have so much to tell you.

I can’t believe it’s been four years since the Rebbe first introduced Mivtza Arba Minim. Now that Sholom and I are older, we even joined Tatty yesterday when he went to bentch lulav with the patients and Jewish doctors at the hospital, just like the Rebbe wants.

Mivtza Recruitment

Tzivos Hashem
Print PDF

So, today I flew on a dreidel to Alaska for a giant menorah lighting!

But what I do have to tell you is way more exciting than that! Today, I went to a Chanukah rally! Wait, what am I saying? It was a military parade! (That’s more like it.) And our General, the Rebbe, gave us an important mission.

I don’t know how much you know about armies, dear diary, so I’ll tell you: In an army, if there’s ever a special goal that you need to accomplish, then you must recruit more soldiers. In Hashem’s army, the usual goal is to learn more Torah and do mitzvos extra carefully, but now, we have a special goal from our Commander-in-Chief, Hashem: To bring Moshiach now!!! (Hence, the new song that I can’t stop singing!)

Anyways, to help with this special mission, Hashem is sending reinforcements—more Yiddishe boys and girls—to join us in our fight with our super-strong weapons: the Torah and mitzvos!

It is not enough to simply fight in this war. I must mobilize more kids to volunteer and join the ranks of Tzivos Hashem. Boys drafting boys, girls drafting girls. There is no time to waste. And we need everyone to join in!

Together with the Rebbe leading the way, we will win the fight against the Yetzer Hara and bring Moshiach now!

P.S. Surprise! The Rebbe requested a totally unexpected rally on Chof-Ches Tishrei, and Rabbi JJ Hecht taught our army our anthem (every army has an official song called an “anthem”).

It goes: “Am Yisroel have no fear, Moshiach will be here this year! We want Moshiach now! We don’t want to wait!”

Of course I can’t stop singing it! The Rebbe likes it very much, and even explained today that it’s perfect for our mission!

But why does Shulamis keep telling me to be quiet? Doesn’t she love my singing?

Mivtzoim—they feel like they’ve been around forever! Can you even imagine life without them? Yet, unbelievably, before the Rebbe introduced each of the mitzvah campaigns that we know so well, they simply didn’t exist.

Join us as we explore imaginary old diaries that could have belonged to kids just like you— kids who might have lived during the time when the Rebbe first announced many of these mivtzoim.

It might have been written over 40 years ago, but after you dust off the cover of Zeidy Tzvi’s old diary and take a peek inside, you'll be transported back in time, living the exciting beginnings of Tzivos Hashem for yourself_right here, right now.

Never before have I felt so proud to be a soldier in the strongest army in the world!

Standing at attention with my fellow soldiers while listening to the Rebbe, our General, speaking to us was unreal. We are unstoppable!

In fact, when a boy was blocking me from seeing the podium, I didn’t pour water down his back. No siree! I pleasantly said “excuse me”, and felt my Yetzer Hara shrink away.

The Rebbe spoke about having a “soldier specialty”, which means a specific mission that you’re really good at, more than anything else. Guess what our soldier specialty is? Nope, not being a pilot—I’m scared of heights. And also no, definitely not sea battles! I would totally throw up.

Learning Torah is our specialty! We need to learn Torah so much that it becomes a part of us! And then, what’s the point of the learning? To help us do mitzvos! (Yeah, far better than jumping out of planes in parachutes.)

And the Rebbe made it clear: We’re not just here for ourselves. We need to expand our ranks.

I’m fired up! I already know which Tanya and mishnayos I’ll learn, and I have a full list of kids to recruit. Victory is in sight!

P.S. I will never need encouragement to do my Gemara chazara again. After all, Torah is my specialty! (And I think my mother is sighing with relief.)

If you’re wondering why there are green smudges on this page, it’s because I had some green face paint on my face so I could really get into that soldier mode, and then there was a fly, and … okay, that’s enough information.

Now, there are three things that need to be completed in this world: 1) My homework, 2) My homework, and 3) My homework.

Okay, that’s it for the Adar jokes, ladies and gentlemen. For real, now.

Elul

Elul
Print PDF

and know that it’s their final chance to get on. They can still yell out to him, and he’ll stop the train. Once the conductor sees that no one is trying to get on, he speeds up the train and begins the journey for good.

The same thing happens for us Yidden every year during Chodesh Elul. We want to make sure that everyone will be ready for Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur! So, we blow the shofar to let everyone know that it is time to get ready, just like the conductor blows his whistle.

We blow every day, again and again, giving us all many reminders to prepare to crown Hashem as king. Then comes Rosh Hashana. The train starts leaving the station. But even then, the “train” moves slowly. After Rosh Hashana, we still have a chance to do teshuva until Yom Kippur. And even after Yom Kippur, there's still another chance through rejoicing and dancing on Sukkos, Shmini Atzeres, & Simchas Torah!

We want to make sure that every Yid is written and sealed for a good, sweet new year!

Did you know that Chodesh Elul is kind of like a train departing from the station?

When it gets ready to leave for a long trip, the conductor wants to make sure that all of the passengers get on in time and nobody is left behind. So, with the help of his whistle, he lets everyone know that the train is preparing to leave.

the conductor blows his whistle. Hopefully, passengers will hear it and will be sure to board the train quickly. Every few minutes, the conductor whistles again. He whistles and whistles, giving everyone a chance to get on so they won’t miss the train.

When it’s finally time to go, the conductor doesn’t just zoom out of the station. He starts moving the train slowly. That way, anyone who might have been waiting until the last minute will see the train leaving,

Chodesh Elul is a special time. All over the world, Yidden spend this month preparing to crown Hashem as

King on Rosh Hashana. And as Lubavitcher chassidim,

The Tzemach Tzedek once said that if we knew how powerful the pesukim of Tehillim are, we would never stop saying them!

During the 40 days of Elul and Aseres Yemei Teshuva, we add extra Tehillim so that we finish the whole sefer. Every day, we say three kapitelach after shacharis. (By the time we reach Yom Kippur, we are left with 36 kapitelach which we say throughout that holy Yom Tov.) If you miss a day, first skip ahead to the kapitelach of the current day, and only then go back to say the ones that you missed.

We hear the shofar every day of Chodesh Elul, besides for Shabbos and Erev Rosh Hashana.

The first day of Rosh Chodesh (Lammed Menachem Av) is just for practice. After that, from Alef Elul and on, shofar is blown each day after saying the three special kapitelach.

Many other Yidden blow just four blasts during Chodesh Elul. Minhag Chabad is to blow a full set of ten blasts. Here’s how it’s done: First—Teki’ah, Shevarim, Teru’ah, Teki’ah. Next—Teki’ah, Shevarim, Teki’ah. Then—Teki’ah, Teru’ah, Teki’ah. These ten blasts represent the ten kochos of our neshama. We want our whole neshama to prepare for Rosh Hashana!

Further Reading: Hayom Yom 27 & 30 Menachem-Av, and 1 Elul; Likkutei Sichos vol. 2, p. 446;

Sefer Hasichos 5748 vol 2, p. 610; Toras Menachem vol. 77, pp. 175-177.

“לְדָוִד ה' אֹורִי” is the 27th kapitel of Tehillim. This kapitel is connected to Elul because it speaks about how Hashem is important and dear to us like the light of our lives. It also has hints to the Yomim Tovim of Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur, and Sukkos hidden within it. We say this special kapital during shacharis (as part of Shir Shel Yom, before Ein Kelokeinu) and mincha (before Aleinu), starting from the first day of Rosh Chodesh Elul until Hoshana Rabba.

Since Elul is a time to check our behavior, it’s also a good time to check the things we use for mitzvos. Minhag Chabad is to have our tefillin and mezuzos checked in Elul. Doing so brings more brachos for the coming year.

When the Rebbe first announced that we should check them every year, some people were confused. Shulchan Aruch says that mezuzos need to be checked once every seven years!

The Rebbe explained: Sadly, there are people today who buy tefillin and mezuzos without being careful about what’s inside. Some might contain printed paper instead of handwritten parchment, and some might not have the right pesukim! And even if everything is good, ink nowadays doesn’t last so long. So, it’s very important to have our tefillin and mezuzos checked every year, and help others do the same. Ask your parents if they’ve done it yet, too!

Elul is a time to think. We make a Cheshbon Hanefesh, thinking about all the things that we did in the past year. We think about what we did well and about what we want to do better. This way, we can clean up our mistakes and come to Rosh Hashana freshly prepared to crown Hashem as our King!

Chodesh Elul is such a special time that we even have a special way to greet each other! We wish each other a “ּכְתִיבָה וַחַתִימָה טֹובָה לְׁשָנָה טֹובָה ּומְתּוקָה—that we should be written and sealed by Hashem for a good and sweet new year.” The Rebbe tells us that our brachos to each other during Elul are very powerful, and can help give everyone everything they need in the coming year.

Lived this Yom Tov like a chayol

Yamim Tovim

Yamim Tovim
Print PDF

It was the year תרכ”ה (1865). Four-year-old Reb Shalom Dovber (who grew up to become the Rebbe Rashab) and his older brother, Reb Zalman Aharon, were talking about their Acharon shel Pesach memories.

Reb Shalom Dovber asked his brother, “Do you remember Birchas Kohanim? Do you remember kissing Zeidy, the Tzemach Tzedek’s, tzitzis?”

“Yes!” Reb Zalman Aharon replied, “…it was time for Birchas Kohanim. We were standing near Tatty, and Zeidy motioned for us to come closer to him. We went to Zeidy’s chair and were covered with his tallis. Zeidy followed the pesukim of Birchas Kohanim in the siddur with his finger, and answered the three ‘ameins’ out loud. After davening, Zeidy called me over and allowed me to kiss the tzitzis of his tallis, and then he called you over to kiss them, too!”

As Chabad chassidim, we are very proud of our special

minhagim! There are Chassidishe minhagim for every day of the year, and even more when Yomim Tovim come around! Many of them are specific to a particular Yom Tov,

but some are shayach for every Yom Tov: The unique way that We do Birchas Kohanim, going

on tahalucha, and having special farbrengens. Let’s

One of the most exciting parts of Yom Tov davening is Birchas Kohanim. Our minhag is that all children go under an adult’s tallis during this time, so that we don’t look at the kohanim’s faces while they say these holy brachos.

We also have a special niggun from the Mitteler Rebbe’s Kapelye that the chazzan and kohanim sing before each word. We listen quietly and say “amein” after each of the three brachos.

While the kohanim are singing the niggun before the words “וְיָׂשֵם”, “לְָך“ and “שָׁלֹום”, (but not while they are saying them), we add a special tefillah. This special tefillah is divided into three parts—one for each time the niggun is sung before these words. The Tzemach Tzedek learned about this minhag when he was under the Alter Rebbe’s tallis for Birchas Kohanim, and then he told others about it, too.

These brachos from the kohanim are very powerful and special. Many people even bring their young babies to hear them! Birchas Kohanim takes place during musaf every day of Yom Tov: on Rosh Hashana (Hachayol Issue 621), Yom Kippur (Issue 622) , Sukkos (Issue 623), Shmini Atzeres (Issue 624), Simchas Torah—during shacharis (Issue 624), Pesach (Issue 648) and Shavuos (Issue 656).

Have you ever heard of the mitzvah to walk? That’s right! Walking can sometimes be a mitzvah! For example, it’s a mitzvah to walk to shul for davening, and that’s for all Yidden to do. But we Chabad chassidim have another “walking mitzvah” which happens only three times a year. Can you guess? It’s when we go on tahalucha!

Tahalucha means “a grand march”. Chassidim go on tahalucha on Simchas Torah, Acharon shel Pesach, and the second night of Shavuos. We march to other shuls to bring them extra Yom Tov joy and share with them a vort of the Rebbe’s Torah.

The minhag to go on tahalucha started on Shavuos תשט”ו (1955). That year, Tzeirei Agudas Chabad arranged for some chassidim to go to nearby shuls and say a D’var Torah. At the farbrengen later that day, the Rebbe was very happy. The Rebbe even added that he was jealous of anyone who went! He said l’chaim with them and gave them brachos. From then on, it has become a set minhag.

The Rebbe emphasizes that the steps we take on tahalucha are holy. Therefore, we should take as many of them as possible. The farther we walk, the better! We march with simcha, knowing that each step brings more brachos, more z’chuyos, and more honor.

Some people indeed walk very long distances for tahalucha. For example, if they’re leaving from Crown Heights, they won’t return to 770 until very late at night! This gives the Rebbe tremendous nachas. In fact, in some years, after all of the chassidim had joyously marched back from far-away tahaluchas, the Rebbe himself stood at the steps of 770 to encourage the late-night singing! One year, in א”תנש (1991), the Rebbe did something very unusual. In addition to encouraging the singing, the Rebbe said a short sicha for the tahalucha goers right there on the steps! This happened twice in that same year—once on Acharon shel Pesach, and again on the second night of Shavuos.

Tahalucha isn’t just for fathers or older bochurim. It’s for everyone, from the oldest to the youngest. As children, we chayolim have a special part in the mitzvah of tahalucha. When we visit other Yidden, we can bring extra simcha to them. Make sure to join the tahalucha this Simchas Torah (Hachayol Issue 623), Acharon shel Pesach (Issue 648), and the second night of Shavuos (Issue 656), and bring Chassidishe joy to the Yidden around you!

Further Reading: Toras Menachem vol. 14, p. 119; Toras Menachem vol. 36, pp. 303-304;

There is a special Chabad minhag to hold a farbrengen at the end of each Yom Tov.

At the farbrengen, we sing a niggun from each Rebbe and somebody explains a maamar Chassidus. The farbrengen lasts until Yom Tov is over, followed by maariv right after bentching. We make sure to use the time of the special day for extra singing and Divrei Torah.

When you attend the farbrengen in your city, use your special ko’ach as a chayol to sing with lebedikeit and listen closely to the maamar. Remember, even if you don't understand the maamar, your neshama understands it!

These farbrengens will take place on the second day of Rosh Hashana (Hachayol Issue 621), Simchas Torah (Issue 624), Acharon Shel Pesach (Issue 649), and the second day of Shavuos (Issue 655). Let’s all be there, and give our neshamos this opportunity to enjoy the holy words of Chassidus.

Lived this Yom Tov like a chayol

Rosh Hashana

the army at a very young age. Many of them only knew how to say Tehillim by heart, and had been reciting it while they polished their buttons.

The Tzemach Tzedek told them: “We polish buttons with sand and water, and we polish our neshamos with sand and water, as well. The sand is the words of Tehillim, and the water is the tears we shed while saying them. When saying Tehillim with tears, we polish our neshamos.”

Rosh Hashana is an appropriate time for all of us to polish our neshamos with lots of Tehillim.

The Tzemach Tzedek once traveled to a group of Jewish soldiers called “Cantonistim” who had been drafted into the Russian Army. They were so excited for the Rebbe’s visit that they arranged a whole parade for him!

One of the soldiers came over to the Rebbe, crying. He said, “Rebbe, we polished our buttons for you. Now, please polish our neshamos!”

The Tzemach Tzedek looked around at these special soldiers. They had all been ripped away from their homes and forced into

It’s always important to greet other people with nice words, but on Rosh Hashana, it is actually a minhag. It’s even written about in the machzor! We have a special greeting—to a boy or man, say: “וְתֵחָתֵם לְׁשָנָה טֹובָה ּתִּכָתֵב”, and to a girl or woman, say: “וְתֵחָתֵמִי לְׁשָנָה טֹובָה ּתִּכָתֵבִי”. They both mean, “May you be written and sealed for a good and sweet year!”

When we say this to each other, even the malachim are excited to hear it. The Tzemach Tzedek said that when the two malachim hear us bentching our fellow Yid with a good and sweet year, they go up to Shamayim and demand that Hashem bentch us with a good and sweet year, as well!

Rosh Hashana is the special Yom Tov when we crown Hashem as King. We chassidim have our own minhagim

for this holy time: We write a Pan to the Rebbe before

Yom Tov, say a specific bracha when bentching licht, and are sure to wish each other “L’shana tova” at night.

We also have a special way of dipping the apple in honey, blowing the shofar, and doing Tashlich. So many

One of the most important ways that a chayol prepares for the new year is by writing a נֶפֶׁש ּפִדְיֹון, called a “נ”ַפּ”, to the Rebbe. A Pan is not just a letter. It is a way to express the deep neshama-connection between a chossid and a Rebbe. In a Pan, we ask the Rebbe to daven to Hashem for us.

We try our best to bring our Pan to the Ohel in person, but if we can’t, we make sure to send it in time for Rosh Hashana. Before writing a Pan, men put on a gartel, and everyone thinks carefully about what they want to tell the Rebbe.

Rosh Hashana is not just any Yom Tov. It is the day when we crown Hashem as King, and remind Him of our special bris with Him.

As Chabad chassidim, we declare how special Rosh Hashana is as soon as it begins—right when we bentch licht!

Many Yidden say “לְהַדְלִיק נֵר ׁשֶל יֹום טֹוב—to light the candle of Yom Tov,” but the Rebbe explains that our minhag is to say “לְהַדְלִיק נֵר ׁשֶל יֹום הַזִּכָרֹון—to light the candle of the Day of Remembering,” specifically mentioning one of Rosh Hashana’s special names. By doing this, we help the ko’ach of the day come down and be revealed even more!

Have you ever seen a courtroom? It is a serious place where everyone sits quietly, waiting for the judge to decide the ruling. Rosh Hashana is like the court case for the whole world, and so it is a serious time. It’s so serious that some Chabad chassidim are careful not to talk at all for the entire Rosh Hashana! The minhag of our Rebbeim was mainly not to talk throughout the first night of Rosh Hashana.

But we don’t just sit quietly doing nothing. Instead of talking, we say Tehillim. We try to fill every spare moment of Rosh Hashana with these holy words. The Frierdiker Rebbe encouraged all chassidim to sleep less and spend more time learning Torah and saying Tehillim. We make sure to add at least a little extra time saying Tehillim on this holy and serious day.

What’s your favorite part of the Rosh Hashana meal? For many people, it’s the apple dipped in honey!

Our minhag is to dip the apple in honey right after kiddush. We say the bracha of “Ha’eitz”, and then, before taking a bite, we add, “יְהִי רָצֹון מִלְפָנֶיָך ׁשֶּתְחַדֵש עָלֵינּו ׁשָנָה טֹובָה ּומְתּוקָה—May it be Your will [Hashem] that the new year be good and sweet for us.”

Many people have the minhag to say the Yehi Ratzon after first eating some of the apple. The Alter Rebbe even says to do that in his Shulchan Aruch! But in Hayom Yom, the Rebbe notes that we say it before eating, and explains in a letter that this causes the Yehi Ratzon to become part of the bracha itself. You see, a bracha has more power to make things actually happen in this world than a Yehi Ratzon does. So, by including the Yehi Ratzon in the bracha of “Ha’eitz”, we give it the same super-power as a bracha, making sure that our new year will be good and sweet for sure!

Whenever children come to shul and answer “אָמֵן” and “יְהֵא ׁשְמֵי'ה רַּבָה”, powerful malachim are created. But the Rebbe says that on Rosh Hashana, it’s even more powerful and important to do so! Precious Yiddishe children saying these words with the minyan can tip the scales of Hashem’s judgment, and bring a good year to the entire world.

Let’s be sure to come to shul and answer “amein” loudly and clearly!

Celebrate Like A Chayol

Yom Kippur

Yom Kippur
Print PDF

Erev Yom Kippur was a very serious time for the Rebbe Rashab. He would wake up early and finish his seudah before 12:00 p.m., so he could say extra Tehillim.

The year תרמ”ח or תרמ”ט (1887 or 1888) was like any other. As usual, the Rebbe Rashab woke up early, and was soon sitting with a sefer in his study. Then, there was a knock at the door, and in walked the chossid Reb Zalman from Cherbin. He boomed out in a cheerful voice, “Rebbe! Gut Yom Tov!”

The Rebbe Rashab replied solemnly, “It is true that today is a Yom Tov, but we must use the day to do teshuva and make hachlatos. It is a serious time.”

Reb Zalman responded, “Rebbe, we are soldiers. Erev Yom Kippur is a Yom Tov, and we are commanded by Hashem to be happy on Yom Tov. So, as soldiers of Hashem, our mission today is to do our avodah with joy.

The Rebbe Rashab was very happy with Reb Zalman’s answer, and handed him a piece of lekach.

The holiest time of the year is coming! As chayolim, Erev Yom Kippur and Yom Kippur are full of special minhagim.

Erev Yom Kippur starts early with kaparos. Then, we ask for lekach and receive brachos from our parents. On Yom

Kippur itself, we completely skip the bracha of ”“ׁשֶעָשָׂה לִי ּכָל צָרְּכִי and sing a special niggun right before the

end of the fast. Let’s learn about these minhagei Chabad!

Erev Yom Kippur starts early in the morning with kaparos. (This minhag can also be done throughout Aseres Yemei Teshuva.) Boys take a male chicken and girls take a female chicken. We wave the chicken over our heads, and say the tefillah of “זֶה חֲלִיפָתִי” for males, and “זֹאת חֲלִיפָתִי” for females. Then, the chicken is shechted and given to the poor. We hope that by giving it to tzedakah, it will help to bring us a kapara for our aveiros.

Kaparos is a minhag done with seriousness and care. The Rebbe would hold his chicken very gently and with both hands, so as not to hurt it, chas v’shalom.

Kaparos is also a chance to do a mitzvah that doesn’t come up very often, called “ּכִיסּוי הַדָם”. We take some dirt, cover the blood of the chicken that was shechted, and make a special bracha.

What’s the sweetest way to prepare for Yom Kippur? With lekach (honey cake), of course!

Our minhag is to ask someone on Erev Yom Kippur to give us lekach. The Rebbe himself would stand and give out lekach for hours on this holy day. It’s explained that the person giving out lekach is a shliach of Hashem. This means that the lekach doesn’t just come from them, but from Hashem Himself!

Do you know why we are davka supposed to ask for lekach, and not just take it? That’s because this minhag of asking for lekach isn’t just about getting honey cake. It’s for a very deep reason: If Hashem decreed that we are supposed to beg for tzedakah this year, we want the request for lekach on Erev Yom Kippur to fulfill this gezeira, leaving us with no need to ask or beg for anything else in the coming year.

When the Baal Shem Tov would give out lekach, he would say: “I am giving you lekach, and Hashem should give you a good, sweet year!”

Erev Yom Kippur is also a time when fathers give brachos to their children, known as “Birchas Habanim”. And so, each year before Kol Nidrei, the Rebbe would give these special brachos to his children: the Temimim.

This minhag began in תשי”ב )1951(, the first Yom Kippur of the Rebbe’s Nesius. The Rebbe asked that the bochurim gather in his room and told them, “Since you are learning in the Rebbe’s yeshiva, you are the Rebbe’s children!” The Rebbe bentched them with the regular Birchas Habanim, and added a bracha for hatzlacha in their learning with Yiras Shamayim.

We, as chayolim of Tzivos Hashem, are also the Rebbe’s children. We, too, surely receive these special brachos and special kochos to make the Rebbe proud!

One of the happiest moments of Yom Kippur is at the end of the day, during the last kaddish of Ne’ila. Right before we blow the shofar to signal the end of Yom Kippur, our minhag is to sing a special niggun called “Napoleon’s March”.

Napoleon’s March is a tune that the French Army used to sing as they marched off to battle. When the Alter Rebbe heard the tune, he said: “This is a niggun of victory!” Since then, it has become a Chabad niggun.

In תרנ”ט (1898), the Rebbe Rashab asked to sing this niggun during Ne’ila. From then on, it has become our minhag to do so every year. It is always sung with great chayus and joy. In the early years, the Rebbe would jump onto his chair to encourage the singing! People from shuls all around Crown Heights would come to 770 for Ne’ila so they could experience the powerful moment of Napoleon’s March.

After such a serious day, why do we immediately switch to such simcha? It’s because we are confident that our Yom Kippur avodah was successful, and we are all going to have a good year. So of course, we sing and dance with the greatest joy as we get ready for the second part of Tishrei: Z’man Simchaseinu!

There is a bracha in birchos hashachar that we skip on Yom Kippur. Do you know which one it is?

Mission
Lived this Yom Tov like a chayol

Sukkos

Sukkos
Print PDF

It was the year תד”ש )1944(, during World War Two. Things were finally looking better—America had just conquered Italy from the Nazis, yimach shemam! But they still had much to do, and so the war raged on.

At this time, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote a letter to the American government, asking them to get him a Calabria esrog for Sukkos. The Frierdiker Rebbe understood very well that the government was extremely busy—especially while at war!—and only asked because it was so important.

What a powerful lesson we can learn from this story! Using Calabria esrogim is not just a “nice thing”, but truly a necessary minhag.

It’s time to celebrate the Yom Tov of Sukkos! Of course, there are many minhagim for this joyous time. We use a special type of esrog and perform the mitzvah of “living

in the sukkah” in our own way. Every night of Sukkos, we are visited by Chassidishe Ushpizin and celebrate Simchas Beis Hasho’eiva. There are even minhagim for

bentching lulav and esrog. Let’s learn all about them. Calabria

Hashem first gave the mitzvah of arba minim when the Yidden were in the midbar. So, Moshe Rabbeinu sent messengers to find the best esrogim. After traveling around, they found the most mehudar esrogim in Calabria, an area in Italy.

Since that’s where Moshe Rabbeinu’s esrogim came from, Chabad chassidim are careful to use Calabria esrogim, as well (also called “Yanover esrogim”, the name of the port city).

As you walk into a sukkah, you could probably tell right away if it’s a Chabad sukkah or not. Just look around!

You see, many Yidden work hard to decorate their sukkahs with all sorts of beautiful decorations. Minhag Chabad, though, is not to decorate our sukkah. The Rebbe writes in a letter that it’s because the sukkah walls themselves are special. We want to notice and appreciate their kedusha and beauty without covering them over with decorations.

Additionally, the Baal Shem Tov said that his sukkah decorations were the Yidden who stepped inside. With their emunah and kabbalas ol, they brought joy to Shamayim and made his sukkah beautiful.

So, this year, think about the beauty of your special sukkah—complete with plain walls and many precious Yidden!

Although many Yidden have the custom to sleep in the sukkah, Chabad chassidim specifically don’t sleep in the sukkah.

We have this minhag because the sukkah is too holy for sleeping! Once, the Mitteler Rebbe was told that some of the younger chassidim were sleeping in the sukkah. The Mitteler Rebbe was shocked. “How can they sleep in the sukkah? The energy of ‘makif d’bina’ (a very high level of Elokus) is there!

“When a person is awake, he is in control of himself; but while sleeping, he’s not. So how can someone be in a place of makif d’bina when he’s not in control?”

As chayolim, we are mekushar to the Rebbe. If the Rebbe feels the great holiness of the sukkah and therefore cannot allow himself to sleep there, we chassidim don’t sleep there, either.

When was the happiest time in the Beis Hamikdash? Simchas Beis Hasho’eiva! Throughout the year, when the daily karbanos were brought, the kohanim poured wine on the Mizbei’ach. But on Sukkos, they also poured water. And getting (or “drawing”) this water was done with tremendous joy. Each night of Sukkos, before drawing the water, the Yidden held massive celebrations. Huge torches were lit, Levi’im played happy music, and great chachamim juggled fire. Everybody danced all night long. These celebrations are called “ׂשִמְחַת ּבֵית הָהַׁשֹואֵב—The Celebration of the House of Drawing [Water].” But when the Beis Hamikdash was destroyed, Simchas Beis Hasho’eiva was not what it used to be. That is, until the Rebbe reintroduced it with a shturem! On Sukkos תשמ”א )1980(, the Rebbe explained that even today, Simchas Beis Hasho’eiva is a time for great joy. We should be so freilech that our joy “spills out onto the streets”! That night, chassidim danced in the streets of Crown Heights. The same thing happened the next night. And the next! Since then, Chabad chassidim have danced every night of Sukkos, and thousands of others join in—just like the Yidden in the Beis Hamikdash!

Although we don’t sleep in the sukkah, we spend every possible moment there— even when we don’t have to. According to halacha, only important foods and drinks must be eaten in the sukkah, while snacks and water can be enjoyed anywhere. But our minhag is to be extra strict: Men and boys don’t eat or drink anything outside the sukkah—no matter the weather.

Rain or shine, and even if it’s pouring buckets outside, Chabad chassidim only eat in the sukkah. We do the same on Shmini Atzeres, when eating in the sukkah is a minhag, not a mitzvah.

The Sukkah is so holy that we can’t imagine eating anywhere else, even if it means getting soaked! Arba Minim

Picking up a lulav and esrog is not so simple. You might do the mitzvah without realizing it—just by holding them together! See, the mitzvah is not to shake the lulav and esrog, but to hold them together. So, if someone has already held them together, they can no longer make the bracha that day. We want to say the bracha each time we do the mitzvah, so we pick them up carefully. First, we lift the lulav in our main (right) hand and say the bracha, “עַל נְטִילַת לּולָב”. Then, with the other hand, we lift the esrog. On the first day of Sukkos, we keep them apart a bit longer and say “ׁשֶהֶחֱי ָנּו”. Then, we put them together and shake three times in each direction. Right, left, forward; up, down, backwards. Our minhag is to keep the lulav upright and bring the arba minim to our heart after each shake. We also make sure to share our arba minim with others. The Rebbe’s esrog would turn brown from so many chassidim using it, and this brought the Rebbe much joy. “There is no esrog more beautiful than one used by many Yidden,” he wrote. This year, let’s get out there and share our esrogim with as many Yidden as possible. Onwards to mivtzoim!

It was pouring rain one Sukkos in Lubavitch, and the Temimim went to eat in the sukkah anyway. When the Rebbe Rashab was told that they were sitting in the sukkah during the downpour, putting their jackets over their heads for protection, he happily noted, “The spirit of Tomchei Temimim has affected them.”

Further Reading: Toras Menachem vol. 4, pp. 33-35; Sefer Haminhagim p. 65; Igros Kodesh Admur M’horayatz vol. 8, p. 411; Igros Kodesh vol. 16,

p. 153 (Letter of 7 Cheshvan, 5715); Sefer Hasichos 5699 p. 295; Sefer Hasichos 5706 p. 3;

Shimini Atzeres

Shimini Atzeres
Print PDF

On Simchas Torah morning, malachim have extra time. You see, on this day, minyanim start later, because Yidden normally sleep in. They’re exhausted from all the dancing. But malachim wake up early just like any other day, ready to praise Hashem. The problem is, they can only do so when there are Yidden awake and praising Hashem. And on Simchas Torah morning, the Yidden are all sleeping! So, the malachim must wait. One Simchas Torah, they decided to spend this time cleaning up Gan Eiden. To their utter surprise, the malachim found strange objects there: Shoes! Worn-out and tattered shoes. Piles and piles of them. This left the malachim very confused. In Gan Eiden, there’s often tzitzis, maybe tefillin—but shoes?! So off they went to ask Malach Michoel what this was about. He happily replied, “Ah! This is my merchandise!” He explained to the puzzled malachim that these shoes were from the previous night, worn by Yidden who danced and danced. They danced so much that their shoes got completely worn out. And these holy, tattered shoes flew straight up to Gan Eiden. “These,” he pointed to one pile, “are from the village of Kaminka. “Those,” he said, pointing to another, “are from Mezritch. All are among the most cherished items in Shamayim.” The Baal Shem Tov concluded, “And with that, Malach Michoel proudly crafts a spectacular crown for Hashem—from the tattered shoes worn out from Simchas Torah dancing!”

Torah. But do you know what else it means? It also means “on credit”. Credit is when you buy something now and pay for it later. During Hakafos, Hashem lets us “buy” brachos for the whole year and “pay Him back” later, so they are a special time to ask Him for what we need.

How old does a boy have to be to get an aliyah to the Torah? You guessed it: Thirteen! But on Simchas Torah, all boys—even tiny babies!—get an aliyah, too! This aliya, called “ָּל הַּנְעָרִים”, is given to one adult along with all the boys.

We make sure to kiss the gartel, say the brachos loudly and clearly, and listen closely to the kriah. Many shuls spread out a tallis over all of the boys, and say “הַמַלְאְָך הַגֹאֵל” afterwards. Although it’s not Minhag Chabad to do these two things, the Rebbe said that they are indeed good inyanim. At Lubavitcher shuls, they are not done b’gashmiyus, but they are accomplished in a ruchniyus way.

Further Reading: Sefer Haminhagim p. 68; Sefer Hasichos 5694 p. 262; Sefer Hasichos 5695 pp. 489-490; Toras Sholom p. 54;

Sefer Hasichos 5701 pp. 31-32; Toras Menachem vol. 18, p. 80; Ibid. vol. 38, p. 152; Ibid. vol. 41 pp. 145-148.

There is something special that we do on both Shmini Atzeres and Simchas Torah. In fact, it’s something that we spend hours doing! Can you guess what it is? That’s right—dancing!

On this Yom Tov, all Yidden dance together. Whether we are young or old and whether we know lots of Torah or just a little, we dance as one. This is because the Torah is for all of us, no matter who we are.

We also show this by dancing with Sifrei Torah that are all wrapped up in their mantel. On this special Yom Tov, it’s not about who can open up the Torah and learn it better. It’s about the fact that Torah is our life. And for that, we are all equal.

We dance and dance with the Torah, bursting with joy that we are connected to it. And while dancing, keep in mind: Yes, we are happy with the Torah, but is the Torah happy with us? Is the Torah satisfied with our avodah? Think of a hachlata that you can take in limmud Torah this year.

When we dance, the Torah is so happy that it wants to dance, too! But it doesn’t have feet to dance with. Instead, we get to be the Torah’s feet! So, we dance with the Torah and we dance for the Torah.

Have you ever thought of what this dancing accomplishes? The Rebbe Rashab said that every moment of dancing on Shmini Atzeres and Simchas Torah brings down bucketfuls of treasures from Hashem, in both gashmiyus and ruchniyus.

Additonally, dancing on Simchas Torah is so powerful that it causes the Satan to hide in shame. Whenever he tries to say something not good about the Yidden, the malachim exclaim, “Look at them! They bring the whole family to shul just to dance with the Torah!” When the Satan hears this, he has nothing else to say. Case closed.

On these special days, let’s chap arayn and rejoice with the Torah with all our might! After all, there’s nothing that can get in our way now!

There's a special tefillah called “תְּפִלַת גֶשֶׁם” that we add during Chazaras Hashatz of musaf on Shmini Atzeres. It’s said after we have switched to “מֵשִׁיב הָרּוחַ ּומֹורִיד הַגֶּשֶׁם” in the quiet musaf, praising Hashem for sending rain at the right time.

Some Yidden don’t say anything else in this spot of Shemoneh Esrei throughout the summer, so if they miss “mashiv haru’ach”, Shemoneh Esrei is repeated. But since in our nusach we say “מֹורִיד הַטָל” during the summer, if we forget to say “mashiv haru’ach”, we don’t repeat Shemoneh Esrei again.

In many places around the world, there’s no need to ask for rain. In Mitzrayim, for instance, the Nilus overflows and waters the fields without the farmers doing anything. In Eretz Yisroel, however, the rain doesn’t just come automatically. We must daven for it.

This might seem like a bother, but it’s actually a good thing!

Davening for rain reminds us that Hashem is the One in charge, and everything in our lives comes from Him. But some things are obviously from Hashem, and other things are not. Hashem makes the Nilus overflow, but He doesn’t do it in a direct way. He makes it happen through the Mitzrim’s Sar (malach) in Shamayim. Therefore, the Mitzri farmers get everything they need through their Sar, without needing to daven to Hashem.

Imagine your parents hired a babysitter for a few days. They might tell the babysitter to take you to the park or pizza shop, or to do other fun things that you don’t normally do. You have a blast with the babysitter, but you’re much happier when your parents return home. Why is that? Wouldn’t you rather have the fun babysitter take care of you all the time? The answer is, of course, because no matter how nice the babysitter is, they can’t compare to the deep love and connection you have with your parents.

The same is with Hashem. He is our Father Who loves us deeply and always wants our connection.

The Mitzrim (and all other nations), l’havdil, are taken care of by Hashem’s “babysitters”, so it looks like they have it better. We Yidden must daven for what we need and want—but it’s because we’re with our Father.

And now, as we prepare to bring Tishrei’s ko’ach into everyday life, we ask Hashem to “rain down” our gashmiyus needs.

Surely, He’ll send it happily and plentifully, as a loving Father does.

Celebrate Like A Chayol

Channukah

Channukah
Print PDF

When to Light Halacha says that the menorah must burn for at least half an hour into the night. Many Yidden have the custom to light after ma’ariv, when it is already nighttime, so they just need enough oil or wax to burn for half an hour. But minhag Chabad is to light the menorah before ma’ariv. So, we make sure that the lights last for at least 50 minutes—20 minutes before nighttime and 30 minutes afterwards. On Erev Shabbos, everyone lights the menorah even earlier—after mincha, before Shabbos candles. So, we make sure that the menorah can stay lit for about 90 minutes: until nightfall begins, and for the full half hour afterwards.

The Menorah Itself If you’ve seen menorahs on coins or on shul walls, you’ve probably noticed that the branches are curved. But have you ever seen the menorah in 770? It has straight branches. That’s on purpose. You see, many people think that the menorah in the Beis Hamikdash had curved branches, but the Rambam and others teach us that they were straight (though only seven, of course). For this reason, Chabad Chassidim are careful that the branches on our menorahs are also straight and not curved.

While many Yidden light their menorahs in a window, minhag Chabad is to light it in a doorway in the center of the house—on the left side, opposite the mezuzah, so we are surrounded by mitzvos! This is how the Rebbeim did it, so this is how we chassidim do it, too.

Once the menorah is lit, we sit nearby and don’t do any work for at least half an hour (especially women and girls). The minhag of the Rebbeim was to learn Torah near the licht. This is because the Yevanim tried to stop us from learning Hashem’s Torah, so when we sit and learn davka near the menorah, we show that we’ve won!

Halalu Some Yidden say Haneiros Halalu as soon as the first light is lit, but our minhag is to wait until we’ve lit all of the lights for that night. Our tune comes from chassidim of the Rebbe Maharash. The Rebbeim would face the menorah while saying these words, and we should, too.

One night of Chanukah many years ago, Ephraim Piekarski was playing dreidel with his friend in the hallway of 770. Suddenly, the door swung open. It was the Rebbe.

He walked over to them and said, “I also want to play.”

Ephraim and his friend stared at the Rebbe in shock and didn’t answer. The Rebbe took a dime from his pocket, put it in the game pile, and told one of the boys to spin for him.

The dreidel landed on a “hey”. The Rebbe smiled, “Really, I could take half the pile, but I will leave it for you.” Then, the Rebbe continued walking out.

Rebbe was so busy, but he still took time to to play dreidel on Chanukah!

The Rebbe instructed parents to give their children gelt each night of Chanukah. On one night, they should give extra. Do you know which one? That’s right, the fifth night! What should we do with our gelt? Baruch Hashem, our parents give us food and clothes, so we don’t need to buy those. Instead, we can use the money for mitzvos! First, give some to tzedakah as ma’aser. Then, use the rest for other mitzvos, especially limmud Torah. We can even give gelt to other children!

The Rebbe encouraged us to give menorahs to Yidden who don’t yet have. We want to make sure everyone can do this mitzvah! The Rebbe even sent chassidim with menorahs to every army base. (As you know from last week’s Mivtzoim Mania!) But handing someone a menorah isn’t enough. We must also teach them how to light. It’s especially important that they know the halachos for Erev Shabbos: light before Shabbos licht, and don’t handle the menorah once Shabbos starts.

Minhag Chabad is to use olive oil. Children can use candles that will burn for enough time. (See next section for how long!) Our minhag is to use beeswax candles for the shamash. Beeswax lights easily and burns brightly.

Many Yidden have the custom to put on Shabbos clothes when lighting the menorah, but our minhag is to wear regular clothing. Married men wear a gartel.

Chanukah is an important time for children to get together. This minhag traces back to the Alter Rebbe, who would gather the family and tell special stories on one night of Chanukah. This was called a “-לאַטקֶעס אָוֶוענט—latkes evening,” and was also done by each of the Rebbeim. The Rebbe encouraged us to do the same. Let’s get together on Chanukah to share stories, songs, and the simcha of Yom Tov!

How tall is the biggest menorah in the world? A whopping 32 feet high! That’s just under 20 amos (the tallest possible height for a kosher menorah)—as tall as two giraffes! This giant menorah is lit in Manhattan to fulfill an important part of Chanukah: “נִיסָא פִּרְסּומֵי—to let everyone know about the miracle.” We don’t just celebrate at home, but also in public for all to see. The Rebbe encouraged everyone to arrange public menorah lightings. Nowadays, they’re all over: in malls, parks, and even the White House! These lightings have a huge impact. The Rebbe said that he knows hundreds, even thousands, of Yidden whose neshamos were awakened through a public menorah lighting. Be sure to join one this year! Who knows how many Yidden will be affected? Remember: Public lightings don’t fulfill our individual mitzvah. We still must light at home.

Listening to the Licht The Frierdiker Rebbe explains that we should listen to the message of the Chanukah lights. The story of Chanukah is full of holy and important lessons, and the flickering flames are like its storytellers. What messages can you “hear” while watching the precious lichtelach?

Chanukah is here! For eight days, Yidden all over the world light menorahs to celebrate our miraculous victory over the

Yevanim. As Chassidim, we have special minhagim for how

to light the menorah, and hora’os from the Rebbe about spreading the light of Chanukah all around us: from public menorah lightings to mivtzoim, rallies, and more. Let’s learn

You probably know that Chanukah starts on Chof-Hey Kislev. But do you know what else happened on that day? On Chof-Hey Kislev, the Yidden in the midbar finished building the Mishkan! Although it was celebrated on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, we remember this special occasion during Krias HaTorah each day of Chanukah. We read about the gifts that the nesi’im brought during the Chanukas HaMishkan. The Rebbe explains that we can learn lessons from each nasi and when he brought the presents. Sitting near the Chanukah licht is the perfect time to share words of Torah with your family. Here are eight messages you can say, one for each night:

It’s very hard to be the first one to do something; to be brave when no one else is. But that is exactly what Nachshon ben Aminadav, the nasi of Shevet Yehuda, did. He was the first to have mesiras nefesh and jump into the Yam Suf before it split. On the first day of Chanukah, we read about the karban of Nachshon ben Aminadav. This reminds us to be brave and spread Yiddishkeit even in ways that no one else has done it yet.

Three is the number of shalom. Let's explore why: One of something isn’t shalom—it's just one idea. Nothing to make peace with. Two isn't shalom either, because it’s two ideas against each other. Only when we have a third idea can there be balance that includes the other two ideas, showing that they actually agree with each other! That's true shalom. Chanukah is also shalom. It's not just about the Torah’s light (1), and it's definitely not about the Yevanim fighting the Torah with darkness (2). It's about darkness itself being lit up with the Torah's light (3). Both sides are included. We learn this from the nasi of Zevulun, whom we read about on Day Three. Zevulun didn't stay in the beis midrash learning Torah. He went out and lit up the world with the Torah's light. He brought true shalom, and we can learn from him to do the same.

Did you know that Hashem gave each of us a superpower? That’s right! We have the power to change bad into good; to turn an aveira into a mitzvah! We activate this superpower through teshuva. The first person to do complete teshuva on his own was Reuven. After he moved his father, Yaakov’s, bed without permission, Reuven did teshuva for many years. On the fourth day of Chanukah, we read about the nasi of Reuven and are reminded about our superpower. Let’s use this power today to fix any aveiros and come even closer to Hashem!

Asarah B'Teves

Asarah B'Teves
Print PDF

Do you want to know more details about the miraculous story with Sancheiriv? This wicked king from Ashur was extremely powerful. He conquered many nations and mixed them all up. He even sent ten of the shevatim into golus, and to this day, we don’t know where they settled! But Sancheiriv didn’t stop there. He also wanted to conquer Malchus Yehudah—the remaining Yidden who lived in and around Yerushalayim. He came with a massive army— far bigger than Nevuchadnetzar’s army—and positioned his men outside the city walls. Truthfully, Sancheiriv could have conquered Yerushalayim that very day, but Hashem in His kindness gave the Yidden more time. Sancheiriv decided to first rest for the night. When the Yiddishe king, Chizkiyahu, heard what was happening, he immediately did teshuva. Hashem accepted his tefillos and sent a malach to kill thousands of Sancheiriv’s soldiers that night. The rest of the army, including Sancheiriv himself, was filled with fear and ran away. As we see, in just one night, one hour, and one moment the entire siege was gone and the Yidden emerged with great victory!

Asara B’Teves is the first of the four fasts connected to the destruction of the First Beis Hamikdash. On this day, the armies of Nevuchadnetzar surrounded Yerushalayim with a siege, meaning that nobody and nothing was allowed to come in or go out. For two and a half years, the city was sealed. Much of the food and water had run out, and people were dying of starvation. Seeing that the Yidden were now too weak to properly fight back, Nevuchadnetzar’s men broke into Yerushalayim. They destroyed homes, killed many people, and sent the rest into golus as slaves. Finally, on the tragic day of Tisha B’Av, our holy Beis Hamikdash was set on fire.

As we see, what happened on Asara B’Teves started the entire process leading to the Churban. It is an extra-strict ta’anis because of that. For this reason, we fast and beg Hashem with extra effort to speedily build the third Beis Hamikdash, now!

Further Reading: Likkutei Sichos, vol. 20, pp. 347–359, 519–523; Yalkut Shimoni, Eicha, 1009; Sefer Sichos 5747, vol. 1, p. 240; Ibid, p. 143.

Do you know why we fast on sad days? It isn’t just to make us hungry. Fasting is supposed to refocus us to the sadness and pain of the day so that we’ll do proper teshuva. Many kehillos had a minhag that on every ta’anis, the rav would speak to the community after mincha, encouraging them to do teshuva. These speeches were called “דִבְרֵי ּכִיּבּוׁשִין—words that conquer the heart.” But for whatever reason, as the years continued, most places no longer kept this minhag. On Asara B’Teves of (1977) תשל”ח, the Rebbe announced that we should bring it back. From then on, the Rebbe would say a sicha after mincha of almost every fast day. As chassidim today, we can listen to or learn a sicha after mincha of the ta’anis. This will encourage us to do teshuva and bring Moshiach, transforming the fast day into a true Yom Tov!

Close your eyes and try to remember what life was like for you two and a half years ago. What games did you play? Which snacks did you eat? What did you learn in school?

It’s probably hard to remember so many details from back then. Two and a half years is a long time! Do you know what else took two and a half years? That's right: the siege around Yerushalayim. But why did it take so long?

The Midrash tells us that Hashem made it take such a long time to give the Yidden a chance to do teshuva. Because if they would have done teshuva, there would’ve been no need for the Churban. Hashem would have protected the city and the Beis Hamikdash would not have been destroyed.

If you knew that a special day was coming, how far in advance would you begin preparing? Yidden have the minhag to prepare for 30 days before every Yom Tov (known as “שְׁלֹושִׁים יֹום לִפְנֵי הַחַג”). We prepare for Rosh Hashana during the 30 days of Elul, and begin learning about Pesach on Purim, which is 30 days before. The same thing is true of Yud Shvat. The Rebbe encouraged us to begin preparing for Yud Shvat on Asara B’Teves. What’s the best Yud Shvat hachana? Adding in more good things, of course! The Rebbe said that everyone, even us children, are to learn more Torah, give more tzedaka, and daven with more kavana. We also strengthen our hiskashrus with the Rebbe by learning his teachings, joining farbrengens, and watching Rebbe videos. So, as Yud Shvat approaches, let’s think of the hachlatos we can take on. When we prepare properly, we will be all ready when the heilige day arrives—ready to greet Moshiach!

That’s actually what happened many years before the siege. Generations earlier, Sancheiriv, the king of Ashur, also wanted to conquer Yerushalayim. But the Yiddishe king, Chizkiyahu, did teshuva, and Hashem ruined Sancheiriv’s plans.

The same thing would have happened to Nevuchadnetzar and his plan if the Yidden would have done teshuva. So, Hashem waited for two and half years to see if they would. Sadly, they didn’t, and the city fell.

The lesson for us is clear. Sometimes, Hashem sends challenges as opportunities for teshuva. He waits to see if we’ll learn from our mistakes and come closer to Him. When we do, Hashem fixes things in a moment.

So, the next time something doesn’t seem to be going right, remember that it might be a reminder from Hashem that it is time to do teshuva! How can we think, speak, or act better? How can we come closer to Hashem? Let’s use the reminder of Asara B’Teves to do teshuva and bring Moshiach now!

Asara B’Teves comes with special lessons and minhagim for us chassidim.

We say slichos and Avinu Malkeinu, learn divrei kibushim, and begin preparing for Yud Shvat (which is now a month away)! Let’s learn about

Celebrate Like A Chayol

Chamisha Asar B'shvat

Chamisha Asar B'shvat
Print PDF

A kindergarten class once sent the Rebbe a collection of their pictures and drawings. The Rebbe writes back to them:

Rebbe had for all Yiddishe sons and daughters … especially the young ones, as he cared for their chinuch and well- being wherever they may be. In every child, he saw a sapling that will grow into a beautiful tree with good, delicious fruit.

But this [growth] is dependent on the will of every boy and girl, as [we learn from] the mashal of a tree.

When we plant a seed or sapling, we must guard it from weeds and all sorts of damaging things, and we must supply it with water etc., until it grows and becomes a tree which gives good fruits.

The same is true with every boy and girl, about whom Hashem says through His navi that they are “נֵצֶר מַטָעַי מַעֲׂשֵה יָדַי לְהִתְּפָאֵר—the branch of My planting and the work of My hands, of which I am so proud.”

Hashem, the Creator, has planted within you a holy neshama, a “חֵלֶק אֱלֹוּקַ מִמַעַל מַמָש—a piece of Hashem above, literally.” You must protect this G-dly “seed” from bad weeds and other damaging things, which means inappropriate friends, and you must supply it with “מַיִם חַיִים— healthy, living water”, which means Toras Chayim (“וְאֵין מַיִם אֶלָא ּתֹורָה—and water [here] is only referring to Torah”) and its mitzvos (which are “חַיִים הֵם לְעֹושֵׂיהֶם—life for those who perform them”).

And then, Hashem will “יִּתֵן וְיַחְזֹור וְיִּתֵן—give and give again” His bracha that you will succeed in being “trees” that give good, praiseworthy fruit, to the joy of your parents and teachers and to the pride and beauty of our nation, Am B’nei Yisroel…

Our minhag is to celebrate this holy day by eating fruits. Do you know which fruits we eat? There is actually more than one answer!

First of all, it’s important to eat the special fruits of Eretz Yisroel that are part of the Shiv’as Haminim: grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, and dates.

Second, we eat “חַרּובִים—carobs”. The Gemara tells us that the only food Rabi Chanina ben Dosa ate was just one kav of carobs each week. (That’s like eating only seven apples all week long!) So many miracles happened to this great Tanna that he was known as a "מְלּומָד ּבְנִיסִים—someone who is used to miracles." This shows us that carobs have a special connection to nisim.

The third type of fruit that we eat on Chamisha-Asar B’Shvat is a new fruit; one we haven’t eaten yet this season. This way, we can say the bracha of “ׁשֶהֶחֱיָנו”. There are so many fruits to choose from! What’s the strangest fruit you’ve ever eaten?

Note: Be sure to eat fruits with the bracha “הָעֵץ”, rather than ones which are actually “הָאֲדָמָה”!

There are certain parts of davening known as “tachanun”. These are serious sections asking Hashem to forgive our aveiros. We don’t say tachanun on Shabbos, Yom Tov, and other extra-happy times (like Chamisha-Asar B’Shvat), because the ko’ach of these days turn our aveiros into z’chuyos— through being b’simcha! From mincha on Yud- Daled Shvat until shki’a of Chamisha-Asar B’Shvat, tachanun is not said.

You might be wondering, “What does this have to do with me, a young chayol?” Even though you might not yet say tachanun in davening, there are still parts of your tefilla that are connected to tachanun. Ask your parents or teachers to show you.

Purim

Purim
Print PDF

What kinds of coins do you have?If you’re from America, you probably know about quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies. But have you heard of the half-dollar coin? On Ta’anis Esther, that’s the coin to use!

In the times of the Beis Hamikdash, it was a mitzvah for every Yid to give a half-shekel coin during the month of Adar. These shekalim would help pay for the צִיּבּור קָרְּבָנֹות (karbanos given on behalf of the entire nation, like the קָרְּבַן ּתָמִיד and מּוסַף קָרְּבַן) and other expenses of the Beis Hamikdash.

Nowadays, in order to remember this mitzvah, we also give a “half” coin to tzedaka—half of whatever type of money is used where we live. In America, it’s a half-dollar; in England, it’s 50 pence, etc. Our minhag is actually to give three of these “half” coins, since the Torah says the word “ּתְרּומָה—donation” three times when describing this mitzvah.

The Shulchan Aruch writes that from the age of 13, all Yidden should give machatzis hashekel. In תשנ”ב )1992(; during the last weekday sicha before Chof-Zayin Adar the Rebbe added that children who are younger than 13 should give machatzis hashekel, too! If possible, it should come from our own money.

Have you ever been to the Rebbe’s library near 770? If you go there, you might be able to see a Megilla written by the Rebbe Maharash himself! It has a different style than other Megillos. The Rebbe Maharash’s version shows us how a Megilla is to be written according to minhag Chabad.

Here are the differences: Some Megillos are arranged so that every column starts with the word “הַמֶלְֶך”. Chabad Megillos do not do that. Additionally, our Megillos have the ten sons of Haman written in regular size, not large letters that fill a whole column.

During the Megilla reading, we have the minhag to unroll our Megilla and fold it into three parts to look like an “אִגֶרֶת” (letter), as the pesukim describe it to be.

Haman’s name is found many, many times throughout the Megilla. Did you know that our minhag is not to make noise every time it’s written? Minhag Chabad is only to drown out Haman’s name when he is described with a title like “הָאַגָגִי—from King Agag”, or “הָרָע—the evil one”.

Sometimes, shaking our graggers by Haman’s name can get pretty noisy! Some people think that children shouldn’t come to kri’as haMegilla at all because their noisy graggers could disturb the reading. But the Rebbe says that children should come, and the noise from our graggers is a good thing! We just need to conduct the kri’ah in a way that everyone can still hear.

The Rebbe's advice is that each time Haman’s name is read, the person leining Megilla should pause and wait for everyone to finish making noise before continuing. This way, everyone will be able to clearly hear each word.

Are you ready to drown out Haman’s name with lots of noise and listen carefully to each word?

Another Purim mitzvah to make people happy is Matanos L’evyonim. We give tzedaka to at least two poor people. Since the money is meant to bring them joy on Purim, we don’t just put the money into a pushka. We either give it directly to poor people or to someone (or an organization) who will give it for us.

Purim is also a time to reach out to Yidden around us. The Rebbe explains that some people are poor because they don’t have money, and other people are poor because they don’t have knowledge. Besides giving Matanos L’evyonim money, it is also our job as chayolim to give ruchniyus’dik Matanos L’evyonim by helping

We go around to Yidden who don’t yet know about the mitzvos of Purim and help them to properly celebrate this holy day. This includes leining Megilla with them, inviting them to our se’uda, giving them Mishloach Manos to pass along to another Yid, or telling them about the mitzvah to give extra tzedaka. Let’s get out there and share the joy of Purim with others!

Did you know that this exciting mitzvah is not about getting Mishlo’ach Manos, but about giving them? The true purpose of Mishlo’ach Manos is to make other Yidden happy on Purim. We give at least two different types of food to at least one person. Boys give to boys, and girls give to girls. The Rebbe’s minhag was to give to a Kohen, a Levi, and a Yisrael. Think of how you can do this mitzvah in the most beautiful way. Perhaps you know someone who lives alone, or maybe a classmate who doesn’t have many friends? Imagine how happy they’ll be if you show up at their door with Mishlo’ach Manos! And that’s what this mitzvah is truly about.

The fourth mitzvah of Purim is to have a seuda. The Purim seuda is often so chayus’dik and long that people may forget to bentch. The Rema, the rav of Krakow, would go from house to house after seudas Purim and remind people to bentch for their meal.

(Learning from this, the Rebbe would end all of his farbrengens throughout the year with a reminder: “דִי וואָס דאַרפן מאַכן אַ בְּרָכָה ַ אַחֲרֹונָה, וֶועלן זִיכער מאַכן א ּבְרָכָה אַחֲרֹונָה—Whoever needs to say a bracha acharona will surely say a bracha acharona.”)

May this year’s seuda be full of chayus and joy. And remember to bentch!

Hooray! Purim is in the air! This Yom Tov is full of missions, between the four mitzvos of the day plus our

own Chabad minhagim. We give machatzis hashekel from the youngest age, we have a special way to write

and read the Megilla, we give Mishlo’ach Manos and Matanos L’evyonim properly and beautifully, have a seuda, dress up in holy themes, and go on mivtzoim. Let’s

learn all about how to celebrate Purim as Chassidim!

585; Sichos Kodesh 5752, vol. 2, p. 788; Sefer Hasichos 5702, pp. 82–83; Likkutei Sichos, vol. 31, pp. 279–280.

Pesach
Print PDF

The Rebbe’s mechiras chametz document. (It's one of the only times when the Rebbe signed his name with “ben Harav Levi Yitzchak.")

When the Alter Rebbe first returned home after studying with the Mezritcher Maggid in the year תקכ”ה )1765(, he wanted to do the mitzvah of bedikas chametz with as much kavana as possible. He was so busy preparing that he didn’t even eat the whole day. And, when it was finally time to do the mitzvah, the Alter Rebbe spent the entire night searching for chametz, even though he had just one small room!

There’s an important mitzvah that we do on the night before Erev Pesach. This mitzvah is so important that we aren’t allowed to let anything distract us—not even limmud Torah! Do you know what this mitzvah is? That’s right: ּבְדִיקַת חָמֵץ—searching for chametz.

But, after spending so much time and effort cleaning the house, there might not be any chametz to be found! That’s totally fine, because the mitzvah is just to look for chametz. We don’t have to actually find chametz.

Still, our minhag is to purposefully hide chametz around the house so that we will find some when we search. We hide ten small pieces, making sure that they’re wrapped carefully so no crumbs fall out.

During bedikas chametz, we look around the house with a candle (beeswax is best), a feather, and wooden spoon. Once all of the pieces have been found, we tie the supplies together in a bag (to be burned with the chametz the next morning), and we say “ּכָל חֲמִירָא” to nullify any remaining chametz..

As you surely know, one of the main mitzvos of Pesach is to not own any chametz. But that doesn’t mean we have to throw it all out before Yom Tov!

The Shulchan Aruch says that we can do what’s called מְכִירַת חָמֵץ: We put our chametz into a place where it won’t be seen or touched throughout Pesach and then sell it all to a non- Jew. This way, the chametz doesn’t belong to us anymore, and it can stay in our homes.

There are different ways to do mechiras chametz. The Alter Rebbe says that the best way is to use a method known as “קַּבְּלָן עָרֵב—a guarantor or ‘backup’ person” who takes responsibility for the sale if something goes wrong with the seller. Having an areiv kablan shows that mechiras chametz is a serious sale; we don’t chas v’shalom want to be left owning chametz on Pesach! To make sure that everything is done properly, we first give all of our chametz to the rav, and then he sells it to a non-Jew.

On the morning of Erev Pesach, we do another special mitzvah called “חָמֵץ ּבִיעּור—burning the chametz.” We take the chametz from the night before and burn it in a fire. As it burns, we say Kol Chamira again, plus a special Yehi Ratzon that Hashem should get rid of our Yetzer Hara just as we are getting rid of the chametz. Chametz

A Chassid who spent Pesach of תרע”ד )1914(in Lubavitch with the Rebbe Rashab described bi’ur chametz:

The Rebbe [Rashab] burned his chametz in the furnace of Tomchei Temimim’s zal (study hall). The fire was started very early in the morning so that the flames would be scorching hot by the time bi’ur chametz took place.

When he finished burning the chametz, the Rebbe [Rashab] turned to the temimim and said, “Just like we burned the gashmiyus’dik chametz, we must also burn our ruchniyus’dik chametz.”

The chachamim established a certain fast day that’s only for a specific type of Yid. Do you know which one? It’s the fast called “ּבְכֹורִים ּתַעֲנִית,” and it’s just for bechorim—firstborn men or boys. As we know from the story of Yetzi’as Mitzrayim, Hashem saved the Yiddishe bechorim during Makas Bechoros. To remember this neis, bechorim fast on Erev Pesach. If a bechor is under bar mitzvah, his father fasts for him.

However, the minhag is actually for bechorim not to fast—instead, they try to participate in a siyum on Erev Pesach. This way, they can eat at the siyum’s seudas mitzvah and throughout the rest of the day.

Pesach is a Yom Tov that is packed with mitzvos! For us chayolim, it is also packed with Chabad minhagim. We have special ways to sell chametz, search for chametz,

and burn chametz; our own way to set up the Seder plate; and minhagim for almost every step of the Seder.
