Do you like asking questions? I hope so. Questions are so important for learning!

The Seder is full of questions. Even the חָכָם ּבֶן, the wisest of the Four Sons, has questions. The Rebbe tells us that this teaches us a big lesson: That we must ask, ask, ask!

We are soldiers in Hashem’s Army, and we have Kabbalas Ol to do everything that Hashem tells us— whether we understand it or not. But, once we’ve committed to following Hashem’s command no matter what, we are also supposed to understand the reasons for the mitzvos. This helps us to have more chayus when we do them!

So, on the Seder Night and throughout the whole year, always ask questions. Ask why we do the mitzvos and ask about each of their reasons. Ask about our minhagim and our Chassidishe ways. Ask away until you really understand. Ask until every single mission is done with true chayus and bren!

Shevi'i V'acharon Shel Pesach

Shevi'i V'acharon Shel Pesach
Print PDF

Note: These images are for illustrative purposes only and are not meant to be an accurate depiction of the holy faces of the Tzaddikim.

In the year תרכ”ה )1865(, the Rebbe Maharash was sitting at the Yom Tov table with his family. Four- year-old (future Rebbe) Rashab asked, “Why is the last day of Pesach a Yom Tov?” His ten- year-old sister, Devorah Leah, answered, “The Yidden have been careful not to eat chametz for seven days straight! So, we make a Yom Tov to celebrate our fulfillment of this mitzvah.” Smiling, the Rebbe Maharash complimented his daughter, “You have a good head!”

When the Rebbe Maharash went with his children to visit his father, the Tzemach Tzedek, he repeated the conversation. The Tzemach Tzedek agreed that Devorah Leah gave a good, logical answer. He then called the children closer, and told them another answer. “Today is called ‘ּפֶסַַח ׁשֶל אַחֲרֹון—The Last Day of Pesach’ because we’ve finished the avodah of Pesach, when Hashem redeemed us from Golus Mitzrayim. Acharon shel Pesach celebrates Hashem redeeming us from this final Golus.”

On the night of Acharon shel Pesach תרס"ו )1906(, the Rebbe Rashab heard his granddaughters arguing. One girl said that Acharon shel Pesach is a regular Yom Tov, but young Chaya Mushka (our Rebbetzin) said: “No, it’s not! The proof is that we don’t say shehecheyanu on Acharon shel Pesach [showing that it’s different from all other Yomim Tovim]!”

When the Rebbe Rashab heard that, he was reminded of the story with his sister Devorah Leah.

On Shvi’i and Acharon shel Pesach, we don’t say the bracha of שֶׁהֶחֱיָנּו, unlike any other Yom Tov. Do you know why? The simple answer is because the whole Pesach is one long Yom Tov, so the last days are not “new”. But there is also a deeper answer. You’ll never guess who figured it out. It was our rebbetzin, Rebbetzin Chaya Mushka, when she was only five years old!

When’s the latest you’ve ever gone to sleep? If you’re old enough, there might be times when you stay up all night! That’s because there are a few times throughout the year when we have the minhag not to go to sleep. One of those nights is Shvi’i shel Pesach. Do you know why? Let’s think of what happened on the first Shvi’i shel Pesach: The Yidden left Mitzrayim on Tes-Vov Nissan, and then, on Chof-Alef Nissan (Shvi’i shel Pesach), Hashem made the wondrous neis of Kri’as Yam Suf! The Torah teaches us that Kri’as Yam Suf wasn’t just a gashmiyus neis of water splitting. It was also a time of incredible giluy Elokus. In fact, simple maidservants saw deeper levels of Elokus there than even the great navi Yechezkel saw with nevu’a years later! Because the ruchniyus energy of a Yom Tov happens again each year (and on an even greater level than before!), we want to be awake for these special giluyim. Minhag Chabad is to stay up all night until dawn. What do we do all night? We learn Torah— especially Chassidus. The Frierdiker Rebbe began staying up all night when he was nine years old.

vol. 22, pp. 30–38; Toras Menachem, vol. 33, pp. 336–341.

That’s right: Until now, we were very careful about gebroks. But on Acharon shel Pesach, that all changes. Now, we specifically wet our matzah. Do you know why?

Chametz represents ga’ava. It rises and is full of air, like a person full of pride. Matzah is flat and low, which represents being humble. On Pesach, we work very hard to have zero traces of ga’ava. So, we have zero chametz—not even gebroks, which is just a tiny chance of chametz.

But pride is not always bad. We’re supposed to be proud of who we are. Aren’t you proud to be a chayol in Hashem’s Army? As long as we remember that everything comes from Hashem, we can and should be proud.

So, once we’ve practiced being humble for the whole week of Pesach, we can start having ga’ava again—the right kind. On Acharon shel Pesach, we bring in a little bit of pride by eating gebroks. (And on Shavuos, when the avodah of Pesach is complete, we bring actual chametz onto the mizbe’ach!) This way, we can be proud chayolim the whole year while remembering that Hashem is the One in control!

Our Rebbe explained how the two stories are connected:

According to Devorah Leah, this Yom Tov celebrates not eating chametz, which is connected to our Yetzer Hara and Golus—so it is similar to other Yomim Tovim. However, our Rebbetzin’s argument is similar to the Tzemach Tzedek’s answer, connecting Acharon shel Pesach to the Geulah. It’s different from all other Yomim Tovim.

When the end of Pesach comes—after we’ve worked hard for a whole week to leave Golus— but Moshiach still isn’t here yet, it’s very painful, so we don’t say shehecheyanu. But when we celebrate Acharon shel Pesach with simcha and emuna, it makes it happen for real!

How many cups of wine (or grape juice) do Chassidim drink that are connected specifically to Pesach? The answer is 12! Four at each Seder night, and another four at Moshiach’s Seuda.

Moshiach’s Seuda was started by the Baal Shem Tov. Our Rebbeim explain that a ray of Moshiach’s energy shines during this time. We tap into it with a special seuda! Since Moshiach will affect even (and especially!) our gashmiyus world, we use gashmiyus to celebrate. We eat matzah and, as the Rebbe Rashab added, we drink four cups of wine.

Ever wonder why there’s no maror at Moshiach’s Seudah? That’s because we are focused on Geulah, when there will be no more sadness or pain. We can serve Hashem with pure simcha!

Therefore, when drinking the wine (which brings simcha and geshmak), be sure to think about the Geulah—may it happen immediately!

Sefiras Haomer

Sefiras Haomer
Print PDF

The Alter Rebbe had a wealthy Chassid named Reb Gavriel Nos’ei Chein. After 25 years of marriage, Reb Gavriel and his wife, Chana Rivka, still had no children. Then, sadly, Reb Gavriel had difficulties in business, and lost most of his wealth.

Around that time, the Alter Rebbe was collecting money for Pidyon Sh’vuyim. Reb Gavriel was asked to donate a large amount like he used to give. But Reb Gavriel didn’t have the money. He was devastated.

Chana Rivka immediately sold all her jewelry. There was now money for tzedakah! But first, she polished the coins until they shined brightly, davening that their fortune should also shine. Then, she wrapped up the coins and sent them with her husband.

The mitzvah of Sefiras HaOmer is to count from Pesach to Shavuos.

When we count Sefira, we focus on both the days and the weeks. Do you know how many there are? You got it: There are 49 days; exactly 7 weeks. Now, hold on to those numbers.

Each one of us also has a special connection to 7: our neshama contains 7 middos! Ready for some math? Each midda itself contains 7 parts. So, 7 (middos) x 7 (parts) gets us back to the number 49! 49 days and 49 midda-parts. During each of the 7 weeks, we focus on improving one main midda, and on each of the 49 days, we

focus on a different part of that midda. This way, by the time we reach Shavuos, we’ll have worked on our middos very well—ready to receive the Torah!

The words we say and think when counting Sefira reminds us of these inyanim:

1) We say the number of the day and week. 2) We say kapitel ס”ז in Tehillim (which has 49 words), thinking of one word each day. 3) We think of one letter from passuk ’ה of that kapitel. (49 letters from the word “יִשְׂמְחּו” until “סֶלָה”) 4) We say the tefillah “ַאָנָא ּבְכֹח”, thinking of one word or roshei teivos. (42 words plus 7 roshei teivos, equals … 49!) 5) We say a special רִּבֹונֹו שֶׁל עֹולָם, mentioning the midda of the day.

You probably know that there are 24 hours in a day, but do you know how many hours there are in a year? The answer is 8,496.

The Rebbe Rashab said that when we “count” our hours and live each one fully and carefully, then the days will also be counted—and not just the days of Sefira. We want to make the most of every precious moment from Hashem. So, when He gives us 8,496 hours each year, we’ll be sure to fill each one with Torah and mitzvos! And, as Chassidim, we’ll see to it that tomorrow will be much better than today.

Further Reading: Hayom Yom, 1 Iyar; Ibid., 10 Iyar; Sefer

Hasichos 5701, p. 116; Likkutei Sichos, vol. 4, pp. 1300-1301; Igros Kodesh, vol.

12, p. 441; Sefer Hasichos 5749, vol. 2, p. 745; Likkutei Sichos, vol. 3, p. 997; lgros Kodesh, vol. 20, p. 112; Ibid. p. 148.

The days of Sefira are a serious time; the students of Rabi Akiva passed away. For this reason, we don’t do certain things that bring joy:

We don’t say the bracha of ׁשֶהֶחֱיָנּו, except on Shabbos.

We don’t get haircuts (except on Lag BaOmer). Some people have the minhag to get haircuts three days before Shavuos, but minhag Chabad is only to do so on Erev Shavuos. The same is for a boy who turns three during Sefira: His upshern is celebrated either on Lag BaOmer or Erev Shavuos (whichever is on, or after, his birthday).

We also don’t listen to music or make weddings during Sefira, except on Lag BaOmer. We can celebrate engagements, but without music.

Shavuos also has another name: “עֲצֶרֶת”, meaning “stop” or “end”. One reason is because Shavuos is really the end of Pesach. But how?

The Rebbe explains that Pesach is about becoming free. Real freedom doesn’t come from just leaving Mitzrayim. We’re truly free when we keep Torah and mitzvos! So, Pesach’s freedom is only complete with Matan Torah. Today, too, we work hard to become truly free in Avodas Hashem, using these special days of Sefira as proud chayolim do: preparing for Matan Torah! Shining Our Middos

Here’s another connection between Sefira and our middos: Do you know what “סְפִירָה” means? If you said “counting”, you’re right! And if you said “shining”, you’re also right! It means both.

The Maggid of Mezritch taught that working on our middos, especially during Sefira, makes our neshama shine bright.

What time is it right now? There are many right answers. If you’re in Yerushalayim, it’s one time. If you’re in New York, it’s another. In Hawaii, it’s many hours later. What if you keep going west, into the Pacific Ocean? If you go far enough, you’ll reach the International Date Line—the imaginary line that separates days. On one side of the line, it’s one day, and on the other side, it’s a different day. The Rebbe ruled that if someone crosses the Date Line during Sefira, they keep counting Sefira as they were before, even if it’s different from the people around them. So, if someone flies to Australia from America (by going west), they’ll count a different day of Sefira than the people in Australia. The Rebbe recommended not to do that. But, if someone does, they’ll need to celebrate Shavuos either a day earlier or a day later than everyone else, depending on which direction they traveled. For this reason, people who travel to/from Australia for Pesach will often get flights that don’t cross the Date Line, even if it’s a much longer trip.

Pesach Sheini

Pesach Sheini
Print PDF

In Liozna, there was a Chassid called “קֶענֶער דֶער חַּיִים—Chayim Who Can”. He was poor and had a hard life, but he was always smiling. Whenever anything difficult would happen to him, he would say “I can!”

Reb Chayim once explained what he meant with those words. It was a hora'ah he had learned from the Alter Rebbe on a piece of Gemara: In Gemara Maseches Nidda, it says that when the neshama is in shamayim—before it is born into a body—it’s made to promise that it will be a tzaddik. The word for “they make it promise—מַׁשְּבִיעִים", has the same letters as the word "מַׂשְּבִיעִים- they give it the ability.” The Alter Rebbe explained that this means

our neshamos are given the ability to overcome all of the challenges that we will encounter in life!

Chayim der Kener took this to heart. Whenever something not good happened to him, he would remember that his neshama was given the ko'ach to handle it. He

would smile and shout “I can!”, no matter what challenge he faced.

Chayolim, all of our neshamos were given that same ko'ach. We are all able to face any challenge or struggle in life. Hashem gave us the ability to overcome it even before we were born. Let’s always remember that “we can”!

Just like on every Yom Tov, we don’t say tachanun on Pesach Sheini. But here’s a difference between Pesach Sheini and other Yomim Tovim: Usually, besides not saying tachanun on the Yom Tov itself, we also don’t say it during mincha of the day before, which is Erev Yom Tov, as a preparation. However, we do say tachanun during mincha of Erev Pesach Sheini (Yud-Gimmel Iyar). Here’s why:

Pesach Sheini is really like Erev Pesach, rather than Pesach itself. This is because it’s not a second chance to celebrate the entire Yom Tov; it’s specifically a second chance to bring the Karban Pesach. The Karban Pesach is brought on Yud-Daled Nissan—Erev Pesach—and Pesach Sheini is exactly one month later, on Yud-Daled Iyar. Both times, the karban is brought on Yud-Daled and eaten that night, on Tes-Vov. We see that Pesach Sheini is already more like an “erev” itself—and we do say tachanun in mincha on the day before an “erev” (i.e. Erev-Erev Yom Tov).

However, it’s interesting to note that the Rebbe discusses the night after Pesach Sheini—the night of Tes-Vov. The Rebbe says it’s possible that we should not say tachanun in Krias Shema she’al Hamita that night, because it’s still a special time; it’s when the karban was actually eaten.

How is Pesach Sheini different from all other Yomim Tovim? It’s the only Yom Tov in the Torah that was created because we Yidden asked for it!

Here’s what happened: When the Yidden were in the midbar, some people couldn't bring a Karban Pesach because they were tamei. But they also didn’t want to miss out on this precious mitzvah! So they asked Moshe: “נִגָרַע לָמָה— why should we miss out?” Give us a second chance! When Moshe told Hashem what they wanted, Hashem agreed to give them another opportunity! He said to bring the Karban Pesach exactly one month later, on Yud-Daled Iyar. We call that day Pesach Sheini.

The Rebbe shows an important lesson here: If the Yidden at that time did everything possible so they wouldn’t miss out on just one mitzvah, how much more so nowadays, when there are so many mitzvos that we can’t fulfill without a Beis Hamikdash, should we demand from Hashem to bring the Geulah now! נִגָרַע לָמָה?!

113–116; Hayom Yom, 14 Iyar; Likkutei Sichos, vol.

The theme of Pesach Sheini is that it’s never too late to fix what we’ve done. Even if we make mistakes, there’s always a second chance. In fact, Hashem gives us second chances even if we mess up on purpose! As soon as we do teshuva, we can come close to Him again. It’s never too late to change.

The Rebbe points out that Pesach Sheini happens in Iyar, not in Nissan. Nissan is the month of miracles, when Hashem takes us out of Mitzrayim in a wondrous way. Iyar, however, is the month of avodah, when we work hard on our middos.

This teaches us a deep lesson: Sometimes, Hashem gives us extra-special brachos and energy in a “Nissan” way. But if we miss them, we can still make them up— with extra effort and working on our middos, we can get a second chance.

Do you miss eating matzah once Pesach is over? Well, there is still one more day when we’re supposed to eat it: Pesach Sheini! On Yud-Daled Iyar, we eat matzah to remember this second chance that Hashem gave us to bring the Karban Pesach. But, even though on Pesach we eat matzah at night, our minhag on Pesach Sheini is to eat it during the day, when the karban was brought on the mizbei’ach (as you read in the previous section). However, the Rebbe also mentioned the minhag to eat matzah on the night following Pesach Sheini, the night of Tes-Vov, which, as you know, is when the karban was eaten.

Can you think of three things that are called “שֵׁנִי—second”? There’s a saying of Chassidim about what those three “sheini’s” are:

1. The Nefesh Elokis: Our neshama is called the “הַשֵׁנִית נֶפֶׁש— the second neshama”, because it comes in addition to our Nefesh Habehamis.

2. The Cheder Sheini: Many Chabad shuls have a second room called a ׁשֵנִי חֵדֶר, where Chassidim could spend a long time davening and doing hisbonenus (thinking deeply about Chassidus) undisturbed.

All of these “sheini’s” are connected. When we listen to our Nefesh Elokis, it will help us to spend more time davening and thinking about ideas of Chassidus, which will help us to properly do teshuva and have a Pesach Sheini—a second

chance to fix all of our aveiros and come closer to

It’s time for a Yom Tov that we asked Hashem for! While Pesach Sheini is a special day for all Yidden, it has a special

message for us chayolim. We eat matzah, we don’t say tachanun, and we learn the deeper meaning of the Yom Tov.

Lag Baomer

Lag Baomer
Print PDF

One year, as hundreds of children marched by the Rebbe in a Lag BaOmer parade, the

that can make them feel like bossing other people around. Chayolim, on the other hand, can wear a crown without becoming

that the message of a crown is that we are leaders. True, we Yidden are often not the biggest group

in our city. There are usually only a few of us compared to everyone else. And there are even fewer of us chayolim! But we must always remember that no matter what, we are leaders, not followers. When we march in the streets on Lag BaOmer, we remember that this is the day of the great leader, Rabi Shimon bar Yochai. He was one of the first tanna’im, and his teachings continue to be learned until today!

Therefore, we wear special crowns, shout the pesukim really loudly, and remember that each of us are leaders, too!

We have a special minhag to eat carobs (called “ּבאָקְסעֶר” in Yiddish) on Lag BaOmer. This is because Lag BaOmer is when Rabi Shimon bar Yochai (“Rashbi”) passed away. When he and his son were hiding in a cave for thirteen years, they survived by eating carobs that miraculously grew outside the cave. To remember the neis, we eat carobs, too. Be sure to check for bugs before eating, and careful not to crack your teeth!

On Lag BaOmer, the Rebbe encouraged everyone to give tzedaka in multiples of 18. (Can you name three such multiples?) Lag BaOmer falls on Chai (Yud-Ches) Iyar—the gematria of 18. This day gives chayus to the whole month’s avoda, so it’s a good day to give tzedaka in amounts connected to 18.

Let’s back up. The reason why we do mourn during Sefira is because most of Rabi Akiva’s talmidim passed away. They didn’t have proper Ahavas Yisroel. But on Lag BaOmer, they stopped dying! The Rebbe told us children that it’s our job throughout the month of Iyar—and specifically on Lag BaOmer—to behave with extra Ahavas Yisroel. This will help bring Moshiach much faster, and then we’ll never need to mourn during Sefira

Further Reading: Likkutei Sichos, vol. 32, pp. 254–256;

Toras Menachem, vol. 3, pp. 77–81; Der Rebbe Redt Tzu Kinder, vol. 3, pp.

157–160, 231–234; Sichos Kodesh 5740, vol. 3, pp. 201–202.

Do you know which sefer Rabi Shimon bar Yochai wrote?

He wrote the Zohar Hakadosh, a very special sefer about Pnimiyus HaTorah. Rashbi was one of the first people to write down such deep Torah secrets, and on the day that he passed away, there was a tremendous giluy of these secrets for all of Klal Yisroel. And guess what? Rashbi says that the same thing will happen for the generation that ends Golus and greets Moshiach—both adults and children alike will learn the deepest secrets of the Torah, and through this bring the Geulah!

Lag BaOmer is a happy day. It is a day to sing, dance, and rejoice with extra simcha! Here’s a story about how important it is to be happy on this day:

A certain talmid of the Arizal felt so broken about the Churban Beis Hamikdash that he would say “נַחֵם” (a tefilla we say on Tisha B’Av) every day of the year. One Lag BaOmer, he came with the Arizal to Meiron, where Rashbi is buried. That day, he said “nacheim” as usual.

Rashbi soon appeared to the Arizal with a message. He told him that on such a happy day like Lag BaOmer, his talmid should not say “nacheim”. For doing so, he would be punished.

We can all take a lesson from this to be happy on Lag BaOmer. Even someone who truly mourned the Beis Hamikdash was not allowed to do so on Lag BaOmer. Let’s be sure to fill ourselves with simcha this Lag BaOmer! Gut Yom Tov!

Lag BaOmer has a specific toy connected to it: the bow and arrow! “Bow” in Hebrew is a קֶשֶׁת, which is also the word for rainbow. Rainbows are Hashem’s reminder that He won’t destroy the world with another Mabul. But as long as Rashbi was alive, not a single rainbow was needed; his z’chus protected the world! To remember this, we play with bows and arrows.

The Rebbe also teaches us a deep lesson from how a bow is used: When you pull the arrow towards yourself, it can fly forward. Only when it’s pulled back really far—all the way to your heart—will the arrow fly powerfully.

The same is with Avodas Hashem. In order to serve Hashem properly, we need to “pull the string” of bittul close to our heart. This means that by learning Torah with humility (and not because “I am so great and smart”), our “arrow” can fly powerfully against the Yetzer Hara!

Are you ready to practice your aim this Lag BaOmer?

Parades are a great way to show that we are proud to be Yidden! The Rebbe arranged children’s parades in front of 770 even before he became Rebbe! תשט”ז )1956( was the first Lag BaOmer “marching parade”. Originally, the parades didn’t happen every year. They would only be arranged when Lag BaOmer fell out on a Sunday, so public school children could attend. The Rebbe spoke at many of them; the last such parade was in תש”נ)1990(. But in תש”מ )1980(, the Rebbe instructed that we should make a parade every Lag BaOmer in neighborhoods and cities all over. This way, we show the world how proud we are to be chayolim, following in the ways of Pnimiyus HaTorah that Rashbi gave us. At the parades, we make sure to say the twelve pesukim loudly and proudly, and march with smiles on our faces and our heads held high!

It’s time to pause the mourning of Sefira for a day of

joy! Lag Ba’Omer is here. As Chassidim, we have our own way of celebrating. We eat carobs, give tzedaka,

Shavuos

Shavuos
Print PDF

It was the day before Shavuos in )1885( תרמ”ה, when the Frierdiker Rebbe was still a four- year-old boy in cheder. His teacher gathered the children and said: “The Torah tells us that Moshe gathered the Yidden and took them to Har Sinai to get the Torah. Come with me! I will take you to Matan Torah!”

All 30–35 students followed the melamed to the shul. There, he told them, “Tomorrow is Shavuos. I want you all to come to shul a whole hour early to be ready to get the Torah.”

The next morning, the Frierdiker Rebbe woke up at 7 am. His mother, Rebbetzin Shterna Sara, tried offering him something to eat, but he refused, saying that he wouldn’t eat before getting the Torah. The young Frierdiker Rebbe went to shul and found the rest of his classmates there. After davening, their melamed took them on a walk.

As we see, even in the times of the Frierdiker Rebbe, young children would come to shul on Shavuos, to hear the Aseres Hadibros!

Every year, we receive the Torah on Shavuos just like the Yidden in the midbar! We learn from them how to prepare and celebrate properly. Do you know what hachanos they did?

For three days before Matan Torah, they made sure not to get tamei, they cleaned their clothes, and a fence was put up around Har Sinai so they would make sure not to go on the mountain.

Because of that, the three days before Shavuos are called the “ׁשְֹלׁשֶת יְמֵי הַגְּבָלָה— three days of limitation”, when the Yidden limited their weekday activities and increased their kedusha. Since we are also getting the Torah, this is a time to start making ourselves more holy, too.

The Rebbe teaches us how: First, we need to put up a “fence” in our own lives. We do this by focusing on the fact that Hashem chose us as His nation—we are “fenced” in to be connected to Him. This will block the Yetzer Hara from being able to tell us what to do.

Next, we take actual steps to become more holy. This includes being careful to say Modeh Ani and wash our hands every morning, as soon as we wake up. We must also make sure not to touch anything before we wash negel vasser.

When we are careful to start our day with a mitzvah, then our whole day becomes holy! And when we do this every day of the Shloshes Yemei Hagbala, we are surely ready to get the Torah!

Further Reading: Der Rebbe Redt Tzu Kinder, vol. 3, pp. 243–245; Likkutei Sichos, vol. 23, pp. 250–259; Ibid., vol. 28, p. 315; Sefer Hasichos 5705, pp. 100–101; Toras Menachem, vol. 8, pp. 210–211; Toras Menachem, vol. 43 p. 378; Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim, 494:16.

continue exploring our Shavuos minhagim in Part Two next week. Stay tuned!

Shavuos is a special time to eat milchigs. Do you know why? There are actually many different reasons. Some say the reason is because the Torah was given on Shabbos. From the moment the Yidden got the Torah, they had to follow the halachos of shechting animals in order to eat meat. And since they couldn’t shecht on Shabbos, they could only eat milchigs. But the Rebbe says this reason cannot be correct. Why not? It’s because there’s a mitzvah to eat meat each Yom Tov, including Shavuos. Certainly, Hashem wouldn’t give the Yidden a mitzvah without a way to fulfill it! Additionally, the Rebbe explains, the Yidden were already shechting meat before Matan Torah, so they could have eaten that meat. The Rebbe says that it must have been for other reasons. One reason is because the Torah is compared to milk, which we see in a passuk describing the Torah as “דְבַׁש וְחָלָב ּתַחַת לְׁשֹונְֵך—honey and milk are under your tongue.” Learning Torah fills us with a geshmak, like delicious foods made with milk and honey. Therefore, it’s fitting that we celebrate the Torah with milchigs.

When Hashem prepared for Matan Torah, He wanted to find “guarantors”, meaning people who could absolutely make sure that the Torah would be kept, no matter what. The Yidden suggested all sorts of ideas for guarantors—big tzaddikim like the Avos and the Nevi’im—but Hashem wasn’t satisfied.

But when they finally suggested the children, Hashem agreed. That’s right: Hashem gave the Torah to the entire Yiddishe nation only because He trusted that we children would learn it, keep it, and teach it to others!

Because of this, the Rebbe said that we children are the “main guests” in shul every Shavuos. In תש”מ )1980(, the Rebbe started a new mivtza. He instructed that every child, even young babies just one month old (!), should come to shul to hear the Aseres Hadibros.

The Rebbe emphasized that just like every single Yid was there at Har Sinai, we must try to make sure that every Yid comes to hear the Torah on Shavuos.

We can see how important it is, even for little babies, from the story of Rabi Yehoshua ben Chananya. When this great tanna was very young, his mother would bring his cradle to the beis midrash. He grew up hearing people study Torah, and that helped him grow into one of the greatest talmidei chachamim.

The Rebbe said that if this is true about listening to people discuss how they understand the Torah, how much more so is it true about hearing Krias HaTorah—pure words of Torah—in shul. When we children, even very young ones, are brought to shul to hear the Aseres Hadibros, it affects us and awakens our neshamos.

Let’s make sure to be in shul for the Aseres Hadibros, and bring our parents, siblings, and friends along with us! Stand quietly, face the bima, and do your best to hear every word of the Aseres Hadibros. After all, Hashem is giving you the Torah again—right at that moment!

learn some of our special minhagim: how a Chassid prepares for Shavuos, hears the Aseres Hadibros, eats milchigs, and more.

Reb Peretz Beshenkovitzer was a Chassid of the Rebbe Maharash. His grandfather had been a great Chassid of the Tzemach Tzedek, so the Rebbe Maharash would often show Reb Peretz a special closeness. But Reb Peretz was a poor melamed, and didn’t think of himself as an important person.

For many years, Reb Peretz would travel to Lubavitch for Shavuos. One year, as Reb Peretz was coming into town, the Rebbe Maharash was taking a walk and silently noticed the humble Chassid’s arrival. When Reb Peretz indeed entered the town, he saw that Lubavitch was packed! There were so many visitors that he was sure that he would not be called in for yechidus that year.

However, much to his surprise, it wasn’t long before the Rebbe Maharash’s gabbai, Reb Leivik, walked over to him. “The Rebbe wants to see you for yechidus.”

I guess I should start this journal with a little introduction. When my sister went off to seminary, she left behind a box of all her old stuff and said I can have whatever I want. That’s when I discovered this empty notebook—exactly what I was looking for. You see, one day I’m going to be a five-star general in Tzivos Hashem and everyone will want to know how I got there.

“No need to ask,” I’ll say, “just read my journal, and you, too, will know how to be a five-star general.”

Till then, this journal is TOP SECRET. Permission to read is granted to absolutely no one. Well…unless whoever reads it can help me figure out how to get enough stickers from my apples to cover my Chumash notebook before Mimi does, and how to reach the top of the 40-foot tree in Blueberry Forest, and maybe even help me understand the stuff my teacher teaches—’cause somehow I always manage to get mixed up…

You’ll never guess what my friend Rivky and I are planning.

See, it’s the end of Elul. We’ve had a month when, as my teacher taught us, “מֶלְֶך ּבַׂשָדֶה—the King is in the field.” Hashem comes to visit all of us simple people, and smiles and laughs with us, reminding us that we are all His children.

But now it’s almost Tishrei, when the King goes back to the palace. So Rivky and I are making a goodbye party for Hashem.

Tomorrow she’s gonna come over, and we’re going to bake a seven-layer chocolate cake with blueberries, marshmallows and spicy chips on top. Then we’ll invite all our friends for a big party, and we’ll make goodbye cards for Hashem. I can’t believe no one thought of this before. It makes so much sense.

I have a lot to write about because I’ve been planning my big Rosh Hashanah mission: the mission to bring the mitzvah of shofar to everyone.

See, Mrs. Feigenbaum (our new fourth grade teacher) taught us about what goes on in shul on Rosh Hashana. Turns out, it’s something nobody would want to miss.

Imagine thousands of people dressed in their finest, gathered together with open mouths and trembling knees, craning their necks to see their brand-new king. Royal servants blow trumpets, and a golden crown is placed on top of the king’s head. This is their new ruler; the one person who makes all the country’s rules. Whatever the king decides is immediately carried out. Everybody, even the oldest, the smartest, and the most important people, must listen to him.

That, explained Mrs. Feigenbaum, is what happens on Rosh Hashana!

Except that Hashem is a much greater King than a person-king, which might make you feel like He’s way too up-there to pay attention to us fourth graders down here in Berryville. But no! When we hear the shofar and crown Hashem as King, then Hashem is actually the closest to us than any other time, paying a lot of attention to us.

And that’s why I’m doing Operation Shofar: so no one will miss out on being so close to Hashem at the greatest time of the year.

Every Rosh Hashana, Tatty goes to the retirement home and blows the shofar for people who can’t make it to shul. I asked Tatty if I could come with him this year, and he said yes! Bump-pa-da-dum— Operation Shofar, here we come!

Don't read! (Unless you can help me with my plans to become a five star general and blast

There isn’t going to be a goodbye party after all. But don’t worry—it’s actually a good thing.

You see, we were busy baking our masterpiece when Tatty came in to see what was going on. Like every time Rivky and I bake, things were getting exciting.

After digging out the huge cake mixer, being careful not to use salt instead of sugar like last time, and asking my sister Mushky to check the eggs, we turned on the mixer.

That’s when the bowl started spinning like a dreidel, faster and faster, splashing batter onto the ceiling, until it flew across

the kitchen and out the window. Rivky and I covered our heads with our hands, screaming for help.

Anyway, it’s a good thing Tatty walked by at that moment. He turned off the machine and asked what was going on.

I said that we were just trying to make a goodbye party for Hashem.

And then Tatty told us one pretty important detail: It’s true that the King goes back to the palace—but we go together with Him. And that means we don’t have to say goodbye. In fact, Aseres Yemei Teshuva, the days from Rosh Hashana till Yom Kippur, is a time when Hashem comes the closest ever to us.

Really, all year round Hashem is close to us, like we say in the 12 Pesukim, “'וֽהִנֵה ה נִצָּב עָלָיו—Hashem is standing over us.” He watches proudly, delighted every time we do a mitzvah or learn Torah. But during these ten days, we are even closer to Hashem than usual—right with Him in His palace. All we have to do is realize where we are, and turn to Hashem with more tefillah, Torah and mitzvos, ‘cause that’s how we come closer to Him. It’s like a huge hug, back and forth.

It was hard not to talk about the surprise all Shabbos long. But like always, I had lots of smart questions at the Shabbos table, which is a good thing—otherwise I would have slipped for sure.

See, Yom Kippur is coming up and I wanted to know what it’s all about. On Rosh Hashana we went to shul and davened. How is Yom Kippur any different?

Tatty asked, “Do you remember going to shul last Yom Kippur?”

Of course I did. For Yom Kippur, we rent out the big building at the

other side of Blueberry Forest. That’s because a bajillion more people come to shul on Yom Kippur than any other day, and we need a ginormous room to fit everyone.

“So many Yidden!” explained Tatty, “The smart ones and the simple ones, the rich and the poor, the big and the little, all come together on Yom Kippur for one thing: to make Hashem our King.”

“But Tatty,” I said, “We did that on Rosh Hashana!! We already crowned Hashem as King!”

“That’s right,” Tatty said, “We did. And on Yom Kippur we finish that job, by sealing the deal. Like when you make a card for someone and put it in an envelope, and then you glue the envelope closed so

“That’s why,” continued Tatty, “at the end of Yom Kippur, we all shout together, “ׁשְמַע יִׂשְרָאֵל—there is only one Hashem!” Then we say “בָּרּוְך שֵׁם”, announcing that Hashem is the King of the whole universe.”

I get it now. On Yom Kippur, all the Yidden get together like one person with one job: to announce that Hashem is the One Ruler.

Through being one with each other, we can be one with Hashem, too. What a onederful day!

And after Yom Kippur, Mommy’s birthday will be a wonderful day too. I can’t wait to show her all the surprises we’ve got planned.

I can’t believe we managed to keep Mommy’s birthday surprise a secret. She wasn’t expecting it at all! We decorated the room with yellow daisies (Mommy’s favorite flower) and the yellow streamers and balloons that I bought. The best part was when we presented Mommy with our project: a huge yellow polka-dot scrapbook with eight pages. Each page has a picture of a different kid

in the family, and next to the pictures are letters we wrote for Mommy wishing her lots of brachos.

Mommy loved our present. And funny enough, she said what gave her the most nachas was that we all worked together to make it. Aidel was right—the best present for a mommy is seeing all her kids getting along with each other.

True, being nice to brothers and sisters is hard…we

never seem to all agree with each other. So why did this birthday plan work? Maybe because we all had one goal: to make Mommy happy.

Which makes me wonder— imagine how much nachas Hashem has when all His Yidden come together in shul on Yom Kippur, with one project: making Him our King.

There were all kinds of people in shul today. Sitting next to me was a lady with a huge purple hat and a glittery purse. I guess she didn’t know that we can’t bring purses to shul on Yom Kippur. But I helped her find the pages in the machzor and follow along with the chazan, and I told her when to stand up and sit down.

At the end of Ne'ila, we all said “Shema Yisroel,” “Baruch Sheim,” and “Hashem Hu Ha’Elokim” really loud together. We announced once and for all that Hashem is King over us. The verdict has been stamped and sealed. Finally, we did it!

The men and boys sang Napoleon’s March and danced. The lady with the purple hat looked a little confused, so I smiled my biggest smile, and told her that we won over the Yetzer Hara and this is our victory march.

Suddenly I heard the loud blast of the shofar, and everyone shouted, “לְשָׁנָה הַבָּאָה בְּיְרּושָׁלָיִם—Next year in Yerushalayim!”

On Yom Tov, Tatty came home from shul singing and dancing (as usual) to the tune of “V’samachta b’chagecha…You must be happy, very, very happy…”

But this time I actually thought about it. “What do you mean,” I asked Tatty, “do we really have to be happy?”

“Yes!” Tatty said. “On Sukkos, being happy is a mitzvah. We are happy because we are so close to Hashem, doing the special mitzvos of sukkah, lulav, and davening, and Hashem is happy with us. That’s why Sukkos is called זמן שמחתינו—the time of our happinesses; us Yidden, and Hashem!”

I wasn’t so sure, though. Mitzvos aren’t always easy for me to do. Hachnasas orchim can be pretty tough…( Is it really possible to feel happy just because you’re doing a mitzvah?

Last night I learned what it means to be happy for real.

After dinner, we all went to the Simchas Beis Hasho’eva at a big shul. It was the funnest in the world! We stayed up three hours past our bedtime, the music was blasting, and there were cotton candy, ices, sour belts and soda. After the clown show, everyone started dancing and hyper kids were running around everywhere. My friends, cousins, and I were all laughing and spinning in a big circle, faster and faster, until I was fainting from the dizziness and sweat.

I was so relieved when my sister Mushky saved the day and brought me a bottle of water.

“Thank youuu!” I said, and put it right to my mouth.

Just then, in the middle of the blasting music and spinning dancing circles, I remembered what Tatty had said: “We are happy because we are doing Hashem’s mitzvos.”

We’re not just dancing for no reason; we’re dancing to celebrate our mitzvos. And making a bracha is a very important mitzvah.

So I stopped right there, in the middle of all the excitement, and I said the bracha carefully. Then I drank and drank and drank.

A funny thing happened. Instead of being annoyed that I had to stop and say a bracha, I actually felt happier.

I know what the Yetzer Hara tries to do. He tries to get kids all wild

and carried away and forget to do the right thing. But the best kind of being happy is when I remember Who is in charge, and the super-fantabulous power that He gave me to do His mitzvos—even when it’s hard.

Because that’s what a chayol needs to do: Be happy, really happy, and at the same time be smart and strong and do the right thing.

As I was thinking all this, I saw my new neighbor, Ruthie, standing on the side all alone. I ran over to her and danced her into the circle with all my cousins and friends. Her face lit up, and I knew she felt simcha shel mitzvah too.

Sicha 1

Did you know there’s a fast day this Friday? I didn’t even know there could be a fast on Erev Shabbos. But on our kitchen calendar, the Friday box says “Fast of Asara B’Teves” with a picture of Yerushalayim.

So I asked my mother, “What’s this fast all about? It can’t be

the destruction of the Beis Hamikdash—that’s Tisha B’Av! Are you really gonna fast even though it’s Erev Shabbos?”

“Sure,” Mommy said. “Asara B’Teves is so serious that even if it fell on Shabbos itself, we would fast. Luckily, that doesn’t happen because of the way our calendar is set up. It’s so serious because it’s the day that Nevuchadnetzar’s army surrounded Yerushalayim,

That made sense in the moment, but now that I think about it, I’m not sure I get it. I mean, I could think of some awful places to be stuck in—like the elevator at my school that barely works, or a giant can of mushrooms (not my taste!). But being stuck in Yerushalayim sounds wonderful to me. So why in the world is it a fast day? ׳ טבת ה

Sometimes I wonder: Do other kids have a sneaky, pesky, stinky Yetzer Hara like me? Does he also get other kids so frustrated at their siblings, that they’ll almost do something really, really not nice to them?

This morning started off like any good Sunday morning. I said Modeh Ani, washed negel vasser, davened, and did all the important things a chayol should do—especially on a day like today, Hey Teves.

I looked out the window and greeting me was the most luscious, sparkly sea of snow I’ve ever dreamed of. Before you could say “Meet you outside!” I was bundled up and knee-deep in that cold, delicious frost.

Then came the snowman: I rolled each ball carefully, from one end of the yard to the next, back and forth, till they were perfectly round and big as bike tires, and stacked each one neatly on top of the other.

Just then, little Menucha ran outside. “I wanna make a snowman!” she squealed, and, as fast as she could trudge through the snow, came hurtling towards my masterpiece.

“No Menucha,” I said, “this is my snowman! You can make your own, over there.”

But Menucha didn’t listen. She reached my snowman and started patting on her own snow.

Take Menucha away!!!” But Mommy didn’t hear. I could feel my heart pounding. And then it happened— Plop. Crunch.

My perfect, shining piece of art came smashing down, head first into the snow.

I wasn’t even thinking. I saw my gloved-up hands lift themselves and aim for Menucha, ready to push her down. No one was watching.

I looked up and remembered something important. Even though I can’t see anyone around, there is always Someone watching. And I wanted that Someone to be proud of me.

I took a step back, and breathed in real deep…then out…and in again.

It had just been my Yetzer Hara trying to take hold of me. Getting Menucha back wouldn’t make anything better anyway.

“Okay Menucha,” I heard myself say, “don’t worry about it. It’s just a snowman. We can make a new one.”

I’m still upset about my snowman breaking. But I sure am glad that I didn’t get into a fight with Menucha. At lunchtime, Mommy helped me talk with her about not touching my things and I hope she understood.

But…why is it so hard to hold myself back? This time I did it, but I’m not always successful. Why did Hashem give us a Yetzer Hara anyway?

It’s all coming together now. The reason why we have a stinky Yetzer Hara, why it picks on me so much, and why there’s a fast day on Friday.

It all happened this morning. I was getting my coat on quickly so I could make the school bus on time, when I saw Menucha running off down the hallway with my boots on her feet. I was about to really give it to her. Enough is enough! But before I could, I heard my smart big sister say, “Esty, I know you’re frustrated and in a rush, but don’t let your Yetzer Hara get you, once it does—you’re trapped!”

I wondered about that all the way to school. I had a long way to walk, since I did miss the bus. What does that mean, once the Yetzer Hara gets you, you’re trapped?

“Hmm…” said Mushkie, “I have a bedtime story that can help you with that.”

was hers. Of course, she knew that it was an aveirah, but the big, mean, Yetzer Hara was too strong to fight!

As I flew down the stairs toward the front door, I saw Mushkie sitting on the couch. “What?” I said. “Aren’t you coming?”

know the story of Mordechai and the three cheder boys? They knew that Haman was watching them, but they were not afraid to act like Yidden and speak like Yidden, even in front of their biggest enemy. When we do the right thing, we don’t need to be afraid of what other people think!”

Right then, Mommy passed by. She heard what I said and added, “That’s right Esty. It’s the job of the Yidden to be a shining light for all to see. We can be a light for everyone just by practicing Torah and mitzvos wherever we go.”

Mushkie agreed to go if Mommy would come too. So the whole family went together to the nursing home this year. Tatty read the megillah, and we handed out shalach manos. Then we girls went to a room where there were only ladies, and we sang and danced with them. You should have seen the smiles on their faces! Everyone was so happy. Even the non-Jewish workers joined in our dancing.

The best part is that I forgot about my fears of the Yetzer Hara, and

Mushkie got over her fears of looking weird. And in the end, we both saw there was nothing to be afraid of.

Instead, we made our little part of the world brighter, happier, and closer to Geulah. A happy Purim was had by all.

Yitzy was wrapped in a purple sheet twenty times his size. He was Mordechai, and his friends

The second boy said, “They make an evil plan, but it will be defeated; they make a plot, but it will not succeed, for Hashem is with us.”

The third boy said, “Until you are old, Hashem will be with you.”

Matzah and Me

Pesach
Print PDF
Sichos this piece is built on
Sicha 1Sicha 2

Source: Der Rebbe Redt Tzu Kinder (Second Edition) vol. 3 p. 38. Sicha of 18 Nissan, 5743.

This morning, I came one massive step closer to my ultimate goal: I, Esty from Berryville, was promoted to a three-star general! The first thing I did was make sure that everyone knew about it.

I made a new sign for my bedroom door. It says, “Esty, Three-Star General” in fancy letters that Mushkie wrote with her calligraphy pen. It’s decorated with precious stones that Baila and Yitzy, my little siblings, gathered for me from the backyard. And it’s taped onto a background of silver foil. (I thought gold foil would be more

appropriate, but my mother didn’t have any. I sure hope she gets some in time for my five- star general promotion!)

Well, it’s already 6:35 p.m., and a three-star general must get plenty of rest for the day ahead. I’m sure everyone will have lots of questions to ask me about my high-ranking position. Good night.

When I got to school, I saw another girl going to put her school bag in her locker. As the prestigious three-star general that I am, I gave her mine and said, “Locker number 302. Thank you.” and went off to class. But when I went to get my snack at recess time, I found my school bag on the floor—right in the middle of the hall.

Then, when Mrs. Feigenbaum asked for yesterday’s homework, I realized that I hadn’t finished the second page. Thinking quickly, I said, “With all due respect, Mrs.

Feigenbaum, I am a three-star general, so I am very busy.”

But Mrs. Feigenbaum just gave me an “incomplete” for the homework assignment, and with report cards coming up soon, that’s not helpful.

At lunchtime, I sat at the head of our class’s lunch table, expecting everyone to fight over who would sit near me. But everyone just sat at their usual places and chatted as always.

When I got home, I realized that I didn’t feel so good inside. The more honor I expected, the more people seemed to ignore me. I wonder if there’s a better way.

Today, Mrs. Feigenbaum took our class on a special trip to the matzah bakery.

We got to make our own matzah. It was hard work because we had to do everything fast. You only have eighteen minutes from mixing the flour and water ‘till taking the matzah out of the oven. When I help my mother make challah, she doesn’t rush like that! We leave the dough in a big bowl on the counter, covered with a towel. When we come back two hours later, the dough is a hundred times bigger.

At the bakery, we got to meet the head matzah baker, Rabbi Izzy Cohen. He asked us to tell him what’s special about matzah. I answered that matzah is special because it doesn’t rise. It’s flat and crispy.

Rabbi Izzy told us a special lesson we can learn from matzah: on

Pesach, we are careful not to eat chametz—dough that had time to rise and grow bigger. When we think too highly of ourselves, we are like chametz. On the other hand, when we are humble, we are like matzah. “No matter how great and important you become,” said Rabbi Izzy, “always try to be humble like matzah.”

That’s when it hit me. That’s what was behind my stomach ache all this time: the Yetzer Hara. He’s been trying to make me think I need lots of honor in order to feel happy and successful, but that’s not true! In fact, I think I feel a lot better when I focus on being kind and helping others instead of showing off and thinking about myself too much.

I decided to try out the humble thing because I was feeling awful. For the rest of the day, I went out of my way to think about others before myself. I tossed Yitzy a few baseballs to help him practice pitching. I gave Menucha a bath and read her a bedtime story. And when my friend Rivky called

to ask a question about homework, I gladly helped her.

My stomach ache is gone now, baruch Hashem, and I think my suspicions were correct. It’s a lot more fun to help others than to sit around all day, thinking about what everyone else can do for me.

This year’s Pesach sedarim were the best. I never ate so much matzah in my life. I’m trying to be as humble as possible, so I need all the help I can get—and what could help better than eating tons of matzah, the humblest food?

Before rachtza, Tatty told everybody that right after we say Hamotzi, we will say the special bracha for matzah: “Al achilas matzah.” We want to show that we are not eating regular bread, chas v’shalom, but pure matzah. And he asked, “Does anyone know why this is so important?”

I gladly shared the answer, I learned it in school: Pesach has two names: “Chag Hamatzos,” which means The Yom Tov of matzos, and “Zman Cheiruseinu,” which means The Time of Our Freedom.

If we act like the matzah, small and humble, then Chag Hamatzos becomes a time of freedom—free of the arrogant words of the Yetzer Hara.

Source: Der Rebbe Redt tzu Kinder (New Edition) Vol. 3 p. 9. Sicha of Rosh Chodesh Nissan, 5740.

שביעי של פסח When the Sea Split for Me Secret Journal!

Today I had my own Krias Yam Suf. That’s right, the sea split before my very own eyes.

It happened this morning as the sun's rays peeked through my bedroom curtains. I said Modeh Ani and washed negel vasser, then curled right back up under my blanket. Ahead of me was a big day with lots of missions and I didn’t know how I would do them all. There was shacharis with Hallel and Musaf, helping to cook for Shabbos, and taking a shower with a smile (ugh). Don’t forget Sefiras Ha’Omer! Oh, and continuing to eat lots of matzah to help me stay humble in my YH battle.

I felt like I would drown in the huge pile of to-do’s. I put my head under my pillow, blocking out the sun which was now shining even brighter into my room, and started to doze off to sleep again.

I jumped up, hearing my big sister’s voice calling. “We have six hundred more potatoes to peel. Do you want to have kugel this Shabbos or not?!”

“Six hundred potatoes?” I moaned, “I would rather stay in bed.”

As I said that, I looked over into the negel vasser water sitting there in the bowl. Spilling it out was yet another task on my endless list.

Suddenly, I wasn’t staring at a little bowl of water, but at the deep blue water of the Yam Suf 3,336 years ago. All around me are thousands of Yidden with sheep and donkeys and lots of little kids jumping up and down, excited to leave Mitzrayim once and for all. But the adults are arguing amongst themselves, “The Mitzrim caught up to us! They’re about to attack and shlep us all back to Mitzrayim!”

Moshe Rabbeinu’s voice can be heard, loud and clear: “Hashem has instructed us to keep going! Travel forward to Har Sinai and receive the Torah!”

Then, from within the crowd, a noble-looking man confidently steps forward—and jumps straight into the deep, blue sea of water. Nothing was going to stop Nachshon ben Aminadav. Deeper and deeper he walks until the water is up to his nose.

Suddenly, a massive miracle happens right before our very eyes! The water gushes away to the right and to the left, and then stands frozen in two great walls as high as the sky. We Yidden sing and dance as we walk forward on the dry ground.

Blinking and shaking my head, I was back in my room. Peering into my negel vasser again, I wondered, could I also be like Nachshon?

I jumped out of bed. Nothing could stop me. I have instructions from Hashem, and missions to accomplish. That sneaky Yetzer Hara was the one trying to tie me down with worries and fears.

The day flew by with amazing success. Thanks to all of us working together, we finished preparing for Shabbos early, and even had time to go to the park. Now I’m all ready in my Shabbos clothes an hour before licht bentchen!

And I learned an important lesson: Plunge forward and do great things. With Hashem’s help, it will work out in ways you can’t imagine.

So you see, Krias Yam Suf does happen to us, just in different ways. Like the story that happened a few days ago, on Erev Pesach. But maybe I’ll save that for another day.

I was standing in the kitchen squeezing oranges when I heard Mushky call out from the next room, “We forgot about Mrs. Goldfarb!”

During the past few days, we had brought matzah to all our neighbors who needed it. But Mrs. Goldbarb wasn’t home when we knocked on her door, and we decided we would try again before Pesach.

I looked outside. Good thing we’d finished burning the chametz already, because it was now pouring rain. And from the look of the dark gray sky, it wasn’t going to stop any time soon.

“I’m not sure we should go,” I told Mushky, who was now standing in the kitchen. “Who says she’ll even be home this time? She probably has some machine-made matzah she can use instead. With rain like this, the matzah will get all wet, and so will we.”

Thinking back, that was my Yetzer Hara trying to get me worried instead of moving ahead. I’m glad Mushky never gave me a chance to listen.

“No way,” she said, “Every Yid should have shmurah matzah for the seder.”

give tzedakah to Yidden in Eretz Yisroel, but I don’t have much money of my own. Now I had an idea. I called up my friend Dina, and we made a plan.

Today I learned a new trick. It’s a trick that can help me be a happier person. It can help me not to be such a kvetch. Maybe … just maybe … it can help me send that YH flying.

I first tried this trick at lunch when Rosie had pizza delivered

to the class in honor of her birthday. You know when those

boxes open and the smell of steaming, cheesy deliciousness

fills the classroom … everyone is thinking just one thing: I

Of course, the slices are never cut evenly. The pizza man

doesn’t use a ruler to measure each one (that’s what I

would do). And of course, I didn’t get a big slice; my

teacher handed me a perfectly medium one. Now, usually I would grumble, at least to myself, that everyone else got more pizza than I did. But today I noticed that some of the other slices in the box were, in fact, smaller than mine. And I appreciated that mine was bigger, and I didn’t look around to see if anyone else got more than me. I was much happier.

I tried this new way of thinking again when I got off

the school bus. My house has always seemed so small

I looked at it and counted the floors: one, two, three. I thought about the people in Africa who live in tiny wooden shacks and sleep on the floor. I thought about the robin who squeezes herself into the birdhouse hanging from our tree. I would not want to live there. Suddenly, when I walked through my front door, my house felt like a palace.

You may be wondering where I got this whole idea from. It all started with a mishna in Pirkei Avos class today: “Who is truly rich? Someone who is happy with what they have.”

Today I wanted to feel really rich, so I tried to be really happy with what I have. I woke

my desk. All twelve of them! Usually, I would look at my rank and say,

I get to the top. How am I ever gonna finish?! But today, I decided to be

happy with what I had. After all, so many kids have way less medals than me.

Before davening, I thought I’d be happy with the Tanya I’ve already memorized

this year, so I didn’t sing the new lines with my class.

I took my Chumash test, but I don’t think I did very well. I told myself I didn’t need to study, because if I just passed, I could be happy with my small accomplishment. After all, I’m sure there’s someone else in the universe who didn’t do as well as me.

I didn’t choose any vegetables from the school lunch today, since I’ve already eaten so many healthy foods in my lifetime, and I thought I could be happy with what I’ve already had.

But by the end of the day, I didn’t feel so happy and I realized that the Yetzer Hara was getting stronger.

This can’t be what the Mishna was talking about. I don’t think being satisfied with our mitzvos is a good thing.

Mussie’s father said it was something that usually only adults get to learn, because it’s full of difficult ideas. I didn’t understand a lot, but

my plans to become a five- star general and blast away

that when Moshiach comes, we’ll get to dig up the hidden treasures of Torah.

Every Shabbos, after davening in shul, my friends and I head downstairs to the kiddush. At a table in the back, we have cup-stacking contests, read the jokes in the shul

newsletter, and finish off trays of steaming kugel.

This past Shabbos, there was a new family in town. I saw

my mother welcoming them into shul. I asked her about them a few minutes later, and she told me that they had

By the time I skipped down the stairs after davening, I had forgotten all about the new family. But when everyone was settled at their tables, talking and eating, I saw them sitting quietly at the table in the back. One of the girls glanced in our direction—kind of like she wanted to join us, but was too shy. I was about to invite her over, but just then, my friend Malky asked me to pass the kugel, and I got completely distracted. Anyway, I was nervous. I’ve never met anyone from France before, and I don’t speak a word of French. What would I say to her?

Only six days till Shavuos! Do you know what happened on this day 3,336 years ago? The Yidden arrived at Har Sinai, and something unusual happened. As they set up their tents, washed their clothes, and got ready to receive the Torah from Hashem, nobody fought with each other! That might not sound like a big deal, but we’re talking about millions of people—from old bubbies to little babies—all camping out together.

Last summer, my family went on a camping trip to the forest and we all slept in tents. It was a lot of fun, but let’s just say it’s not easy to get along with all your sisters in one squishy tent…

Actually, as I’m writing this, I think I know how all the Yidden got along so nicely. It’s like that time my whole family piled into our van and drove to New York for Uncle Berel’s wedding. We were packed like pickles in a jar, but we were so excited for the wedding that we forgot to kvetch!

When everyone is excited for one thing together, being nice kind of just happens. And that’s what it must have been like counting down those last few days to Matan Torah. I mean, what could be more exciting than getting the Torah itself?

You know, I’ve been thinking about that new girl from France all week long. I would love to just play with my usual friends and laugh at our jokes (in English!) together, but with Shavuos coming up, I can hear my Yetzer Tov whispering: “Don’t forget about that French girl. Be nice to her, too!”

My sister Mushky had a good idea, as always. She said I don’t have to know French in order to be nice to the new girl in shul. I could just say “Good Shabbos,” and smile. That feels like something I could easily do. I’ll try it, and see what happens next.

Mushky’s idea was great. As it turns out, Rivka Algazi (the

new girl) actually knows lots of English, and she had no

Rivka taught me how to say “bonjour,” which means “hi.” It took me all day because you have to put your teeth together in a weird way to make the French “j” sound. Rivka couldn’t stop laughing while my friends and I tried copying her.

Rivka invited me to her house for “seudat shlishit.” Her family is Sefardi, and they have a big meal at the end of every Shabbos. Well, everything was going great ‘till I saw some cute baby peppers on the table and decided to try one. I took one juicy bite and suddenly my whole mouth felt like a fiery furnace. Rivka quickly passed me some water, but her baby sister couldn’t stop giggling at my face (which was as red as hot tamales).

Aidel is back from Eretz Yisroel (she came for Yom Tov and her best friend’s chasuna), and today she showed me lots of pictures she printed from her year in seminary. I never saw so many different-looking Yidden before. There were men with big, furry hats and long, curly peyos,

and kind before Shavuos, even with people who

all Yidden together. Aidel said that the people in her pictures come from all around the world. They speak different languages and dress in different ways. But they are all Yidden, and all Yidden share the same Torah. That’s what makes us all like one person. On Shavuos, we receive the Torah from Hashem. And the best way to prepare for that is by bringing lots of Yidden together with Torah.

I’m glad I’ve started to be friends with Rivka. It’s easier now that I understand how we’re all one nation of Yidden, like one person, even if we seem different on the outside.

I’m going to ask Rivka if she wants to join Tzivos Hashem. That’s a great way to bring Yidden together to receive the Torah.

I’m sure that when we all unite “like one person with one heart” to receive the Torah, happy and excited, Hashem will give us the greatest brachos.

My name is Yerachmiel Sender Alter. My friends call me Sender,

or Reb Sender. My wife calls me Sender Yerachmiel. My kids call me Tatty, but it’s usually more like,“Taaaaaaa-teeeeeee!”

What ordinary people don’t know is that I’m available twenty-four hours a day, six days a week to answer the calls of my chayol-friends around the world. It all started when a chayol named Benji from Australia had an emergency. He

The Whispered Tefilla

Rosh Hashana
Print PDF

On the first day of Rosh Hashana, which is also called יֹום ַהִַּזִָּכָרֹון—the day of remembering, we read in the Torah how Hashem remembered Sara Imeinu’s barrenness and blessed her with a son, Yitzchak. Here is the story of the haftorah:

Elkana and his wife Chana were childless for many years. Hoping that it would help her be blessed with a child, Chana arranged for her husband to marry a second wife, Penina. However, Penina went on to have ten children, and Chana had none.

Day after day, Chana’s pain grew deeper, her heart aching to have a child of her own. Penina’s constant talk about her own children made it

impossible for Chana to forget her painful situation.

Before each of the Shalosh Regalim, Chana, Penina, and Elkana would travel to the mishkan in Shiloh to spend Yom Tov in the presence of the Shechina. They would bring along their entire family and take a different route each year, gathering Yidden along the way to join them. In this way, Elkana brought many Yidden closer to Torah and mitzvos.

On one of these trips, Chana felt especially sad. As Chana’s pain overcame her, she entered the Mishkan and, facing the Kodesh Hakadoshim, began to weep. Chana poured out her heart, promising that if Hashem would hear her pain and

The Whispered Tefilla 2830, ב'תת"ל | Shiloh, Eretz Yisroel

give her a child, she would dedicate his entire life to Hashem.

As she quietly mouthed her tefilla, Eli the Kohen Gadol entered. The sight of Chana silently swaying back and forth and moving her lips looked strange to him, and Eli thought that she must be drunk. When he rebuked her, Chana answered, “No my master, I am a broken woman. I have drunk no wine, but it is my soul that I poured before Hashem.” Eli, understanding Chana’s greatness, told her that her tefillos would be accepted. Chana left with a happy heart.

A short while later, Chana and Elkana were blessed with a son, Shmuel. For two years, she waited at home, nursing and nurturing her miracle child. When Shmuel was weaned at two years old, Chana once again travelled to Shiloh with the rest of the family. She brought up a korban to thank Hashem, and told Eli, “I am the woman who beseeched Hashem

right here for a son. For this child I davened, and now I’m giving him to you to raise him in Shiloh, the place where Hashem’s Shechina rests.”

Despite having waited so many years to be blessed with a child, Chana willingly sacrificed her own need to bring up her son so that he may be raised in Hashem’s House and serve his nation. She was so overcome with joy that Shmuel would be raised in such a holy way, Chana the prophetess sang shira to Hashem.

In her shira, Chana tells many nevuos. In fact, according to the Targum, her entire song hints to important events in Jewish history all the way to the final geula. She predicts the future of her son, Shmuel Hanavi, who had the great zechus of anointing Dovid Hamelech, the first of all the kings of Yehudah—the last of whom, of course, is Moshiach.

The Most Special Kapparos

Aseres Yemei Teshuvah
Print PDF

One year, on the night before Yom Kippur, a Chassid asked Reb Elimelech of Lizhensk if he could watch how the tzaddik does kapparos.

“Well, how do you do kapparos?” Reb Elimelech replied.

The Chassid lowered his eyes. “I’m just a simple Yid,” he said. “I hold the chicken in one hand and a siddur in the other, and I say the tefillah of ’‘ֶזֶה ֲחֲִלִיָפִָתִי.”

But the Chassid wasn’t satisfied. “Rebbe, for more than twenty years, I’ve come to spend Aseres Yemei Teshuva with the Rebbe. But I’ve never seen the Rebbe do kapparos. I know it must be very special.”

Reb Elimelach looked at him. “You want to see something special? Then go watch how Moshe the Innkeeper does kapparos.”

He traveled to Moshe’s inn at the edge of a nearby town and asked if he could stay for the night.

“I’m sorry, but we don’t have any available beds,” Moshe replied. “You can stay at the inn down the road.”

“Please,” the Chassid begged. “I’m very tired. I can rest in a corner.”

Moshe hesitated, then nodded. “Alright,” he said, letting the Chassid in.

The room inside was filled with Goyishe peasants drinking mashke. But after some time, Moshe sent everyone away for the night. At last, the room was empty.

The Chassid lay down under one of the tables and waited to see what would happen.

Before morning, Moshe got up, washed his hands and quietly said the morning brachos. He then whispered to his wife, “Yentel, it’s time for kapparos. Please bring me the notebook from the shelf.”

The Most Special Kapparos תקל"ג–תקמ"ז (1770s–1780s)

Moshe sat down on a small stool and lit a candle. The soft light flickered across the room. Yentel brought his notebook, and he began to read through a list of all the aveiros he had done that year.

“One day I spoke lashon hara,” he said in a broken voice. “Another day, I woke up too late to daven. Another time I forgot to give tzedakah.”

As he kept reading, his voice began to shake. Tears filled his eyes and ran down his cheeks. Page after page, Moshe read and cried, until he reached the very end.

After a few moments, he called out again. “Yentel, please bring me the second notebook.”

She dutifully brought it over, and Moshe opened it up.

This notebook was different. Here, Moshe had written down every difficulty that had happened to him over the course of that year.

“One day, the peasants beat me,” he read. “Another day, my child became very sick. In the winter, we had no wood and the inn was freezing cold for many nights. Then our cow died, and we had no milk.”

His voice grew quieter with each word. When he finished, Moshe lifted his eyes toward the

sky. “Hashem,” he cried out, “I know I didn’t do everything right. I promised last year that I would be better, but I wasn’t always strong enough.”

He paused, holding the notebook tightly. “But I also trusted You. I asked for a good year, and I believed that You would make that happen.”

The room was very still. “Hashem, today is Erev Yom Kippur,” Moshe continued. “It’s a time when we forgive each other.”

A Mitzvah's Reward

Print PDF

The weary traveler to Berditchev shook his head. “No,” he said. “You cannot have my esrog. Let me continue on my way, for I must hurry home for Yom Tov.”

“But you can spend it here with us, in Berditchev,” pleaded the Chossid. “And then Reb Levi Yitzchok and our entire town will be able to fulfill the mitzvah of lulav and esrog!”

Despite the Chossid’s heartfelt pleas, the traveler refused to stay.

Word of the esrog's departure reached Reb Levi Yitzchok, who hurried to meet the traveler. “Please, consider staying with us for Yom Tov,” Reb Levi Yitzchak begged. “There is not one esrog in the entire town of Berditchev. You are our only hope!”

The traveler, determined to spend Yom Tov at home, wasn’t convinced.

Reb Levi Yitzchak’s desire to fulfill the mitzvah of lulav and esrog overcame him, and he turned to the visitor once more. “If you stay and allow us to use your esrog, you will share in my portion of Olam Haba.”

Stunned, the traveler agreed. The people of Berditchev were overjoyed.

A few hours before Yom Tov, a messenger appeared at the traveler’s inn. “I have instructions for you from Reb Levi Yitzchok,” he informed the innkeeper. “Don’t allow the traveler with the esrog inside your sukkah!” The messenger continued on his way, passing on the instructions to everyone in Berditchev.

On the first night of Sukkos, the traveler returned from shul ready to make kiddush and eat the Yom Tov seuda. But as he tried to enter the sukkah, the innkeeper blocked his way!

“Please let me in,” said the traveler. “I can’t make kiddush outside of the sukkah!”

The traveler had to look elsewhere for a place to eat. He walked to the neighbor’s sukkah and asked if he could celebrate Sukkos with them. To his utter bewilderment, the neighbor refused. As he continued looking for a place to make kiddush, the answer was always no.

The traveler grew suspicious. Why was everyone turning him down? He questioned some of the residents, pestering them until they revealed Reb Levi Yitzchok’s instructions.

Frustrated, he ran to Reb Levi Yitzchok, and cried, “Is this how you repay me?”

“If you disregard my promise of being with me in Gan Eden,” replied Reb Levi Yitzchok, “I will let you enter my sukkah.”

The traveler stood rooted to the spot. How could he choose? It took some moments before he concluded: fulfilling the mitzvah of sitting inside a sukkah is more important than all the rewards of Olam Haba! “I agree,” he said.

Reb Levi Yitzchok invited the traveler to eat in his sukkah. He turned to him and remarked: “I made a promise to you, and I will keep it. You will indeed get a share in my Olam Haba. But it was necessary that you should work to deserve it. Once you showed that you were willing to give up the share in order to do a mitzvah, you were able to receive this lofty reward.”

A Mitzvah’s Reward תק”ע-ֻסֻּכֹות תק”כ (Late 1700s) Berditchev, Ukraine

The Very Stones Were Dancing

For many years, Reb Levik was the rav of Yekaterinoslav, a large city in Ukraine, helping Yidden stay strong in their Yiddishkeit. But one day, everything changed. The police arrested Reb Levik for spreading Torah and mitzvos, and sent him to a small, faraway village in Kazakhstan called Chi'ili. His wife, Rebbetzin Chana, bravely traveled there to be with him.

Sukkos was coming, but all that Reb Levik and Rebbetzin Chana had was one small rented room. There was no shul, no minyan, and hardly any other Yidden. How would they get a sukkah for Yom Tov?

She looked at the unfinished hut. “And where is the roof?”

“We don’t have enough money yet,” Reb Levik answered. “For now, we will use leaves. Before winter comes, we will build it properly.”

Sukkos soon arrived. One other Yid joined them for the Yom Tov meals. They ate the little food they had, feeling so happy to be sitting in a sukkah.

Back home, they would celebrate with hundreds of Yidden at Reb Levik’s shul. But here, there was no shul, no crowd, and not even a Sefer Torah. It was just the two of them and their small room.

The Very Stones Were Dancing ֲעֲֶצֶֶרֶת תש״ג ְׁשִׁמִיִנִי

The familiar words of ַָאַָּתָה ָהְָרְֵאֵָת filled the room. Then, Reb Levik began to dance. Step by step, he danced around the narrow space between his bed and the table, singing the same special tune that he would sing back home—the one famously called “Reb Levik’s Niggun”. As the night continued, his voice rose higher, his steps grew quicker, and his dancing became more alive as his deep love for the Torah shone brightly on his face.

Rebbetzin Chana was filled with emotion as she watched her husband dance. She remembered how it was back at home: When Reb Levik would dance on Simchas Torah, it seemed like the very stones danced with him!”

And that night, as Reb Levik danced alone in the tiny room, it felt the same way.

Over the following year, more Yidden arrived in the village. On Rosh Hashana, they all gathered together to daven. They even got hold of a Sefer Torah! But who would lead? None of them knew how.

And so, Reb Levik stepped forward. He led the davening, leined from the Torah, and blew the shofar that Rebbetzin Chana had brought from home. He did it all in his special, heartfelt way, leaving many people deeply inspired.

Thankfully, that Simchas Torah, he didn't have to celebrate alone. Full of joy, Reb Levik sang and danced together with the other Yidden. And in those moments, many of them forgot their troubles. They felt uplifted to a higher, holier place.

This is how Reb Levik spent his last two years of Simchas Torah, תש”ג )1942( and תד"ש )1943(:

One year, he danced alone in a small room, and the next, he shared the joy with fellow Yidden, carrying them above their pain and filling them with simcha.

No matter his surroundings, Reb Levik rose above them all and celebrated with holiness and joy, uplifting others along with him— until the very stones were dancing, too.

The Gift of Giving

Channukah

Benny ran outside for recess, but stopped on the stairs. He had noticed the new boy, Aizik, standing alone.

He never joins in our games, Benny thought. Maybe it’s because he doesn’t know much English yet. He just arrived here after the war with other refugee boys. He must miss his family back in Europe so much.

“Hey, Aizik,” he called out. “Can you believe it’s almost Chanukah? I already went to the store to choose the new bike I’m getting with my Chanukah gelt! What are you doing with your gelt?”

“Oh, I wish I’d get some,” Aizik said sadly. “I just got a letter that my little sister Golda is very krank and needs penicillin*

to get better. But my parents can’t afford the medicine.”

During afternoon classes, Benny just couldn’t concentrate. The minute the last bell rang, he gathered his friends and repeated the conversation he’d had with Aizik. “We have to do something!”

“You know how much I wanted that bike, but I think I’m going to give my gelt to Aizik, and if we all chip in…”

Everyone readily agreed. That night, Benny wrote a letter.

I put a blue bicycle on hold in your back room so that I could purchase it with my Chanukah allowance. However, my friends and I have decided to pool our money for a better purpose, so that our classmate Aizik can send medicine to an ill family member in Europe. Please sell the bike to another customer.

Chanukah came. All the boys gathered around Aizik during recess. “This is a present for Golda,” Benny said shyly, stepping forward and handing him a package. Aizik tore it open.

“Penicillin!” Aizik cried out, tears welling in his eyes. “How can I ever thank you?”

“It’s nothing,” the other boys mumbled. They, too, were crying.

That evening, after lighting the menorah, Benny’s father said, “A letter came for you in the mail today.”

Benny opened the letter from Best Brooklyn Bicycles nervously. Were they asking him why he didn't pick up his bike? Had the letter with his instructions about the bicycle gotten lost?

Thank you for your letter in which you told us why you wouldn’t be buying a bike from us. Benny, we think that you and your friends did a remarkable thing and we have decided to keep that bike in the back room—until you can come to the store and claim it as a gift.

P.S. Tell your friends to come with you. We have a present for each one of them. And one for Aizik, too.

“Oh!” Benny exclaimed. “This is the best Chanukah ever!”

*Nowadays you can easily get this antibiotic from your doctor, but in Aizik and Benny’s time, it was rare and expensive.
