The Seventy-Two Rooms

Asarah B'Teves
Print PDF

It’s Asara B’Teves. Everyone bends over their siddurim, saying selichos in low, serious voices. Line by line, they remember the tragedies that happened to the Yidden in the month of Teves.

Soon, they reach the words: “ּוֶמֶֶלְֶך ָיָָוָן ִאְִנְַסִַנִי ִלְִכְֹּתֹב ָדָת ְיְָוִָנִית—And the Greek king forced me to write the Torah in Greek.”

When was the Torah translated to Greek? And why is that sad enough to mention in selichos?

*** More than two thousand years ago, the powerful King Talmai (Ptolemy) ruled over Mitzrayim and Yavan (Greece).

He had wealth, power, and a vast empire. But what he loved most was his enormous library, filled with books and scrolls from around the world.

“I want the Torah in my library,” King Talmai declared. “But it’s in Hebrew, and I can’t understand it. I must have it translated into Greek!”

When a king gives an order, no one dares to refuse. “Guards!” he commanded. “Bring me seventy-two of the greatest Jewish sages!”

The officers hurried to obey. Soon, seventy-two talmidei chachamim stood before the king.

But King Talmai didn’t tell them why they had been brought there. Before they could speak to one another, he sent each talmid chacham into a separate room. Then, going from room to room, he gave them all the same command: “Translate the Torah into Greek!”

The Seventy-Two Rooms 8 Teves, 3515 (Just over 100 years before the Chanuka miracle)

But soon, they all realized the same problem: In thirteen places, a correct translation could cause King Talmai to misunderstand the Torah. They would have to change the words to express the Torah's true meaning.

But what if each talmid chacham made different changes? What if the translations didn’t match? King Talmai would be furious!

There was no way to know what the others were writing. They each had to decide on their own.

Finally, on Ches Teves, the translations were finished.

“Lay out the scrolls and compare them!” King Talmai ordered.

The guards obeyed. To the chachamim's amazement, every translation was identical. All seventy-two chachamim had made the exact same thirteen changes!

But surprisingly, the chachamim didn't celebrate. They saw this as one of the saddest days in Jewish history—as tragic as the day the Yidden made the Eigel Hazahav.

Chazal didn’t compare the translation to bowing to the Eigel. They compared it to the day that the Eigel was made.

On that day, no one had worshipped it yet. But what had been created? The possibility for the aveira to happen later.

The same was true on Ches Teves. The chachamim had translated the Torah carefully, and Hashem even made a neis to protect them.

But still, they saw what could happen later. Now that the Torah was available in Greek, anyone could learn it anywhere. Instead of being taught in an environment of warmth and kedusha by teachers with Yiras Shamayim, it could be misunderstood and even misused. This possibility is what made Ches Teves such a sad day.

We can learn from this, too. Sometimes, things seem fine at first—a new book, an exciting game, a funny comment.

But a Yid stops and thinks: Where could this lead? Will it still be good later?

The Poisonous Plot

Chof Teves

Throughout Cairo and the surrounding lands, the Rambam was famous as both a great talmid chacham and a brilliant doctor. So when the sultan chose him to be his personal doctor, everyone was happy.

I used to be the sultan’s doctor, Hakim fumed. Now nobody thinks I’m important, all because of the Rambam!

Each day, Hakim grew more jealous. I must get rid of him, he thought.

He rushed to the palace and bowed low before the sultan. “Your Majesty,” he declared. “I have discovered that the Rambam is planning to poison you!”

“I will prove it.” Hakim’s eyes flashed. “Tell both of us that someone is trying to poison you, and order us to prepare a medicine that will save your life.

“All doctors know,” the evil man continued, “that a stronger poison can stop a weaker poison from working. The honest doctor will bring the strongest poison possible, because he wants to save you. But the one who is really plotting against you will bring a weaker poison, so that the poison in your food will still work.”

The sultan narrowed his eyes. “How will I know whose poison is stronger?”

“We will do a little test,” Hakim said, his smile widening. “I will drink the Rambam’s poison first, and then my own. If I live, it will show that my poison is stronger. Then the Rambam will drink mine, and then his own. If he dies, you will know that his poison was weaker, and that he was the one plotting against you.”

The sultan agreed to the plan. The next day, he called both doctors to the palace and told them about the dangerous test.

As the Rambam rode home, he wondered why Hakim looked so smug. Surely Hakim knew that the Rambam could prepare a stronger poison. What trick was he hiding?

But at home, there was no more time to wonder. His waiting room was full of patients and people with Torah questions. The Rambam helped each one, then davened ma’ariv, learned, and wrote late into the night.

Only when he lay down to rest did the Rambam understand Hakim’s plot. I know what to do, he thought.

The next morning, after davening and learning, the Rambam prepared a mixture of red wine and water. Then, he rode to the palace.

At the sultan’s signal, the two doctors exchanged bottles and drank both mixtures.

For a few moments, no one moved. Suddenly, Hakim cried out in pain and fell

“Your Majesty,” the Rambam said, “I didn’t kill Hakim. His own plan killed himself.”

“What do you mean?” The sultan asked in amazement.

“You see,” the Rambam explained, “Hakim drank a slow poison before coming to the palace. Then he gave me a harmless drink, expecting me to bring a strong poison. He thought my poison would save him, but would make me die.

“I realized his trick, so I also brought a harmless mixture. Since Hakim never received the poison he was counting on, the slow poison he had already taken caused him to die.”

The sultan laughed in amazement. “Rambam, you are not only the greatest doctor. You are also the wisest of men! From now on, you will be my advisor, as well.”

Indeed, the Rambam faithfully served the sultan as both royal doctor and advisor. Yet, despite the honor, he stayed humble; helping the sick, teaching Torah, and writing the sefarim that continue to guide Yidden today.

The Secret Inside the Trees

Chamisha Asar B'shvat

“Yankel, please read the next letter,” the melamed said.

Yankel bent over his page. His finger rested on the letter, but his eyes were looking out the window.

He looked around the room. One boy was drawing something in the frost on the window. Another was whispering to the boy next to him. The melamed closed the siddur for a moment and took a deep breath.

These boys weren’t trying to make trouble. They were farm boys. They loved running in the fields, helping their fathers stack the hay, and taking care

of the animals. Sitting in cheder was hard for them.

Still, the melamed felt discouraged. If they can barely read the alef-beis, he thought, how will they ever learn Torah?

On Chamisha-Asar B’Shvat, the melamed had a day off. He wrapped himself in his worn coat and walked out of the village toward the forest. How do trees celebrate their Rosh Hashana? he wondered, as the snow crunched under his boots.

He looked at the forest and stopped. The trees were bare. Their branches were covered with thick white snow. They don’t look like they’re celebrating, thought the melamed. They look almost dead.

Just then, a strong wind blew through the trees. The branches swayed and the snow sparkled in the sunlight. To the melamed, the white snow now looked like Yom Kippur talleisim and kittelach, and the wind sounded like whispered tefillos.

He stood very still and listened. Suddenly, everything changed before his eyes.

The melamed could see through the sparkling snow and through the bumpy bark, as if the trees were made of clear glass.

And deep inside the branches, tiny green sprouts were pushing closer to the outside. They hadn’t come out yet, because the world was still too cold. But no doubt, life was stirring. New buds were waiting for the right time to blossom, when Hashem would send warmth and sunshine.

The melamed stared in wonder. “These trees are not dead,” he whispered. “They are full of life inside.”

A gust of wind blew snow into his face. He closed his eyes. When he opened them again, the forest looked back to normal. The trees were still white and bare; no hints of growth in sight.

As he walked back to the village, he thought about his students.

I only see the outside, he thought. I see boys who mix up daled and reish. I see boys who draw on the windows instead of focusing. But inside every one of them is a neshama. Inside, every one of them has hidden kochos, waiting to bud and blossom.

The next day, Yankel mixed up the letters again. This time, the melamed didn’t sigh. He bent down gently and pointed.

“Look carefully,” he said with warmth. “A daled has a little corner. Try again.”

Tatty’s shlichus felt unimportant. Was it worth the effort?

Tatty and Mommy always dreamed of being shluchim of the Rebbe. But when they couldn’t find a place to go on shlichus, they decided to move to Postville, Iowa, where Tatty became a shochet.

Never giving up on his dream to be a shliach, Tatty worked hard to help the Yidden in Postville connect to Hashem. He taught Chassidus to the frum families and workers in town. He traveled to faraway places to meet Jewish people who weren’t frum and teach them about Yiddishkeit. Tatty also sent bochurim on mivtzoyim to find more Yidden and help them do mitzvos.

Over time, Tatty officially became the shliach of Northeast Iowa, and we opened a Chabad House with a library and visitor center.

But sometimes, he felt unsure. While other shluchim were making big events for hundreds of people, Tatty and Mommy were only helping one or two Yidden at a time.

Does our shlichus really matter? He wondered. Maybe we should move somewhere else, where we’ll be able to have a bigger impact.

One year on Gimmel Tammuz, this question was bothering Tatty a lot. He went to the Ohel

and poured out his heart to the Rebbe. Please, Rebbe, show me if our shlichus in Postville is making a difference.

After leaving the Ohel, Tatty checked his phone and noticed an email from someone named Rabbi Martin Rosenfeld. He didn’t recognize the name at first, but when he read the email, his eyes widened in surprise.

Rabbi Rosenfeld was writing to let Tatty know that he was printing an article in The Jewish Link, a publication sent to families across the Tri-State area of New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut. Titled, “Making a Difference in the World of Kiruv,” the article was all about how Tatty’s shlichus had inspired him!

In the article, Rabbi Rosenfeld described his visit to Postville years before:

I was once in Postville and met a Chabad shliach named Rabbi Schimmel. I asked him, “How do you spend your day as a shliach if everyone in your community is already frum?”

Rabbi Schimmel told me what he does for the local Yidden. Then, he described how he travels to nearby towns to find Yidden and share Torah and mitzvos with them—one Yid at a time.

Submitted by Yosef Yitzchok, 12 Shneior Zalman, 9 Meshulam Zushe Schimmel, 7

Rabbi Schimmel’s shlichus taught me that you can’t wait for Jewish people to come to you; you need to go out and find them. He inspired me to do this in my own life and look for Yidden whom I can help.

Rabbi Rosenfeld ended the article by encouraging others to do the same: Anyone can make a difference and help another Yid. You just have to go out and look for them.

Tatty stared at his phone screen in shock. Just minutes after asking the Rebbe to show him if his shlichus was making a difference, this email had arrived at his inbox!

Not only was a Yid (whom Tatty barely remembered!) deeply inspired by our shlichus, but he was encouraging thousands of others to learn from Tatty and do the same!

All of Tatty’s doubts vanished in an instant. He began working with much more chayus, knowing that his shlichus was making a big difference.

This year, Tatty felt doubts creep up again. Are we really needed here? he wondered. Maybe we should move somewhere else, where we could have a bigger impact.

At that very moment, Tatty received a message from Hachayol, asking if they could publish this story in an upcoming magazine.

This is amazing! Tatty thought. Once again, the Rebbe heard my difficulties. And once again, he found a way to tell me that my shlichus is making a difference, however hard it may be.

And of course, once again, Tatty resolved to continue our important shlichus in the way that the Rebbe wants—one Yid at a time.

My family is on shlichus in the tropical city of Cairns, Australia, very far from other frum families. The closest shliach lives so far away that it takes more than a whole day to drive there!

Cairns is a beautiful place. Our Chabad house is surrounded by wonders of Hashem’s world, including the ocean’s Great Barrier Reef and the leafy-green Daintree Rainforest.

But living in Cairns also means living with something dangerous: cyclones. A cyclone is a huge storm with strong winds and heavy rain. Cyclones are so powerful that they can flood houses and push trees to the ground. In other parts of the world, this type of storm is called a hurricane.

Years ago, a cyclone swept through Cairns, and many people lost their homes. Baruch Hashem, our Chabad House remained safe, and we opened our doors to Jewish families who needed somewhere to stay until they could find a new place to live.

In the month of Shvat, 5781 (2021), just before one of our big community events,

we heard worrisome news: Tropical Cyclone Kimi was on its way, headed straight toward Cairns.

The whole city began to prepare. Shops closed, windows were boarded up, and many people left for safer places.

Inside of our house, though, everything felt calm. Tatty told us that he was going to write to the Rebbe for a bracha, and we knew that the Rebbe would help.

Tatty went into his office and sat down at his desk. If the cyclone comes, he thought, the streets will flood and the event will be canceled. He picked up his pen to ask for a bracha that the event should go on as planned.

Then, Tatty paused. There’s something more important than the event: I should ask that no one gets hurt.

LAST TIME: The Maharal and Rav Betzalel return from Worms, greatly impressed with Reb Eliyahu Baal Shem’s love and care for his fellow Jews, as well as his scholarship. They resolve to fight to defend his reputation against those proposing a cherem against him. A New Kind

The original Pinsk yeshiva was supported by an orphan from Karlin named Tevel. Tevel was a humble, kind, but unlearned Jew who hid the wealth which he’d gained from growing his father’s beekeeping business. Tevel regularly gave large sums of money to the Rav of Pinsk to distribute anonymously.

Early one morning, as young Tevel hurried to the shul in Karlin for shacharis, he heard muffled sounds coming from a garden nearby. He listened more closely, and realized that it was a young girl crying. He felt both pity for the poor girl’s suffering, and also curiosity. The Jewish owners of the inn, as far as he knew, led a coarse lifestyle similar to their customers, the local peasants.

Tevel discovered that the young woman was the inn’s newly-hired maid. An orphan from a young age, Chava Devorah had no one to look after her. She had to put up with harsh working conditions and much verbal abuse at the hands of the innkeeper and his wife. With the help of his mentor, the Rav of Pinsk, Tevel rescued Chava Devorah from the inn. He eventually married her, and gave her half of his fortune to use as she pleased.

Chava Devorah had taught herself to read and understand the basic Hebrew of Chumash, which made her the more learned of the two. She began to teach Tevel what she knew. As the young couple advanced in their studies, they hired a young Torah scholar to live with them and teach them more Torah. Over time, they both became quite knowledgeable. But, like the money that they gave to tzedakah, they kept their learning a secret.

Meanwhile, the old Rav of Pinsk left and was replaced by Rav Naftali Katz of Prague (who we will meet in the following chapter). Rav Naftali soon insisted that Tevel and Chava Devorah reveal their generosity to the public, so that all of Pinsk may learn from and model their kindness. They agreed to do so, but only if they could avoid any resulting honor by moving far away. Thus, after forty years of supporting the Pinsk yeshiva in secret, the middle-aged couple moved on to Cracow—but not before the local yeshiva received a new name due to their generous support: Tevel and Chava Devorah’s Yeshiva.

There were three distinguished yeshivos in Pinsk. The first and oldest one was “Tevel and Chava Devorah’s Yeshiva”, another was called “Reb Shimon’s Yeshiva”, and the one most recently built was known as “Bubbe Golda Leah’s Yeshiva”. Each of those men and women were Baalei tzedakah who supported the yeshivos, and each had a fascinating story behind their donation.

The second famous Pinsk yeshiva was called Reb Shimon’s Yeshiva. Reb Shimon was a nephew of the Maharshal, Reb Shlomo Luria. Reb Shimon did not have the head for learning, but he loved Torah with all his heart. So, when Reb Shimon went into the diamond business, he was determined to use his wealth to support yeshivos. His first project was in his hometown of Pinsk: he convinced a learned relative to come to Pinsk to found a new yeshiva, and promised to fund it.

But he didn’t stop there. During his many business travels, Reb Shimon observed how the poor kehillos of Poland and Lithuania lacked structured schools of learning. And so, he dedicated his efforts to helping these communities establish yeshivos, too.

Once, on his birthday, he and his wife discovered a buried treasure of many clay pitchers brimming with gold coins. He drew up a contract with the Rav, whereby they committed most of the buried treasure to support hundreds of yeshivos throughout Eastern Europe.

“Bubbe” Golda Leah was a midwife by profession, who was at the side of every woman in town who gave birth. But this extraordinary lady was involved in helping the Pinsk community in many other ways, too. Most of all, she dedicated herself for the sick, visiting their homes to care for them and their families personally. She often pulled her husband away from his work as a tailor to help in these vital efforts.

She was also a mikvah attendant and Torah teacher. She taught the local women how to completely live their lives according to the Torah, influencing them to refine their middos and inspiring them with stories of righteous women through the ages.

Bubbe Golda Leah was also known to give brachos to women who were suffering from miscarriage, stillborns, or sickly children. News of her success spread throughout the region, far beyond Pinsk. She refused payment for her services, but when a woman insisted, she would pass the funds on for a newly- established yeshiva. While the other two yeshivos in Pinsk were mainly for married men, this yeshiva was unique in that it was for younger bachurim.

Bubbe Golda Leah soon became the yeshiva’s main donor. Over time, as her fame increased, her contributions grew, and the yeshiva became known as “Bubbe Golda Leah’s Yeshiva”.

And during davening, he would gather all the little ones around him and help them say “Amen”, “Baruch Hu Uvaruch Shemo”, and the words of kedusha at the appropriate times.

Unfortunately though, one by one, all of Reb Yisrael Chaim’s children passed away when they were still babies. One son, Simcha, lived longer. Reb Yisrael Chaim and his wife were so hopeful that this time, Hashem had granted them what they were waiting for! But sadly, at age five, little Simcha passed away as well.

The whole community showed up to Simcha’s funeral. There wasn’t a dry eye in the crowd; everyone felt the pain of Reb Yisrael Chaim and his wife. Reb Yisrael Chaim himself appeared quiet and calm. “We hoped this son would live,” said Reb Yisrael Chaim, his eyes downcast. “But Hashem gives, and Hashem takes; may Hashem’s name be blessed.”

Just then, a very old, disheveled- looking man pushed to the front. His name was Asher Yehonasan; everyone in Posen knew him as the town meshugane. He never talked to anyone, and mostly spent his time in the attic of the shul muttering to himself and pacing back and forth. So everyone was shocked when they heard Reb Asher Yehonasan give the following speech:

“My fellow Jews. It has been some fifteen years since the Satan

became jealous of this righteous couple's holy behavior. The Satan was afraid that Reb Yisrael Chaim would force him out of his job, for because of his efforts with Yiddishe children, they were doing more mitzvos than a v e i r o s !

“The Satan therefore asked permission to put Reb Yisrael Chaim to the test, and see if he would continue to be as dedicated to Torah and mitzvos even through pain and suffering. That is why they have been struck with this terrible tragedy. Rabosai, I am now ninety-four years old. Two months from now, I will be leaving this world. When I arrive in the olam ha-emes, I promise to call the Satan to a din Torah for having caused Reb Yisrael Chaim and his wife so much suffering! Enough is enough!”

Reb Asher Yehonasan turned towards Reb Yisrael Chaim. “I will insist that you be blessed with a healthy son; a son who will live for many years, have great talents, and grow up to be a leader among our people. On one condition: you must name your son after me, Asher Yehonasan.”

With that, Reb Asher Yehonasan disappeared back into the crowd.

People didn’t know what to think. Was Reb Asher Yehonasan really a hidden tzaddik, someone with access to what was going on in shamayim? Or was this all just a fantasy he made up, another symptom of his craziness?

At first the townspeople were split. But when exactly two months later, a healthy-looking Reb Asher Yehonasan passed away,

there were no more doubts. Reb Asher Yehonasan’s crazy behavior had all been an act to disguise his tzidkus.

In the year 5425 (1665), exciting news started to spread throughout Jewish communities across Europe: Moshiach was on his way! A man named Shabsai Tzvi had declared himself to be Moshiach ben Dovid. Jews began to sell their businesses and properties, and prepared to rush to Eretz Yisrael as soon as Shabsai Tzvi would announce it was time.

The Jewish people were so broken from years of suffering and persecution, that they so desperately wanted to believe Moshiach had indeed arrived. And so, they trusted Shabsai Tzvi’s words, despite a few warning signs that something was not quite right: Shabsai Tzvi did certain actions publicly that were against halacha: he said the Shem Hameforash2 out loud; he ate cheilev3; and he ate and drank on fast days. He excused it all by saying that though these things were forbidden by the revealed halacha, they were permitted according to the secrets of kabbalah. Some rabbanim sent out letters as soon as they noticed these things, warning people that this Shabsai Tzvi was not the real Moshiach. But unfortunately, many weren’t aware of—or didn’t pay attention to—these issues.

Shabsai Tzvi continued to travel around and spread word that he was Moshiach, until reaching the Middle East along with his assistant, Nassan of Gaza. When he arrived in Constantinople, in the year 5426 (1666), he was arrested by the Sultan for the crime of trying to overthrow the crown. The Sultan gave Shabsai Tzvi two choices: either convert to Islam, or be put to death for treason. Shabsai Tzvi chose to convert, rachmana litzlan. It was this action that proved once and for all that Shabsai Tzvi was not Moshiach.

The whole saga of Shabsai Tzvi had devastating effects for Jews all over Europe. It shattered countless hopes and dreams, and weakened the emunah of many. Some Jews, unfortunately, continued to believe in Shabsai Tzvi. And

the story of Shabsai Tzvi proved that teaching kabbalah was just too dangerous. If kabbalah had led to the Shabsai Tzvi tragedy, who knew what else it could lead to?

Oh, hi. You must be Ovadia? We’re the Levin kids, and we’re excited to host you on our podcast!

Reb Ovadia, can you tell us what the coronation ceremony is like? It’s probably super fancy, right?

Wow, I never knew that before. What else are you doing for the king’s coronation?

Oh, there are some very special things that you soldiers in Tzivos Hashem do, which He really appreciates. In fact, they are the very reason why He created the world!

Sounds like a good trick to me! Does it work for you?

That means that the Yetzer Hara had no power over the Yidden then?

Parshas Bereishis! Who should we bring to our podcast? Adam or Chava?

Come on, Yossi. You can’t be serious. The moon is sooo far away, and it’s not even a person! What could the moon teach us?

Didn’t the Rebbe say that we have to learn from each day of creation? Well, today is Wednesday, the fourth day of the week. And the moon was created on Day Four, so let’s find out what we can learn from Day Four.

He’s right. We do have to learn what Hashem, our Commander-in-Chief, made each day, so that we can learn from Hashem’s example. Plus, the moon is a good example, because the Yidden are compared to the moon.

Okay, okay, let’s call the moon. I just hope there’s good reception in the moon’s atmosphere.

Hey, hey everyone! Thank you for bringing me to the Parsha Podcast. You kids are awesome—I listen to your podcast every week on my long trips around Earth. But what do you want from me? I’m just a little moon from the big dark sky.

We want to know what we can learn from you. Why did Hashem make you?

Hmm, it’s a very simple story from a very simple moon, but if it’ll help you, I’ll tell it.

Well, Hashem made me to be ‘the little light. My job is to come out at night when it’s very dark, and share my light.

Good question. Since I don’t have any light of my own, Hashem gave me a special power: I can reflect light from the big sun! So when it’s dark, and the sun is far away, I can still come and bring the sun’s light into the world.

Whoa. I think I just counted three things we can learn from you.

Number one: The Yidden are compared to the moon, and just like the moon is small, we are also called small. And just like parents love and get special nachas from their small children, Hashem loves and gets nachas from every Yid.

Ooh, I think I know the second thing! Just like the moon lights up the dark night, we Chayolim in Tzivos Hashem need to light up the dark Galus. We spread Torah and mitzvos to every part of the world!

…And number three ties them all together! This is neat, listen closely: the little moon can only light up the world when it reflects light from the great big sun.

Us too! We’re just Hashem’s little children, but we can light up the night of Galus. How? Because Hashem gave us the power to reflect His great big light into this world.

Wow. Okay, let's talk practical. We know that we light up Galus by spreading Torah and mitzvos with mivtzoyim.

But how do we reflect Hashem’s light the way the moon reflects the sun’s?

Oh, you chayolim do it all day long, by doing mitzvos the Torah way. When you make a bracha on kosher food, say Modeh Ani in the morning, and Shema three times a day—

—And all the mitzvos in our Tzivos Hashem missions!

I think it’s pretty obvious who we should bring this time!

Yaakov Avinu! Parshas Vayeitzei is all about Yaakov and his family.

Yep. I’m calling already! Let’s hope we get through this time…

Ah! My children! How are the Parsha Podcasters doing? Are you using the bracha that Hashem gave me in this week’s parsha?

”“ּופָרַצְּתָ יָמָה וָקֵדְמָה וְצָפֹנָה וָנֶגְּבָה—That I should grow strong and spread out to the west, east, north, and south!

Well … um, actually, we’ve kinda just been staying here in our secret headquarters...

Wait—is that the bracha that teaches us how to attack the Yetzer Hara like a real army does? With four special divisions?

Yes, exactly. Every army has divisions, and each division has its specialty, something that it is best at doing.

Like an air force for sky attacks, the navy for the ocean, cavalry for the tanks and trucks, and infantry on their feet!

Hey, I think I’m remembering something about this. Tzivos Hashem also has four divisions—the east, north, west, and south!

Right on! “Yama vakeidma v’tzafona v’negba!” Each division also has leaders: My grandparents Avraham and Sara lead the south. My father, Yitzchak, and mother, Rivka, lead the north. Leah and I, Yaakov, lead the east. And Dovid and Rochel lead the west.

We each lead different attacks on the Yetzer Hara. Just like the navy is used when the army needs to attack from the sea, Avraham and Sara’s division— the south—is used when the Yetzer Hara needs to be attacked with mitzvos of tzedakah and chessed.

Oh, that’s because we learn about mitzvos of chessed from Avraham and Sara, so we look to them to lead us in those things. What if the Yetzer Hara is trying to stop Yidden from learning Torah? Who leads then?

That would be Leah and I from the east. Tell the Yetzer Hara that you’re following in Yaakov’s lead! I would sit and learn Torah, unlike Eisav who would go out to hunt.

So basically, whichever division the Yetzer Hara is attacking, that one has to be the strongest and lead the fight!

But what if the Yetzer Hara figures that out? Like, what if when we’re busy fighting hard and learning a lot of Torah, he’ll attack Avraham and Sara’s division of the south? He’ll see that they’re not fighting because we’re too busy with Torah, so he’ll easily win and get us to stop giving tzedakah!

Good point, Chaim. That’s why we’ve got to make sure that every division is always on guard. North, east, west, and south. When one side is leading the fight, the others must stay on guard and make sure that the Yetzer Hara doesn’t get through to them, either.

Just because we’re learning all day, doesn’t mean we can’t help Mommy prepare for Shabbos!

Well, Moshe and Aharon had told Paroh that we were just going on a three day trip to serve Hashem in the midbar. Paroh wanted to make sure that we would do just that, and then come back.

He wanted you back? After all those makos? After you were already gone for three days?

Oh, you obviously don’t understand Paroh! Quite foolishly, he never gave up on us being his slaves. No matter what, he kept trying to get us back. Even after we were far, far away from him.

Well, when the three days were up, they tried telling us it was time to go back to Mitzrayim. We pretty much just laughed at them! Of course we wouldn’t go back. We only go where Hashem tells us to go, not Paroh.

So the agents just went back all alone? They were probably so embarrassed!

Yup! And we Yidden followed Moshe, who first took us backward a bit, where we rested close to Mitzrayim. Then we headed toward Har Sinai to get the Torah!

Um, can I ask why you first went backward? Paroh probably thought you were going back!

Moshe wanted to show Paroh that we weren’t afraid of him. He could chase us if he dares! We were just resting up so we’d be ready to head to Har Sinai.

You know, Paroh is just like my Yetzer Hara. He also never gives up! Even when I’m so good and I ignore him for so long. He just pops in my head, as if he’s a mighty king, and says I should listen to him. Then he tells me to quickly put food in my mouth— without thinking of saying a bracha.

Or without making sure the food is a good hechsher, or without saying thank you.

Yeah! Mine too! The Yetzer Hara never stops bothering us kids.

Aha... So you must do what we did. Laugh at him, don’t give him any attention. Only follow Hashem’s commands. Then run far away from him, until there’s not a trace of Yetzer Hara left. What can we do when the Yetzer Hara pops back up?

…and that’s another fabulous episode of the Parsha Podcast. Ancient Yid, thank you for joining us again! We’ll be sure to think the question over. See you all chayolim next week!

You got it! And then, once you bring your guf and nefesh habehamis on board, you can receive the Torah!

It all makes sense now! Because Torah is so special, we need to use something special in order to understand its lessons. We need our “Yisro” to help us!

Ohhh! So it’s called Parshas Yisro because we need our “Yisro” to accept and want Hashem, and then we can get the Torah!

Exactly! Starting with —“אָנֹכִי ה' אֱֹלקיָך accepting Hashem as the only Power.

And of course, thanks to you, Yisro, we all have the kochos to do this. Because when the Torah teaches us a lesson, it also gives us the ability to make it happen!

So then “inside-out windows” would mean windows that are wider on the outside, and narrower on the inside. Hmm. That would bring the inside light to the outdoors.

Exactly. Because the Bais Hamikdash doesn’t need light from outside. It gets filled with its own light from the menorah. And the light of the menorah spreads out to the whole world.

But we don’t have inside-out windows like the ones in the Bais Hamikdash.

True, not windows that you can see. But these rooms are full of ruchniyus’dik inside-out windows. If someone would step into your home, it would be obvious to them that it’s a true Yiddishe home where Hashem is comfortable to live. They’d feel the kedusha in the air. This feeling of kedusha is like a light that will spread out to your neighbors. Its brightness will continue shining along, farther and farther. In fact, with all of your Tzivos Hashem missions, you will light up the whole world.

Then we’ll bring Moshiach, when we’ll see you light the menorah in the greatest home of all—the Bais Hamikdash! And the whole world will be completely lit up!

And I think we’re the only ones who celebrate Shabbos each week!

Parshas Vayikra talks about robbers. It says, “וְהֵׁשִיב אֶת הַגְזֵלָה אֲׁשֶר גָזָל” That means that robbers have to return whatever they stole.

Okay, I’m calling a robber who had to return what he stole...

Aaah! You scary Yetzer Hara! What are you doing here? Yossi was dialing a robber!

But of course, I am the best robber there is. I am the king of robbers! I invented robbery!

What do I steal? I steal from Hashem! I steal all of the kedusha that I can!

Well, we’re not going to let you do that anymore. You’re never going to steal any mitzvos from me! Never ever again! You’re gonna go out of business and fall off the planet forever and ever!

Oh, but it’s too late. I already stole a lot from Hashem. What are you gonna do about that? Huh?

We’re gonna get it back from you. We’re gonna get all of the kedusha back by using everything in the world for Hashem, until there’s no kelipa left!

Then everything will be kedusha, and the Geulah will be here! Yay!

Hello, my young heroes! How is everything going today?

Something from this week’s parsha has been bothering me all week.

Our guest is Reb Shloime. He was a chossid of the Alter Rebbe, so I’m sure he’ll be able to help.

Baruch Hashem, good, but I’m really struggling with an idea in this week’s parsha. Could you help? As a chossid of the Alter Rebbe, I’m sure you know a lot.

In this week's parsha, Chassidus explains that Avraham Avinu represents the neshama and Sara Imeinu represents the guf. But last week Hashem told Avraham Avinu “ּכֹל אֲשֶׁר תֹּאמַר אֵלֶיָך שָׂרָה שְׁמַע בְּקֹלָּה—Whatever Sara tells you, listen to her voice.” That just doesn’t make sense together.

Yeah! Why should the neshama listen to the body? It should be the opposite!

Beautiful question! Once, when the Alter Rebbe was davening on Rosh Hashana or Yom Kippur, and he got to the words, “…ּובְכֵן ּתֵן פַּחְדְָך—And so, Hashem, put a fear of You on everything You made,” he was unable to get the words out, and he began rolling on the floor.

Because the Rebbe was so overcome by the meaning of the tefillah, that he felt it in his whole body.

I get it. Sometimes we feel something so strongly that it affects our whole body. For the Alter Rebbe, it was his connection to Hashem.

That is exactly right! Our Rebbeim always showed us that when we do mitzvos, it does change our whole body. And so, the best way to do a mitzva is by showing how it affects your guf.

Sometimes I get really excited about doing a mitzvah and I jump up and down. Like when we got to help our neighbor build his sukkah.

And sometimes when Mommy is davening, she sways back and forth and cries. Does that mean she’s davening with her whole body?

Yes! These examples show that the body feels its ruchniyus connection to Hashem.

But that’s still the guf listening to the neshama. They’re connected, but it’s still Sara listening to Avraham. Hashem told Avraham to listen to Sara.

Well, now that we’re discussing this, I realize that things were probably different for Avraham and Sara because they’re tzaddikim.

A kluger kop! Tzaddikim live with the reality of Geulah. And what will be of the guf then?

Right again! In a way, the guf is greater than the neshama. While we are in Golus, though, we don’t see it. Our bodies seem gashmiyus and grub. But in Moshiach tzeiten, the greatness of the Yiddishe body will finally be obvious. We’ll recognize that it’s from a higher place, and constantly use it for Hashem!

But even now, we can show how amazing our guf is by doing mitzvos with our whole self. This gives us a taste of Moshiach!

Oh, yeah! And when we live with a Moshiach mindset by doing mitzvos with our full body, then Moshiach will come in a fully revealed way!

Amen! Exactly! And now let’s ask all the other chayolim to think about it: How will you show the ma’alah of your guf and use it for Hashem?

I’m calling Eisav. He was really rich. Maybe he’ll get you a new bike!

Eisav?! But Yossi! He’s not nice and happy—he’s scary!

Nah, I’m not that bad. In fact, I just made peace with my brother.

Hey, kid, calm down. I don’t even have an army anymore. They all left. Your Zeidy Yaakov scared them off.

I sure am! Listen, I was going to attack Yaakov to get him back for tricking me out of the brachos. And I thought I had the perfect chance: after he had spent twenty years in Charan, surrounded by resha’im like Lavan. I was sure that by then, he had lost his kedusha-power. When he said “ּגַרְּתִי”, he meant that the whole time he was in Charan, he was there in a way of “גֵירּות”, like a stranger. He didn’t become part of the people; he knew he was just traveling.

He did. He built a house for himself and his family to live in and learn Torah. But for his gashmiyus belongings, he only made temporary huts. That’s the thing: Yaakov kept all of his belongings at a distance. To him, they were just a bunch of stuff that he needed while traveling. His only real concern was his family’s ruchniyus life. And so, his kedusha-power remained with him stronger than ever.

The Mezritcher Maggid would say that golus is like when you’re traveling and staying somewhere random. In your home, you want everything to be perfect, but you don’t care as much when you’re travelling. You know it's just temporary.

Right. Torah and mitzvos are ruchniyus, so they last forever. But everything else is just temporary.

Y’know, I guess it’s not so bad that my bike got a scratch. It’s only gashmiyus. At least my D’var Torah didn’t fall in the mud! I’m gonna try to remember that gashmiyus things are temporary, and we should just focus on the ruchniyus.

…And on using the gashmiyus for the ruchniyus, just like Yossi said.

You kids got it! Your Zeidy Yaakov must be so proud of you. And now let’s ask all the other chayolim to think about it: How will you use your gashmiyus in a way that brings Moshiach sooner?

Ah my friend, there is much more to this jumping. This is the jumping that made the sea split! We were all stuck at the big Yam Suf with the evil Mirzrim chasing right behind us, threatening to bring us back to slavery. Hashem needed us to go right in. Right into the mighty waters— not knowing what would happen next.

With complete mesiras nefesh— that’s why the sea split for you!

Yes! Yes! I would’ve done it! I love jumping into water! And then the sea would have split and I would've marched right through, waving at my friends through the “water-wall windows” and holding my shevet’s flag for all to see!

Umm, sorry Nachshon, my brother’s a bit on the adventurous side. Don’t mind him.

Oh, I love it! This boy is going to split some seas! Now, I’ve got one for you— a place where you can do this jump.

Dive right into Torah!. Everyone out there is telling you that you need to play all day long, and that you have no time to do Torah and mitzvos b’hiddur—beautifully and carefully. But, do you know what those messages really are? They’re a big, giant Yam Suf blocking your way, saying that you can’t do what Hashem wants.

But nowadays, no one tells us that we can’t do what Hashem wants! If Hashem says to do something, I’ll for sure jump right in!

Perfect! So then, don’t let anyone stop you from learning Torah in your spare time. Just jump right into it! Here, let’s open a sefer up and learn together. You’ll see all your distractions slip away; see how doing mitzvos b’hiddur is very possible. And when you do incredible things for Hashem, Hashem does incredible miracles for you.

Okay! I’m in! Hey, Chaim, maybe you were right after all…

And now, let’s ask all the other chayolim to think about it: What will you do in your spare time to jump into the “Yam Suf”?

…and that’s another fabulous episode of the Parsha Podcast. Thank you, Nachshon ben Aminadav, for joining us! We’ll be sure to think the question over. See you all chayolim next week!

We were all camped in the shape of a square with the Mishkan in the middle, because Hashem said, “סָבִיב לְאֹהֶל מֹועֵד יַחֲנּו”. So, three shevatim camped on each side, creating a big box. Inside that box was Shevet Levi, camped around in a smaller square…

…and inside the Mishkan was the Kodesh Hakadashim, and inside the Kodesh Hakadashim was the aron, and inside the aron—in the innermost box—were the luchos!

Hmm, it’s almost like the luchos were given layers and layers of protection.

It was a desert, remember? There were probably snakes, scorpions, and big scary spiders!

Exactly! There are many dangers in a desert. Our mission as Yidden was to protect the Torah.

Basya, when Hashem told Bnei Yisroel to build the Mishkan, He didn’t say, “Build me a Mishkan so that I can rest in it.” Hashem said “וְׁשָכַנְּתִי ּבְתֹוכָם—so that I can rest in them.” Hashem is always with us, and His presence rests in every one of us, even today!

That’s right! Don’t be sad, Basya. We all have our own ruchniyusdik Beis Hamikdash.

Hey, neat! So we can guard the luchos and the Torah? Umm … but what are we protecting it from?

Well, like the desert, Golus is also full of dangers. C’mon Basya, think of the Yetzer Hara! It’s scary!

He’s right. So when we finish recording this podcast and I study for my Chumash test instead of pulling out the new board game, I’m protecting my Mikdash?

You got it, Mimi! But there’s more. Did you kids know that your house is also called a Mikdash?

It sure is! When you protect the Yiddishkeit of your home, Hashem responds by filling it with brachos.

So maybe it’s time to get rid of those questionable CDs we found in the attic.

And throw away the candy with a not-so-great hechsher that I accidentally bought yesterday.

Perfect! By guarding the kedusha of your heart and your home, you’ll reach the same place that the Yidden in the desert reached: Eretz Yisroel!

Yes! All Yidden will leave Golus and greet Moshiach in the gashmiyus Beis Hamikdash!

This Shabbos is Shavuos. So, instead of reading the regular parsha in shul, we read a part of the Torah specifically for Shavuos.

Ooh, yay! I love Shavuos! We get ice cream and cheesecake and blintzes and so many other yummy things!

Yeah, but it’s also really hard to sit quietly and listen to the whole Aseres Hadibros. I wish we could get the ice cream without all that.

Yeah, I guess so. Anyway, I miss Zeidy, so we’re calling him today.

Kinderlach! So good to hear from you! Are you ready for Shavuos?

Oh yeah! We already made five cheesecakes and bought three flavors of ice cream!

And yesterday, we sat and learned all ten of the Aseres Hadibros so we can follow along and know what’s going on.

Baruch Hashem! So nice, so nice. What about invitations? Did you invite everyone?

Uh well, Mommy and Tatty invited some people. But that’s not really our job, is it?

But how is it our party? Isn’t the Torah for everyone?

Yes, yes, the Torah is for everyone. But we really only got it thanks to you kinderlach. Hashem wouldn’t give us the Torah until we chose someone to guarantee that it would be treasured and kept. And it wasn’t the zeidies, bubbies, teachers, or even Kohanim who could guarantee that. Do you know who did?

Exactly! As soon as we said that the kinderlach will be the guarantors for the Torah, Hashem agreed, and Matan Torah was able to happen.

I see. It’s only because of the kids that the Torah was given to us in the first place. Therefore, the celebration of Shavuos is for us. When everyone goes to shul to hear the Aseres Hadibros, it’s actually our party.

Well then, Zeidy, will you join us at shul to hear the Aseres Hadibros?

Ah, thank you for the invitation, Basyale. Yes, I will join you, b’ezras Hashem. And now, let’s ask all the other chayolim to think about it: How will you show your important part of this year's Matan Torah?

…and that’s another fabulous episode of the Parsha Podcast. Thank you, Zeidy, for joining us! We’ll be sure to think the question over. See you all chayolim next week!

Note: These images are for illustrative purposes only and are not meant to be an accurate depiction of the holy faces of the Tzaddikim.

Hey! One of the options for this week is the leader of a big, mean highway gang! What can we learn from someone like that?!

I don’t know! Those guys used to rob and kill people. He probably does a lot of aveiros.

Oy vey. I hope this isn’t going to be another scary one…

Don’t worry, Basya. I have a hunch about this. I say let’s go for it!

Okay, I’m kinda curious anyway, so I’ll trust you, Chaim, that he’s a safe person…

Baruch Hashem! I’m in the middle of reviewing a mishna. I must go over it at least forty times before the next shiur from my teacher, Rabi Yochanan.

That’s because it’s not. My hunch was correct! You’re Reish Lakish, right?

That’s what I’m called, yes. How can I help you children? Is there a part of Torah that you’re unclear about? The whole world exists because of the learning of you Yiddishe kids!

Whoa. I am so confused right now. Yossi, didn’t you say that you called a highway gang leader? I’m pretty sure people like that don’t learn with Rabi Yochanan. Reish Lakish sounds like a tzaddik!

Oh—ah, well, it seems your brother wasn’t completely wrong. A few years ago, I was a gang leader.

Yes. See, I was always big and strong. Back then, I used all my strength for aveiros. Big, bad aveiros. Everyone was afraid of me.

But what happened? How did you end up becoming a tzaddik?

Rabi Yochanan inspired me. He said, “You are so strong! If you would put that strength into Torah, you could be a great talmid chacham!”

Well, it took a bit more convincing from Rabi Yochanan, but in the end, yes, I decided to put all my strength into learning. Baruch Hashem, I did teshuva.

But … what about all of those aveiros from the past? How did you just move on?

What a wonderful question! Hashem tells us that when we turn ourselves around by regretting our past, and doing good instead, then our aveiros actually become z’chuyos!

And that’s exactly what we learn in this week’s parsha! It says to admit our aveiros and do teshuva— ”.“וְהִתְוַדּו אֶת חַטָאתָם אֲשֶׁר עָׂשּו

Well said! Sometimes, our Yetzer Hara puts shtus in our head, which can chas v’shalom stop us from doing a mitzvah, or even make us do an aveira. An aveira is also called a “אְחֵט”, which means “something is missing.”

But when we do teshuva, we return everything that was missed, and Hashem forgives us right away?

chayolim just like you. Welcome to our podcast, where

Mimi, you’re playing that niggun beautifully, but can you please take a break so we can record our podcast?

But I really need to keep practicing. Violin is super difficult and if I don’t practice for enough hours a day, I’ll never perfect my technique! Can’t you just do the podcast without me?

No way, Mimi! Besides, you’re obsessed with that violin. You literally practice all day long! Mommy has to call you like a million times for dinner.

Can you all please just leave me alone for a few minutes?

That’s it. I’m going to call our guest. Maybe that’ll snap you out of this.

Ah, shalom! You have reached Lior’s wax studio. How can I help you today?

Wait, you have a studio? Like a real artist? That is so impressive.

Thank you, thank you. I like to make wax sculptures. I make all sorts of different shapes—fruits, instruments, people—and for this week's parsha, I am making a menorah.

How did you learn this craft? I want to become an artist, too!

You know, I used to spend all day locked up in my studio. I love modeling, and all I wanted to do was improve my skill. Eating and sleeping were a waste of time. I was 100% focused on my wax.

I totally get you! I would spend all day with my violin if my siblings weren’t always pulling me away from it.

Ah! But you are forgetting something important. It says in Mishlei, “ֵנֵר ה’ ִנְִׁשְַמַת ָאָָדָם - the neshama of a Yid is Hashem’s candle.” Tell me, who lit the candles in the menorah of the Bais Hamikdash?

Yes! Now let me tell you about the menorah’s flames: Fire usually reaches upwards, but these flames all faced the middle branch. As it says in this week’s parsha, “ְעַת ה ַנֵרֹות אֶל מּול פְּנֵי הַמְנֹורָה יָאִירּו שִׁב”.

Well, do you know what the middle of the menorah represents?

Hashem! Wait, I think I get it. We are the candles, and Hashem is in the center. We learn from the menorah to make Hashem the center of our lives.

Exactly! Now I want you all to do something. Close your eyes for a moment and think about your neshama and of making Hashem the center.

Good question. I'll answer that with another passuk from Mishlei: “ֵנֵר ִמְִצְָוָה ְוְתֹוָר ָה אֹור—a mitzvah is a candle, and Torah is light.”

But what happened to your obsession? I mean you still make sculptures; does that mean that Hashem isn't your focus?

Basya, to me, Reb Lior looks like a great role model for us. He uses his talents and passions, but keeps Hashem as the top priority. The candles he creates are there to add beauty to mitzvos.

Thank you. I do try! It wasn't always this way, but now I make time to eat, sleep, and learn Torah. I know that I need ko’ach to serve Hashem.

chayolim just like you. Welcome to our podcast, where

Chayolim, in what way can this week’s lesson make a difference to you? What changes can you make in your own life?

We have a few options of who to call this week. Hey, guess what? One of them is Mommy’s great-great-great- grandmother, Bubby Basya!

Mommy told me about Elter-Bubby Basya. She lived almost 170 years ago, and she was famous for her challah. The recipe has been passed down to all the mommies in our family, and Mommy still uses it today! I always wished I could have met her!

Yay, this is so exciting! Your wish will finally be granted!

Hi Elter-Elter-Elter-Elter Bubby! I heard that you made the best challah in the world!

Oh, I know! You’re talking about the mitzva of hafrashas challah!

Exactly, zeeskeit. The Torah tells us that “ֵרֵאִׁשׁית ֲעֲִרִֹסֵֹתֵֶכֶם ַח ַָלָה ָּתִּרִימּו ְתְרּוָמָה— The first portion of the dough is given as a present to Hashem.”

Why does Hashem want a piece of dough as a present?

Oh Chaim’ke, it’s much more than just this piece! The Torah uses the term, “ָּתִּרִימּו ”ְתְרּוָמָה, which really means “you shall lift it up as a gift.” With this little pitzele of dough, we elevate the entire batch of challah, making it heilig for Hashem!

Wow, I knew that taking challah is a mitzvah, but I never knew that it affected the whole batch of dough!

Of course, mein kind. And you know, there is a lesson here that applies to much more than just delicious challah dough!

Mommy always says that bubbies give the best advice. Tell us, what lesson can we learn from challah dough?

Well, bread represents all that we need in order to live. Oy, I remember that during the war, we barely even had a crust of black bread … but that’s for another conversation. Anyway, Hashem tells us to set aside the first of our dough for Him. This does not just mean challah dough; it means that the first part of everything we have is given to Hashem. And as a result, the rest of our possessions become heilig!

Just like by saying Modeh Ani, we give the first part of our day for Hashem…

Oh, and all of my books say, “לַה' הָאָרֶץ ּומְלֹואָּה—To Hashem belongs the earth and all that fills it.” So, everything I read is also all for Hashem!

Ooh, and when I give Hashem the first moments of my meal—by making a bracha—then the whole rest of the meal becomes heilig, too! I will make sure to say a bracha before eating my pizza and salad and muffins today!

That’s gevaldik, yes! By making a bracha, sitting and eating nicely, and then using the energy to learn more Torah.

Thanks, Bubby. This will definitely help me do the right thing. Next time my Yetzer Hara starts bugging me to want a milkshake after having chicken soup, I know just what to answer! “You, Yetzer Hara, are a silly fool, saying utter nonsense! I already gave the first part of my day to Hashem, so my entire day is holy! Stop trying to mess up my plans.”

Oy, kinderlach, I’m shepping such nachas! Kein ayin hara, you are all as sharp and zees!

And now, let’s ask all the other chayolim to think about it: How will you start your day so that you lift the rest of it up for Hashem?

…and that’s another fabulous episode of the Parsha Podcast. Thank you, Bubby Feldman, for joining us! We’ll be sure to think the question over. And chayolim, we wish you all a great summer! Stay tuned—we might just be back for more episodes next year! And remember, you can keep your own Parsha Podcast going at the Shabbos table. Whether at home or with your bunkmates at camp, let's all learn about the parsha in a fun and practical way all summer long!
